IN THE SAD SEPTEMBER GLOAMING. In the sad September gloaming, when the pallid mists are
drawn O'er the meadow and the river, like a web of ghostly
lawn, And dark, and still, the moorland rolls, for many a purple mile, 'Tiithen, my love, I miss you most, who miss you all
the while, aur wedded days were sweet as swift, and since we've
_ _ been apart Your mern'ry, like a twilight mist, clings ever round my
heart, Andtefttimes cm a nig,ht like this, I rest beside tho stile. And lose the present in the past, to dream of you awhile. There's. bonnie Bate, and gentle Nell, and others too
_ beside, But if 'twere but to ask, to have a helpmate by my side. I could not patch a broken heart where ancient longings
brood, Or garnish for a second bride its haunted solitude. Through the years, with all their changing, I have held that somewhere still There's a white _soul holds unbroken that old faith no
chine can kill, And I'll keep the troth an angel trusts, though given a
• simple girl, And with clean lips shill meet her kiss within the gates of pearl. —Good Word?.
S. RID.

The affections themselves are a kind of understanding; we cannot understand without them. Affection is a part of insight —it is required to understand the facts of the case. The moral affections, e.g., are the very instrumonts by which we intellectually apprehend good and high human character. All admiration is affection—the admiration of virtue, the admiration of Nature. Affection itself, then, is a kind of intelligence, and we cannot separate the feeling in our nature from the reason. The kite Doctor Ward, of -Yankton, Dakota, was famous for the number of good stories he could tell. Csf the last reconcctions which an old friend had of him was at a banquet of college men, where he related the following of a college classmate who was present. This classmate was a rising young minister, very absent- minded, very earnest, and very sensitive. Hurrying to church one Sundae morning and going into the pulpit late, he was horrified to discover that he had not his carefully-written sermon with him. The service had begun by the singing of the anthem, but be called up one of his neighbour's boys and gave him hurried directions about his study and the nrobable location of the sermon, and sent him to get it, and return as fast as possible. The pos. service needecl, and still the boy did not appear. ;..sr The young peeacher was in agony. He had never preached without nr.l"fee, and the perspiration stood in great beads upon his forehead as he wondered what he would do if the sermon did not come. Finally, just as the last stanza of the hymn which preceded the sermon was being sung the boy appeared, rushed up the aisle conspicuously, and handed' the minister his manuscript. The clergyman took the package ner- vously, opened it, and during profound stillness announced the text. Not until he had spoken it did the meaning of it flash over him. It was this:—" Re- joice with me, for I have found the piece which I had lost!" This was too much for the audience. The people laughed outright. But the lesson was a good one for the minister, who never forgot his sermon again while in that parish. In the current number of the " Universal Review Mr. Sydney Hall, the well-known " Graphic " artist, revives his recollections of the Franco-Prussian War, under the head of "Twenty Years Ago." He tells one story which is quite of a novel character. Staying in the suburbs of Versailles, at the Hotel des Reservoir, he applied to the German feld-post, as usual, for his letters. One day the officer of the feid-post asked if he would take charge of a letter for a man named King. " Did he know such a man at the Hotel?" He gave Mr. Hall the letter and it was addressed thus :—" To Bloody King William of Prussia, Versailles." He made no further in- quiries, and thought it better to appropriate the letter than forward it to his Imperial Majesty. It was found to be written by twenty English ladies to warn the Emperor to desist from the war.

The Prince of Wales, it was said on Monday morn- ing by an important member of the Court, will be greatly displeased by the speech which Lord Pairhyn, without permission or any authority, has made, apparently on his Royal Highness's behalf. The Prince is really a master ot royal method in public appearances of the sort referred to, and the assertion that his absence from the Eisteddfod was because of information received from Lord Penrhyn, whom the Prince well knows to be a bigotted partisan, will be most distasteful to his Royal Highness. The Heir Apparent is exactly the sort of man who, if he were told all that Lord Penrhyn had said as to the parties represented at Bangor, would be likely to form shrewd and decided opinion that nothing would tend so surely to correct party feeling as his own presence in the Princi- pality.

Most people have long since come to the conclu- sion that the Brave General was not at all brave; but it needed the latest of the " revelations" to show how very cowardly he was. The potential saviour of society ran away not merely from his own shadow, but from another man's shadow, in April, 1889. It was 31. Constans who " worked " the famous flight to Brussels in that year. The General had managed to get a friend of his own in the Min- istry of the Interior to watch M. le Minister, and I report. The Minister tried an ancient and a simple dodge. He found out the spy, and he took care that this gentleman should see a paper setting forth a plan for the instant arrest of the General. The hood-winked agent communicated this alarm- ing intelligence to his chief, who promptly bolted; after which the Boulanger game was up. A very astute man, as well as a resolute one, is M. Con- stana.

The visit of the Queen of Roumania to Balmoral will be very. brief, and her stay at the Castle is not likely to exceed two nights. Her Majesty will pro- bably go to Scotland sooner than was expected in order that she may pay a flying visit to the Prince and Princess of Wales at Abergeldie. Queen Eliza- beth is desirous of traversing as much charecteristic Highland scenery as possible, and she will probably go to Balmoral by the old " Royal route," driving from Blairgowrie through the Spittal of Glensbee. If the weather is fine, and October is usually a good month in Scotland, Queen Elizabeth will proceed from Balmoral to Blair Athole by Poll.Tarff and Glen Tilt, a route which the Queen has twice tra- versed, and it affords some of the grandest scenery in Scotland. A visit to Inverness, the voyage by the Caledonian Canal to Oban, a trip to Staffs and lona, the tour of Loch Tay, and finally a brief sojourn at Edinburgh, are the proposed movements of Queen Elizabeth, who also intends to inspect Abbotsford before she returns south.

Mr. Henry lladen, whose death all Lancashire Liberals deplore, was a man of a remarkably fine physique, with a ruddy smiling face. He invariably wore a short jacket and a grey billycock hat, lie was a fine type of a Lancashire man, being in ap- pearance more like a country gentleman than a rich and powerful cotton lord. A model of the Eiffel Tower, a Paris Correspon- dent says, has been erected by a farmer of St. Hilaire in the Meuse. as a monument over the grave of his parents. It is 25 feet high, an lis sur- mounted by across. Theie is a statue of St. Joseph on the first platform, and the names of the departed relatives are engraved on slabs fastened to the four shafts.

At Agnetendorf, on the Riesengbirge (a chain of mountains between Silesia and Bohemia) one Herr. Vogel has trained a dog to perform the duties of a mountain guide. The animal leads the tourist in safety from Agnetendorf to BisrnarckhOhe. Gaily he springs from point to point and gives confidence to the tourist. When there is a spot whence a special view of scenery can be witnessed, he stops and looks about him.

it was a little difficult on Wednesday, in some parts of London, to procure an apple or a pear. Wednesday was the Day of Atonement, or the Fast of Expiation of the Jews (Tom Kippur), and most of our fruiterers' shops are kept by persons of Jewish race, who close their establishments on the occasion of this solemn fast. From the sunset of the ninth day of Tishri, or the 23rd of September, until the rising of three stars on therevening of the following day, the fast is kept by the conforming members of the faith.

How the British burglar is improving in his man- ners! "All right, guv'nor. Don't use violence and we'll come down," was the pleasant remark ad- dressed to the Rev. Robert Ward, when he came home and found "someone in the house." This is quite a new departure in burglary, and a vast im- provement upon shooting the master of the house on his own doormat. It will soon be quite a plea- sure to find a burglar waiting for one in the draw- ing room on a dull evening. This is the result of Board schools—and halfpenny newspapers.

At last there is some definite prospect of a ter- mination of thegreat struggle in Australia. In reply to the men's proposal for arbitration, the employ- ers have agreed to a conference, " provided that freedom of contract be assured." Much will turn upon the meaning of this proviso ; but, at any rate, the door is opened for a settlement. What is more, it is the men who have opened it, by offering to put their case in the hands of three public men—the Chief-Justice of Victoria, the Premier of Queens- land, and the Cardinal Archbishop of Sydney— whose names ought to be perfectly acceptable to the employer class generally.

Judge. Waters, of the Waterford County Court, gave another nasty blow on Wednesday to Mr. Bal- four's campaign against the Irish Press. Yesterday he quashed two convictions of editors by Remov- ables—one in the case of Mr. Redmond, of the " Waterford News," the other that of Mr. Fisher, of the " Munster Express." In both cases Judge Waters held that the mere publication, without comment, of a resolution passed at a League meeting is no offence. Three months' imprisonment was the sentence which the Removables had passed in each case. How many Irish journalists have been sent to goal during the last two years just as illeg- ally ?

A curious accident is reported from Ilirson, on the Northern Railway of France. A drunken man named Lefebvre contrived, unobserved, to mount upon a bcomotive, left at the moment, unattended at the station in that town, and, turning on the steam, started it down the line at an accelerated pace in the direction of Buire. Being ignorant of the practical working of the engine the man was powerless to arrest the mischief and the locomotive,. coming into collision with an empty carriage, dashed it to pieces. Finally, it was somehow turned into a siding, where, colliding with violence with the buffers, it was brought to a stand. Only five minutes later an express train passed down the line. The strangest part of the incident is that the drunken engine-driver is reported to have sustained no serious injury.

Among the working-classes he was extremely popu- lar. If his health had permitted him to comply with the wish of the Liberal Council, of which he was president, and stand against Lord Hartington, , that nobleman must have gone to the wall.

Mr. E. P. Marum, who has unexpectedly died, was one of the earliest members of the Irish Parlia- mentary party. He was always something of a Liberal in politics, and he belonged to the more moderate section of Mr. Parnell's followers. He was, however, a staunch Nationalist and an unswerving supporter of the leader whom he greatly admired and lovod.

Mr. Marum, who represented Kilkenny County, when a young man was one of the most daring riders to hounds in Ireland. About thirty years ago, whilst returning with a few friends from the hunt near the city of Kilkenny, he made a wager that he would ride his horse safely down the "stone steps of St. Canice," leading from the cathedral of that name to the street below. The "stone steps" were thirty to forty in number, four and a half feet wide, and composed of the black marble for which Kilkenny is famed, polished like glass from long usage. He accomplished the feat safely, and in next week's "Punch " appeared the following " Harum-scarum Mulhallen Marum
Rode down St. Canice's steps in Kilkenny; Had his horse stumbled at all, he'd have got a great fall, And knocked out his brains—had he any.

more complete. Before you could say "Jack Robin- son" I was out of the saddle, with the dog in my arms, kissing him and petting him like a good fel- low. He was modest and loving as ever, but I carried him in triumph into Silver Xing, where I heard the rest of the story. Jim Ellison told me that a couple of hours earlier in the day the last mules came in on a sweeping trot, Lovely growling and limping behind them. He began looking for me at once, visiting first one cabin and then another, and whimpering like a child at every fresh disappointment. Jim said they tried their best to make him stop for a rest and a bite to eat; but deaf to all entreaties, Lovely kept right on, gathering up his captives, and setting off on the road he,knew I had gone. Such a hero as he was in camp that night ! Dick fiddled, Jim Elli- son danced a breakdown, and we had a big spread I of pork, beans, and griddle-cakes, with the dog as Iguest of honour.

div.head: THROUGH ST. MARTIN'S WINDOW.
div.p: THROUGH ST. MARTIN'S WINDOW.
Alexis St. Martin was a Canadian trapper. Many years ago, while out hunting, he received a gunshot wound in his abdomen. This finally healed in such a strange way
as to leave an opening into the stomach, with a thin skin over it almost as clear as a pane of glass. Nothing
so remarkable had ever happened before. Through this window, by the aid of a strong light thrown into it, the doctors could see what went on inside his stomach. So
the poor trapper's bad luck proved to be good luck for
the rest of mankind.
Now let us see how we can avail ourselves of the know-

ledge thus obtained. There is a postman by the name of Frederick Green, who :live% at 33, MarsiPst., Short- lands, Kent. Speaking of an occasion about two years ago, he lately said: I couldn't eat meat without experi- encing great pain." What ailed Mr. Green? When the doctors looked into St. Martin's stomach just after he had eaten a meal, they observed that a liquid of a light yellow colour was thrown in great quantities from the lining of the stomach in among the food. Then they noticed that the whole mass began to turn round and round as milk does in a revolving churn. When this process was over, in an hour or two there was nothing to be seen except a gray t uid which looked like broth or soup. The doctors also took note of the fact that when St. Martin ate much meat the stomach required a longer time a3d seemed to labour harder to turn it into the brothlikeluid. The 3, again, there were times when the light yellow liquid hardly came forth at all, the stomach moved, or churned, slowly, and the food ay in St. Martin's body until it became rancid, putrid, and sour. At such times he complained et feeling; ill and

sick and suffering much palm If not soon relieved, his skin turned a eopperiab hue, a nauseating acid arose in his mouth, his head ached and grew hot, he had sharp pains in different parts- ere his body, the kidney secretion was. thick and hig,h,colourecl, he slept badly, couldn't work, and was lbw-spirited, restless, and uneasy. What he suffered from wae- in- digeation, which, long enough cortinued,becomesehronin, dyspepsia and nervous prostration. Now let us see how it fared with our friend Mr. Greem the postman. Be goes on toy "When 1 drew my breath it was like a knife running through my chest.. My apettite was bad, and I fell away•to nothing. As. have to walk twenty miles a day in the discharge of- ris.:lt duties, I found the work in my weaLt.. state was- killing. me by inches. Before I was taken ill I, was a strong,. healthy man, and did my work with ease and.pleasure.. Finally I had to go on the sick-list, and as attended by a physician, for a fortnight, but I felt none the better. There was a load ors my chest, and when I ate anything the food lay on my.stamach like a ton of-lead. ' "One day my wife-said tome: 'Frederick, my-mother used to suffer the way you do, and she alWays frund re— lief by taking Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, Why don't you try it?' After some persuasion I gave up doctoring and got a bottle of 'Seigel's' and began,. The first few doses made- me feel better. I stuck to Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and in a few weeks I got strong and went back to my- work. I have never ailed any- thing since,.and for my recovery I have to thank God and Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup." Mr. Green has been postman in the Shortlands district for fifteen years. arid, bears an excellent character: If there had been a window in his stomach, his physician and friends-might have observed the same trouble that esoasionally appeared in the case of St. Martin.

div.head: MULES' MASTER.
div.p: THE MULES' MASTER.

Ile was the sorriest little dog in the Arizona territory. Such legs! Bowed as barrel hoops, and his dingy hide almost naked, with just enough stiff yellow hair left in patches to prove the original colour. One eye was gone, and he must have been in an awful lot of tights, for both ears and tail were chewed off pretty nearly down to the roots. I picked him up in Tombstone one day, or rather he picked me up, limping at my heels, and then trotting lamely out after me to the cabin that night. lie was such a mean, sickly-looking cur, at first I hated having him about; and whenever the fellows came over from camp they jeered at and plagued Lovely, as they called him, till I had half a mind to drive the ugly beast off. But he wouldn't go, and by the time hs foot got well no one ever saw me without my dog. It was just about this time that I sold enough silver ore to go into the packing business. As soon as I could buy five stout mules, I contracted to carry the mail and merchandise across the mountains be-

tween Tuscon and Total Wreck, Tombstone, and Silver King mining camps. I filled orders at the capital, and usually returned loaded down. with a queer assortment of hams, rope, coffee, nails, boots, candy, stamps, and dynamite. Now it was that Lovely showed up in strong colours, and after our second trip I bragged he was worth a brace of lazy Mexican half-breeds, and that "handsome is as handsome does." As for those mules, he was harder on them than any slave-driver before the war. All day he travelled with his one good eye on the train. If old Molly stopped long enough just to tickle her nose with grass, you should have seen that dog. He would try to eat her up, barking, spitting, and kicking up dust, un- til I'd. ii ave to crack ray whip and set the whole party off at a gallop. It was funny to see him treat them like servants, and I can tell you they were trained, too. There was Mose, stall, black, lumbering creature, vicious and ready to buck if you looked at him. But Lovely never stood foolishness, and the second day out from Tucson he fixed old crosspatch in good fashion. We had trotted pretty briskly since noon, and r was riding ahead, watching the sun wheel down behind great thunder heads hanging low to the mountains, when all of a sudden such a pawing and kicking,. and braying as there was, and Mose bolted by. Lovely stuck on his back like a circus rider. I laughed till I cried at those two • but the dog whip- ped in at the first round, and from that time on, whenever he felt a bit tired, just swarmed up on, one of the mules and rode till he was rested.

The minute we reached camp and unloaded, II turned the whole train over to Lovely. He knew where to find water, drove them to drink, sat by patiently till they were satisfied, and then started the gang off at a canter for the corral or pasture. After finishing myibusiness up at the mines, I always found the mules greedily browsing, and Lovely, his ragged ears erect, keeping a keen lookout to make sure they nlayed him, no tricks. Till I came to re- lieve him, nothing could have induced the dog to desert, and not the sleekest of squirrels ever dis- tracted his attention from that flock. No wonder he declined to trust them, for, in spite of his dilig- ence, they led him a dance. I remember one day in Tombstone when time came to load up'and start off across the country, I called Lovely and told him to drive up the train, which now numbered ten. Away he went, was back in a few minutes, rubbing gently against my leg and wagging his stumpy tail, as if asking appro- val. As I did not stir, he glanced hastily around, and in a flash discovered his mistake. Old Toby, the meanest mule in the drove, was missing. Giving me a bright look, as if to say, "You mind these till I get back,' he was oft like the wind. Down he raced to the corral, flew round and round the scrub to see if Toby was in hiding, and finally darted off on the trail. He returned presently, his ' tongue out and panting furiously, but no Toby in ,sight. He had evidently nursed a hope that the truant would repent and come back, but seeing his mistake, sat on his haunches, reflecting an instant. Then,. as if struck with an idea, he made off for the camp. In and out, smelling at every house corner and shed, went the little yellow shepherd, even up- setting boxes and barrels in his search. After many a sharp turn, sure enough, there was the sly black varmint, cunningly flattened out against the side of a cabin, not a vestige of tail or mane showing on either side. He was chewing a whisp of hay, with a malicious twinkle in his knavish eves. Lovely was mad, I tell you. He barked out his opinion, and after one vicious snap at Toby's heels, dog and mule came dying up like lightning. Before that trip was, over,. Toby wished he had never been born, for Lovely wouldn't even allow him to switch his own tail without a scene.

By this time I learned to trust the dog in every- thing, and loved him too,,for he was as gentle and affectionate with me as he waeharsh and domineer,- ing with the beasts. Besides standing guard half the night, his one eye skinned for Indians ar wolves, he helped mind the drove, kept me com- pany,and was a first-class rabbit hunter. It was nat, however, until my three finest mules disappeared from the corral at Silver King that I appreciat.ed my dependence on him. Lovely was just as mach distressed as I was that morning. Over and over again he went through the herd,.counting them one after another, as plainly, as la Gould myself, and then apparently scratching his head, trying to thinks High and low and up and down he hunted those wretched brutes through half of Pima County. Pen- ning, the remaining seven, I. scoured the county on horseback, Lovely following. Worn out and dis- gusted, I at last abandoned the search, and came to the conclusion they must have been stolen by the thievish Apaches„who had grown daring of late. The evening of the third day after their disap- pearance I was pretty low in my mind, bat next morning got up at daylight, whistling for- Lovely to round up the mules,..so we might get an early start. Seeing nothing of him, 1 supposed he must be off larking, and so thought no more of the mat- ter. All that day passed without one trane• of ray dog. At first I hoped and koked, and then, rag.ed. around, vowing there was foul play, for Lovely would never in all the world walk off and leave me alone. I hung around the camp all the rest of that week, neglecting my work, and getting. bluer with every day that passed. I could not believe that he was really gone, and never gave the mules a thought now in my new trouble about the dog. Finding it was useless to delay any longer, I pressed on for Total Wreck. But instead of riding ahead, as old. when I had someone to bring up, the rear, I was forced to drive that gang of scampish mules, for ever yelling and popping my whip over their stub- born heads. They fretted the life out of me, cutting up all sorts of shines—Molly particularly, who would run half a mile out of her way after three blades of grass. Saturday, returning to the King, doleful as a moulting owl in the dark of the moon. I was think- ing of cutting the whole business, when presently I spied a cloud of dust in the distance. Poking slowly along, and idly wondering what it might be, I could scarcely believe my eyes on recognising one after another of those vagrant mules. But it was all three, sure enough, and smartening our pace, we were soon alongside. Not until I heard a feeble little bark near my stirrup did it occur to me who the detective had been. There was Lovely, all beaten out,too stiff and lame to hobble another step, yet with his longest ear proudly cocked as he scanned the company and counted his flock once

Mnma's achievement soon spread abroad, and all her acquaintances, while blaming her rashness, um- gratulated her upon her very narrow escape and presence of mind. "But)" remarked Minnie, sen- tentiously, "what is the use of having a mind if you don't use it when you are in trouble.' And so thEsdays and weeks passed by. Aroongst those who took an ,carly opportunity to eee tht3Young—girl and congratulate her upon her preservation was Marrnaduke Deane. Ho was the cause of considerable anxiety to his good mother (Lady Deane), for his tastes and habits, far from being aristocratic, as she had fondly endeavoured to make them, were more characteristic of the work- man or the rustic. And for months he paid Minnie great attention. "I wish you wouldn't use such words, Marma- duke," his mother said one day, after a conversation in which her son's language was embellished with some choice ," slang" phrases. "One would think you had never been educated. I'm sure Mr. Boots

the tutor) would never sanction such terms.' "A chap can express himself much more to the point with a hit of slang," was the young " man's " reply. Marmaduke already looked upon himself as a man, and he was certainly very tall and strong for his age. "What's a cove to do 2 Ny pals under. stand me well enough!' "My wishes should be ffufficiont for you; and your ' pals ' as you call them. You are a great deal too much amongst the work people, and I don't at all approve of your going so much to Mrs. Layton's cottage." "Why net ? " asked Marmadnke, doggedly. "She's an old friend of yours." "No, she is a servant and her child isnot at . . .
Well, at auy rate, I wish you to abstabl from going there for the future." _
Minniele all right. I like her very much. She's a clipping girl, Minnie is." "I don't know what a clippinm ' girl may be

Marmaduke, but I trust you will attend to me. The girl is no fitting associate for you. She is not a lady." , "Oh, ain't she!" exclaimed the lad. " Sh&s a jolly sight more a lady than Lily- Watson, who you are always shoving down my tla.rost., A stuck-up, pug-nosed--4.--" " Starseadake ! Hold your tongue this moment. Your vulgarity is insufretable. Datyou understand I entirely disapprove of your association with that girl—Minnie Layton." "Very well. I can't help it. If I see her I'll talk to her. she's a nailer is Minnie?' "Tour idol seems quite a mistress of all trades," remarkeltady Deane, roused to sarcasm. " first she's a clipper, then a nailer. In time we shall hear she 18 a lady perhaps." " Shs will be if I can make her ane,!"remarked young Deane. "I'm going to pop fis question to her some day."' The estolarnatien of horror that To3e from Lady Deane, and the disgrast expressed in her-Lounterranca even disconcerted the reckless youth Marmaduk-e. "Why shouldn't /t" he asked. " Sh,e'fi all right. An awful pretty girl she is, too; the -best in the basket."

"You must-be mad!" was all the comment Lady Deane condescended to offer to this remark, as she sailed out of the room in her most majestic manner. "Oh, thafait, is it? Very well," remarked M&T- maduke to himself, as he turned to the window.. "Then I'll just•spite her by spooning Minnie • when- ever I can. Mad, indeed, am IP" With the nvowed object of disobeying Las Deane, this young ma= took up his hat and vaulted from the window into the garden. Be then struck . across the pathrand asitick, or ill-luck, would have it, encountered Minnie herself. "Bulb, Minnie.l how are you? Been cinder any more engines P" " No," replied Minnie,. quietly. "Once' was quite enough; don't you think so?" ; "Rather," reiponded: the led. "I say you are a: iplucky one! Why everybody thinks you a lieroine !still, and all the peOpletalk about you." "I wish they wouldn't then," said Minnie. "TM ' not worth all that. Ifs- all long past and ever." • "Oh come, that's ,very fine. Quite the modest eetiriag girl. But, Ijsay-, come for a walk ?" "No thank you, Mr. Deane, I must go heme:"' "Jitibbish," was the elegant reply. "I like you, awfully, Minnie. Come along, there's a good girl.. You.'re the only girliin the place worth her salt." "I (rennet go with youi. Of course I can't: Why,. what would mother say and the people andlady Deane?" _ _ -

"Tether Lady Mane, replied Marmadirke. "'Come along, and we'll go into the Leigh Woods am]. find a squirrel, I daresay." "No,' said Minnie, „firrray. "I'm going•homei" " Expecting young,2 Watson, I suppos, I'll punch his head if ho, goes worrying you," sneered rfeane. 'lie does not worry me at all," said the. girl' steadily., "Now, Mr. Deane, good-bye." He extended his hand to meet hers, but instead of 'releasing it, held it firmly in his, and attempted to lead her in the direction opposite to that in, which she wished to proceed,' Let me go," she cried, indignantly.v "Mr- ' Deane„ don't be so stupid. You are very rude awl ; very rough." "'Perhaps I am; but then I want your sweet , society_ That oaf Watson isn't going to keep yoa • from everybody, I can tell you: • "'Mr-Watson is a gentleman, which is:rnere'than I can tell you !" ,13,.,0u are, Then you can't expect me to behave like one," • retorted the passionate youth. "Give, me; a kiss, Minnie, and part frisnds." She made no answer, but struggled to freo;herself. She, had nearly sueoecded, when Marmadvike Deane suddenly seized her'waist, and perhaps might have gained the kiss he, sought had not his collar been firmly seized from behind and a sudden jerk laid him prone upon the-grass. He leapt to his feet, and found "the oa-ZwaMen ' standing before hinah. "-What d 9 you mean by that ?" inquired Manna- k _

"I meant to rakes° this young lady from your insults," replied Edward, "and I have succeeded. I don't wish for your society any longer.'!' " Get out of this, you interloper.. Don't you know this park la my property, and you are tres- passing? have you taken up if you don't look out."

"You miserable ctir ! Come Minnie, let me escort you. These cubs should be chained up when I they become dangerous." Minnie smiled, and gra'infully accepted his offer. "Cubs !" exclaimed Marmaduke,, white with rage as he saw her laugh, and noticed her content- ment in Edward's society. " Do you. mean to call: me a cub, you railway cod?" "If the cap fits you can wear it. You are a low,. cowardly blackguard, for all your grand descent,'?' replied Edward, indignantly, "and deserve a lessen.. Come, Miss,La.yton, let me assist you.' "Miss Layton may go on, and. you, if you are not a coward, will wait here?" "Don't stop," whispered Minnie to Watson. "I know he wants to. hurt you ("me with me, please Mr. Watson."' " You,, need not be alarmad,',' said Watson, a:had. " CowardS mho attack defenoeless girls do not umallY fight with men. Such blackguards are bettor cut or horsewhipped. like curs, as they are." This.retort maddened Marmaduke, and, without considering probable consequences, he ruched at Edward Watson, and before the latter could protect himself, hit him a severe blow upon the cheek. Edward had only time to throw his hold back, for the assault was so sudden that his hands could not, protect hire. The blow reached his cheek, but. his quick movement in some measure saved his eye, at which it was aimed. Minnie screamed, and called for help; but Wat- son took no notice of Marmaduke for a moment, He told Minnie to ran away home, and then but- toning his coat, put himself into a fighting atti- tude, and stood his ground. "I'll teach you to call people curs," said, the spiteful Marmaduke. "You shall have as good a thrashing as ever a cad got. Now, then!" As he finished speaking he rushed suddenly upon Edward, and aimed at his rival a tremendous blow straight from the shoulder with all his force and weight. Watson partly parried it, but the impetus was too groat; he leaned tack, put his foot into a hole in the ground, and fell heavily. Ah, ha," cried the bully. "That will teach you manners, you cad! Get up, will your ' Edward said nothing, but rose slowly. His face was puffed, but the glance he permitted to rest upon his adversary made Deane feel uncomfortable. Once again the young men faced each other—the bully the taller and stronger., Edward Watson, cool and
collected, stood his ground and maintained a defen. sive attitude, breathing quickly between his closed teeth.

Marmaduke Deane faced his late friend, and made another sudden .rush, hoping to overthrow Edward by sheer brute force. But this time hi tactics did not succeed. Watson stepped aside, and as the enraged Deane passed him Edward dealt him a severe blow in the face, which cut his cheek badly and covered his face with blood in an instant.

Unheeding his wound the powerful young squire rushed in a terrible rage upon the calm engineer—. the former with all his evil passions aflame, the latter feeling in a certain sense in the position of a knight-errant, whose aim was to succour damosels in distress; and Edward Watson was quite prepared to assist Minnie Layton, for he felt the influence of her attractions deeply. "A 'z Marmaduke rushed at Edward, who now felt it was time to stir himself. He had learnt a peculiar blow from a young clergyman, an excellent boxer and a pattern priest, who worked down in the canal district, amongst : the boatmen and deck - hands, in which a little knowledge of the noble art was necessary, as I could, if space permitted, prove from an actual occurrence that came under my own know- ledge and observation. This hit was a peculiar one, but I cannot explain it. All I know is, a young friend of mine, a very fair boxer,was knocked across a room, sweeping all the ornaments off a table in his flight, until he finally subsided into the coal-scuttle.

This was the "tap" that Edward Watson now determined to draw upon the excited Deane. As the latter rushed at him Watson parried with his right and retreated one step. Then in a second the " right " somehow advanced and made an opening for the left, which dashed out with a terrific upper cut, and in a moment Marmaduke Deane was lying prone upon the ground with a broken jaw, bleeding from the tongue and teeth --a perfect picture of helplessness and passion unsubdued. Edward Watson stooped down rather amazed at the prompt effect of the "parson's lessons." He endeavoured to rouse his prostree antagonist; but he, whether because he was unwilling or unable to rise, remained resting where he was. His eyes were closed and he lay motionless. "Can't have killed the animal," muttered Edward. *Better let him lie. He is breathing well enough," he added, as he felt his heart. "AU right, Deane?" But Deane, though he heard and well understood fie question, replied not, being more inclined to lie at any time than to speak the truth. So there he lay resting in the grass until Edward went to seek the doctor at best speed. By the time the young engineer had gained the surgeonlehouse Marmaduke had entered the Hall, unperceived by Lady Deane, and sent a servant on hone/Jack for Doctor Prober, who, thanks to Edivard, was already on his way to the Hall. Meantime, Minnie had returned home and-told her mother,-who, in her secret heart rejoiced that 3.l.armadhke Deane (her child) had formed an at. taehment to. Lady,Deane's true daughter, and what! will Sir William say when he finds his heir as he is Yet her-schemes did not look very rosy just then. She had become very much attached to Minnie, and Marmaduke•was always very rude. How was it that the child she had taken to work out revenge had twined around her heart, and the son she had relinquished-'—the son she hoped to work upon, .and who would be heir to tho estate, if she held her tongue and played a waiting game—should be so untutored ancbrough ? She had promised herself vengeance, but the effects of her eeheroing somehow did not leok EO pleasant just then. Edward Watson might oven yet win the prize, and then all her influence-with young Marmaduke would be gone. From him she hoped many things, and did not hesitate to held out Minnie as an inducement or decoy. Mrs; -Dayton wanted money and pleasant surroundings. She must . keep Marmaduko sa good humour.
ORAPTER XXVL WAS IT WORTH THE CANDLE?

Lucy LAYTON'S idbas of vengeance her -notirirP of striking at the man whom she imagined had inflicted a lasting insult upon her, through his or her child) were beginning to assume a less pleasant hue in her eyes. Her intention had been eta, sub- stituto her boy as tils• heir, and when he, the petted and spoiled child of the celebrated and wealthy Sir William Deane—when this lad had grown up a real gentleman—the idol maybe of the county— then she could humiliate his supposed parents, and put forward her cottage-bred child as theirs and daughter lowly brought up instead of the son—the heir the parents had, so long wished and prayed for. This scheme had appeared to the angry Lacy Layton a very refined, and original kind, of feavenge. It had its advantages,. no doubt. She, wasi.on the Spot, and could note the gradual accompliihaaenit of her plans. There were no violent means- to be resorted to. All the fell 'satisfaction of, the mur- derer, or his deadly and dangerous deeds, -mere not anticipated nor desired; but the quick revenge that works in darkness was her's, she fancied. She had brooded over her wrongs—her lost, hus- band, for whose love she in her youth had lied from , home and caused her father's death. Hen-warped and wilful spirit had resented any interference in : her conduct at Mussuri; her vanity had urged her to flirt, and play a dangerous -game; her temper hail' alienated her husband, and then she tarifa upon the first person who interfered. Eating her heart out with the brooding on saious- ness of unsatisfied revenge, and the utter insudi- cieney of her schemes-to promote happiness- or even the fOICCOSS and satisfaction she expected, Lucy Layton ask herself the question, so often asked by those who have plucked the Dead Sea Fruit so ,to speak, and found it all ashes, Was,-the game worth the candle ?" • . .

_ Mr & Ltyton was rapidly coming to the conclu- sion that it was no& She had reckoned without taking Nature into consideration. Her boy, upon whora, she hoped wealth:and honour would descend, and through whom,“when her day of vengeance came, she had some, vague ideas of striking at his (supposed) parents,. had developed into a very commonplace and vulgar young man, one of whom it were certainly unseasonable to be proud. On the other hand, the cottage-girl: she fancied % Minnie would be, Nahl all the ease and appearance of a. gentlewoman. Well-bred and very pretty, every- one remarked the gradual development of her'. beauty, and openly said that the was DLICTO fitted fop, thuhall than the cottage. Here was o. cheek at the outset. The girl's striking likene,s to Sir William Doane, her father., was daily becoming, more marked,. and affected Lady Deane not a little. This circumstance alone was .ennugh to render Lucy mistrustful of the success of her plot which, though so ver7 firm and solid-looking when rst put together, was crumbling away. by degrees, just as some apparently solid and durable stone dis- ' integrates under exposure to weather and such adverse influence.

Was the game worth the cane? This is,the question she had to answer. Is the gains,, aver worth theicandle ? Do not. most forbidden fruits and stolen apples of this life, beautiful, enjoyiw, engrossing as they are when we are plucking Ithem and eatingt turn acid in ourntanths even before we are satisfies?. Do they ever satisfy? Have they not from Adam downwards, breught with their.enjey- ment a punishment, sure' if slaw, certain if belting? The lame goddess is behindius. Nemesis..will yet overtake n% And then we ask,. Was the genes• worth the tandle? Was it? No.

So Mrs. Layton answereeli. and her heartleegan to misgiveher, but she could nee turn back. She had put her hand to the .plough, and was obliged to con- tinue the work, even, though many a furrow were lined upon her awn,fitee, and the turning up of past scenes and buried memories were not pleasant to behold. Was, there any. way out ? ".Marmaduke Deane "had already developed, as abaladhopetat one time he would doe= affection. for Minnie. But the girl detested him. and Mrs-. Layton knew too well, how obstinate. Minnie cord/. be.. In snch, a case no persuasien, would mover ber' and even Lucy herself felt that. Marmaduke was., not a son to be proud of. But there was, another reason why Mrs. Laytem was ill at ease and: already inclined to confess here self beaten. Minnie had frequently shown sYfiiptoms. of a preference far young Watson,. and the events of, the day upon which he and Illarmaduke had met, as already. detailed, served to confirm, the girl in, her previous. estimate of the rival, claimants of her favour. Should Watson ever propose marziage to Minnie, Mrs. Layton was quite sure she would aceept him; but she fancied that the son of the great Sir Walter would never be permitted to unite him. e]l with the daughter of Limy Layton, neeßaymond. There was another consideration which weighed upon the mind of the woman, and that was the in- creasing devotion and, openly - expressed ad - miration of Collier, the inspector for herself. He was becoming importunate, and she had no satisfactory answer to give him. She felt she must decide one way or the other soon, for George Collier was continually pressing her to become his wife., She could give no reply, for no intelligence of he husband's death had reached her. He 'had disappeared; but he might be alive, and then she didn't love George Collier; any more than she did in the old days. Altogether, therefore, it will be perceived that Lucy Layton was in no way comfortable. Her arrange. moats, which had. looked so °levee and which had
%ould

promised so well, were in imminent danger of col.. lapse. She scarcely knew whether to continue her plans or leave the neighbourhood, taking Minnie with her. ZFate, however, solved the question for her, and led .co.a clearing up of events which will now be

explained. The defeat of Marmaduke Deane had, so far from quelling his passion for Minnie, only served to stimulate it. He could not understand that such a common girl could resist him for any length of time, and therefore as soon as he had recovered from his bruises and felt presentable, he made up his mind to wait upon Mrs. Layton and ask her final consent to his paying his addresses to her daughter. He thought he could easily gain her consent. and 10 soon as he obtained the interview he sought, he jiSit tho question to Mrs. Layton, little dreaming that he was asking such a favour from, and con - feting with. his own mother. And she? Did ,he have no ecrupleo, or did shit betray any feeling when, for almost the first time, she found herself tete-a-tete with her child, for whom she could not help feeling a tenderness which he did not, in his selfishness and self importance, remark? When he had broached the object of his visit, he went on to dwell upon the advantages which would accrue to Minnie by such a match "Heir to a large property," he said, "I am about the greatest catch in the county, and nobody can deny that. • "Then why do you wish to marry such a very insignificant person as Minnie?" asked Mrs. Layton. "Because I'm fond of her. Upon my soul I sen, Mrs- Layton, and I will do all I can for her." "Suppose you were not the heir, would you accept your change of position, and be contented to live with her in a cottage such as this?" "Oh, of course, that is all rubbish," he replied. "'What I want is your consent." • "You have it," she rejoined. "But you mast, gain Minnie sas well. I cannot interfere there, Ann your parents must receive her as their daughter." • "Well, I'm not so sure about that, you know. She ought to be quite content to marry me, any way, an can't expect to be received all at once. Surely ll ask her to be my wife it is sufficient for her. Efer position is so very different. By the by, where is she ?" "She is down with Mr. Collier, the local in• epector. He and Minnie are great friends. Bet you will have to think of what I have said.' Mirmie must never be humiliated." "She is awfully like my governor's picture,7 marked Marmaduke. "Sometimes I think that -when he returns and sees her he may wonder at the likeness himself. I have heard— aren't re 'well, Mrs. Layton ?" "Quito well, thank you, Mr. Deane. But' Yeti have rather upset me. You must excuse me for si moment." "I'll be off; don't mind me. I•was only going te. say we had a telegram from the governorrwhe is coming home-at once. He may turn up any day. What fun it will be to meet him! He's never seen me in his life, and won't know me. He will be astonished when he does turn up. Good.bye."' "Good-bye," replied Mrs. Layton, listlesSlY The announced early arrival of General Sir William Deane had given her-much food for reflection. \V° the game worth the candle? Marmaduke walked up to the Hall musing. upon the conversation he had had with Mrs. Layton. That Minnie would never be received by his mother as his wife, Marmaduke was quite convinced. That she could even assume her position as the wife of the heir to the property, Marmaduke had heard enough of his " father " to be convinced would !never be. The pride and exclusiveness of Sir William Deane was well known to his wife, and it was this know- ledge that made her anxious concerning Marmaduke. The young man wandered homewards, aud 00 arrival found the house in confusion—servants hurrying to and fro, and anxiety was depicted uP°l3 every countenance. "Is anything the matter ? "inquired Marreaduke. "What's all the row about, eh?" "Sir William and another gentleman have arrived> sir. They have met with an accident, and. were pet served by a miracle, I'm told, sir. We are all Weil thankful, Mr. Marmaduke," added the. pious font' \

man. " Rather !" replied • the young man. "I'M glad they've arrived. HereTs a go," he rems.rked as ha proceeded to the drawing-room. "Not valsoll•ellance for Minnie now. Hang it!" Heopened the drawing-room door, not very gentlY, and passed in. The blinds were down, hut Marina- duke perceived that a young lady was reclining up° A , the sofa. She took no notice of his approach, se" the young heir came over towards.treading softly upon the thick carpet. "Wonder who she *1 inutterea Martnaduktr 4 I believe she's asleep, No. I beg your pardon', he said aloud. "Not at all, thank you. I am merely resting her* in deference to Lady Deane's wish: there is nothing the matter."- Marmaduke could not believe his eara, o.nd scareel credited his eyes when the young lady rose sn, seating herself upright upon the sofa presented to no bewildered gaze the beautiful face and graeafulionsi et "the signalman's daughter.'. _
