div.head: ADJOURNED BREWSTER SESSIONS AT WARRINGTON
div.p: ADJOURNED BREWSTER SESSIONS AT WARRINGTON

A RENEWAL REFUSED. The adjourned licensing meeting of the justices for the borough of Warrington was held on Tues- day, at the Sessions-room, in Irle.m-st., the proceed- ings lasting over a period of several hours. Great interest was centred in them, and during the whole of the time the-Court was crowded to an uncomfort- able degree. The Mayor was in the chair, and the Other magistrates on the Bench were Aldermen , Sutton, Crosfield, Burgess, Chandley, Harrison, and: Holmes; Councillors J. Platt and \Toney; and Messrs. J. White, R. Garnett, Ridgway, Pairciough, Guest, and Gornall. Amongst those in the body of the Court were Messrs. W. Pierpoint, li. Roberts, J. Walker, Henry Greenall, Hatton, James Ilepherd, William Owen, Dobson, sen., William Bolton, T. J. Down (managing director for Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co.), W. B. Roberts, Joseph Garner, and the Revs. J. J. Langham, E. Moore, and E. C. E. I ICarleten. Before the proceedings commenced, Alderman Davies, who had been adjudicating on some police 1 eases, said that it had been communicated to him that any magistrate adjudicating in licensing mat- ters, who happened to be a shareholder in anry rail- way or shipping company that held a license for the sale of ints.aicating liquors, would be subject to pains and penalties that might be recovered from him. Being concerned more or less in ships and railways, be must decline to adjudicate.—Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, said that this only applied when the magistrate had a share or interest in a license in the immediate or adjoining district.— Alderman Davies then retired, and the licensing business was taken.

UNOPPOSED RENEWALS. THE 'HOP POLE, -EORSEMAREET•ST. Henry Dale, licensee of the Hop Pole nn, Horse-' market-st., applied for a renewal of his license.—The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said the applicant-had only recently become the owner of the house. The former occupier had been fined, but he had no fault to find with Mr. Dale. Formerly the house, which was used as a singing hall, was a notorious place, but nothing objec- tionable now took :place on the premisesi—The license Avugrante'd. THE OLD CHOW, ,FENNEL-ST. John Roberts asked the Bench to renew his lioenae In respect tothe Old Crowlnn, Fennekst., hisapplication being ,supported by Mr. Swift, barrister, :Liverpool, in- structed by Ilfessrs.R. Davies and Co., soliciters.—Mr. .Swift-said that the applicant had -Wen tenant ef the house for three years. and in January last, he was fined 10s. and costs for sellin,gliquor during prohibited hours. At that time, however, he was ill, and his wife by mis- 'take opened the door before the proper hour.—The 'license was granted. „ RENEW-ALS OBJECTED TO. 'MEE ROYAL EXCHANGE, MARKBP-PLACE. The application of :Edward Bullock, for a renewal of 'the license to the Royal Exchange, Market-place, was next taken. Mr. A. Browne, -solicitor, appeared in sup- port of anobjection to-the renewal, and Mr. McKeand, barrister, Manchester, was for the occupier of the house,. the interests of the owner, Councillor Bolton, being , watched by Mr. Segar, barrister, Liverpool.—Mr. Browne -said -that the course he intended to pursue that ' morning was one thabhe thought would meet with ap- proval. He,proposed to-make cue opening for the whole I 1 seven licenses the renewal of which -was objected to, then to call his evidence, and then let learned counsel. 'reply and 'call evidence. He should ask -the Bench to refuse the licenses of the whole of the seven, houses that had been adjourned -for further, consideration. The .sairen objected to were :--- 'The Royal 'Exchange, Market-place; the Swan Inn; liridgast.:: the Bull's heactlnn, Bridge-st,.; the Fox Inn,: Buttermarket-et.:; the Currier's Arms, Buttermarket-st. the Pelican Inn, Buttermarket-st..; and the Shakespeare: Inn, Bank-st. Mr. Browne, in urging the Bench not to ' renew these licenses, said that, besides being supported in that course by :public opinion, the :magistrates had, had a.n example set theinatSearborough, Bradford, and: 21lewcastle-on-Tyne, where zenewals had been refused., An objection that appliedto the whole of-the houses was that they were not required for the necessities of the:, neighbourhood, and another was that -they were not' atructurally.adapted for the,purposes of licensed houses., With one exception, the Royal Exchange, Mr. Browne pointed out,the same houses were on a pre,gous occasion objected to by the otagistrates,acting through a sub-com-' Mince, and it was only owing to a technical-error that, the licenses were necessarily -renewed. as to the Royal Exchangeroccupied 'by Edward Bullock, he was not, he alleged, a fit and proper person to hold a license. Re also had to object 'that the house was not required, that it was not structurally adapted for the purpose, and that tha premises were usedfor the purposes of betting. Mr. Bullock was a book-ntaker, and kept a clerk, named Smith, and the two were in the habit of attending race meetings in different parts of the country. Mr. Browne was proceeding with a charge against the landlord and his cieric„ and said that he should .call the evidence of two girls, when Mr. M'Keand objected onbehalf of theaenant. Mr. Browne had opened,lie eaid.with circumstances that might disclose a crime underthe Criminal Law Amend- ment Act. He was asking the Bench to try a question 'which, as ordinary justices, they had no jurisdiction to try, as the matter as alleged would have had to go be- fore a jury.—Mr. Segar, banister, Liverpool. supported Mr. M'Keand's objection, on behalf of the owner of, the house, Councillor W. Bolton.—Ultimately, after ' considerable legal argument, the bends retired, and on returning, the Mayor intimated that they had decided not to hear the evidence of the witnesses mentioned by Mr. Browne, but police evidence would I be accepted.—Mr. Browne said that he would call police evidence, and went on to say that on the sth C f last August the occupier of the Exchange, accom- panied by his clerk, was publicly making a book at a football sports -at Warrington. Dealing with the question of the premises, Mr. Browne said that they 'were not structurally adapted for the purposes of a licensed house, and, in addition, there were no less than 40 licensed houses within 150 yards. Dealing with the objections to the Swan Inn, occupier Henry Gittens, Mr. Browne said that the cbjections were that the house was not required, was not structurally adapted, that it was used for the purpose of betting, and that its situation was such as not to bring it under the Sufficient supervision of the police. They had nothing against the character of Mr. Gittens,except that he was a bookmaker. Within 150 yards' radius of the Swan there Were 26 houses holding licenses. With regard to the Curriers' Arms, the Fox Inn, the Bull's Head, and the Pelican, he had no possible objection to make to the character of the tenants. They were all good tenants, but he contended that the houses were not required. Mr. Roddy kept the Bull's Head, and there was no pos- sible objection to his character, but there were eleven' ale-houses and two beer-houses within a radius of 150 yards of his house. With all the population taken away from the bottom of Bridge-street, he contended that the Bull's Head was not required. With regard to the public houses in Buttermarket-St. which were objected to, Mr. Browne strongly urged that they were not re- quired. They were, he admitted, also properly conducted, but the fact was that Buttermarket-St. was overwhelmed with public houses, there being nine or ten within 60 yards of Market-gate. In consequence, as was well known, the business houses in the street were prejudici- ally affected, as was also the letting value of the pro- petty.

div.head: ENIDENCE.
div.p: THE ENIDENCE.

Mr. Silcock, architect, Egypt-st., Warrington, pro- duced an ordnance map coloured so as to show the num- ber of public-houses within a radius of 150 yards of the houses which had been objected to. Within that radius of the Royal Exchange, there are 34 ale-houses, two beer- houses, three out-door licenses and one for wine on the Premises, a total of 40 licensed houses. With regard to the Swan there were 22 alehouses, two beerhouses, two out-door licenses—a total of 26 licensed houses within a radius of 150 yards; and within the same radius of the Shakespeare Inn 21 alehouses, two beerhouses and two out-door licenses, total 25 ' • of the Curriers Arms, 32 ale- houses, two beerhouses. three out-door licenses, one for wine on the premises, total 38 ; of the Fox Inn, 34 ale- houses, two beerhouses, three out-door licenses, one for wine on the premises, total 40 ; of the Pelican Vaults 35 alehouses, three beerhouses, three out-door licenses, one for wine on premises, total 42; of the Bulls Head, 11 ale- houses, and two beerhouses, total 13. By Mr. McKeand : The Royal Exchange was near the market, lie could not say that the population about there was very dense. He did not know that the Royal Exchange was the oldest licensed house in the locality, nor did he know that it had been licensed for 86 years at least. He did not know that it was largely frequented by market people,nor did he know that the landlord had to provide tea for a large number of women 'who came there for it. Mr. Browne: If that district is congested with anything it is eengested with publichouses. (Laughter.) In answer to Mr. Swift, Mr. Silcock said he had not taken a radius of 150 yards because that included the largest number of public houses. The public houses out- side the 150 yards radius were:not marked red, but there were public houses outside that limit. Mr. Mulholland said the map ought to have been marked with all the public houses.—Mr. Browne : We Produce a map for our own purpose; you can produce Your own map.—Mr. Swift: Because you want to throw dust in the magistrates' eyes. The map, he held, was a delusion and a snare unless it showed the whole of the number of public houses. Inspector Spinks was the next witness called. He said he had been inspector six years and sergeant before that, and he had been in the police force 24 years. He knew the Royal Exchange. It contained a very small bar par- lour, two taprooms, kitchen, and a small yard with a right of user to the adjoining yard of the Coffee House liotel. Upstairs there were two bedrooms on the first floor and two on the next. The rooms downstairs were Oct very large, in fact none of the rooms were large. He (witness) was at the Football Club sports on Augustßank aoliday, and he eaw Edward Bullock there. Ile was

standing on a ginger beer box betting on the events of the day. Harry Smith. Bullock's assistant, was with him. He (witness) reported what he had seen to the Chief Constable, and as the latter was going towards him Bullock got down from th 6 box, and did not bet after that. tie (witness) had the matter of the girls in hand. —Mr. Browne •: After your inquiry and investigation in the case, do you swear Bullock is a fit and proper person to hold a license.—lnspector Spinks : He is not a fit and proper person.—Mr. Browne: Supposing that was put ' t 3 you when he was applying for a,license 2—lnspector Spinks : I should not report he was a. fit and proper person. By Mr. McKeand : Witness said the occasion mentioned . • was the only occasion on which he had seen Bullock make bets. The Chief CQnstable did not give him instructions to summon Bullock.—Mr. Browne,. Because he could not.—lnspector Spitiks : I knewbefore the Chief Con- stable came that we had no case against Bullock.—Mr. Browne: It was not a place within the meaning of the Act. Mr. Browne further asked if there had been any complaints about betting on Bullock's premises, but Mr. McKeand objected to this que:ltion and it was not answered.

Cross-examined by Mr. Sega; inspector Splnks said he believed that was the first time it had been com- plained that the Royal Exchange was too small. He (witness) was not a teetotaller. 'He did not think that it was within his province to say whether the license of the oldest or the newest house -should be taken away.— Mr. Segar : What is the difference between a member of the Stock Exchange and a man standing on a ginger beer 'box ? (Laughter.)—lnspector Spinks : I don't know, sir.—Mr. Browne: Have you over seen Bullock go anywhere P—lnspector Spinks : I saw him go to the last Manchester races.—Mr. McKeand : How does he know.; he might have gone to a gospel meeting.—lnspec- tor Spinks : I have seen him on excursion trains to races. Inspector Cox said he hathbeen for 18 years in the police force, and having made investigation into Bul- lock's case he considered that be was not a fit and proper person to hold a license. Be heard, too, that Mr. Bullock was a betting man:—Mr. Browne :Have you had any complaints.—Mr. McKeand, however, objected to thisquestion being answered.—Mr. McKeand said there had been a paragraph in ormof the newspapers regard- ing Bullock, and asked if that paragraph was put in by one of the persons objecting Ito the lidense.—lnspector Cox: I don't know.—Mr. McKeand : Has he been threatened witn an action forlibel for putting that in ? —lnspector Cox: Not to my 4knowledge.—Mr. Browne: And he has hot yet.--ContinuinK, Inspector Cox said he thought Bullock was not a fit and proper person because he had heard complaints about his betting. They had net been able to catch him, but they had had plenty of eomplaints. _ _ .

Cross-examined by Mr. Segar, Inspector Cox said he ffid not know who had put the police in action in that case.—Mr. Browneasked why no betting CAIM4 had been gone into against Bullock.—lnspector Cox: Because we could not get suffioient evidence. P.C. Monoghan spoke to having seen Bullock betting at the .Football Club sports. Be was one amongst several bookmakers. After he had got off the box, he still continued betting but did not make so much noise. Be did not think Bullock was a fit and prop ec person to hold a license.

Cross-examined by Mr. McKeand, witness said be came to the conclusion that Bullock was not a fit and proper person beca,nse he had made inquiries in the case referred to, and he believed that Bullock was a bookmaker. He did not know that the young women were persons of bad character.

Chief Constable Hunt said he had been chief constable 24 years, and, having made inquiries into the ease affect- ing Bullock, he should say that if Bullock were making an application that day he (witness) could not recom- mend him as a person to hold a license. Mr. McEeand : Do you base your opinion upon what you know in connection with these two girls ?—The Chief Constable : Two or three years If have had pretty much the same impression that he was scarcely a fit person. —Mr. McKeancP: Why have you had that impression ? The Chief Constable: Because he was a betting man. Further cross-examined by Mr. McKeand, the Chief Constable said hehad never seen Bullock make a bet; 'he had simply had reports against him. One of the girls ilad a good character, and the other a character that was not very good. He had never confronted bullock with the story of the two girls, and be did not feel justified in 'taking criminal proceedings. Cross-examined by Mr. Segar, the Chief Constable wadded that he had reason to believe that Mr. Bolton had bought the Royal Exchange. The affair with the girls 'took place befcre the: 11th Septembez, the time when Mr. 'Bolton bought the house. Mr. Lolton had a good .character with regard to the conduct of his houses. 'There had been no conviction and no charge against any one of them. He would have no ohjection to the license If Bullock was got rid of.
Mr. Browne : But you cannot get rid of him till the Ist fleptember, next. I Mr. Segar : That is a question alas' ;he is bound to do nothing to imperil the license. _

Mr. Mckeand then addressed the Beach on behalf of Mr. Bullock. He contended that the okections to the license were not of a bona-fidecharacter, and the other side shewed that by putting in every postible farm of objection they could. That was an organised attempt against that license and was not brought there for the publk weal. The objection was made by .a, gentleman named :John Walker, and it would have been a good deal moresatisfactory to Lave had John Walker put in the witness box to explain why he objected to the house. They had no right to say that Tallock was , guilty of a certain ,cffence until he had been con- I victed before the mar,ierurates, and there was trat a tittle , of •evidence upon which they would be justiffed in coming to the conclusion that the alleged abduction was true in substance or fact. Referring to the evidence,as to bet- ting, Mr. McKeand said that even if Bullock did make a bet outside his house that was no evidence of bad char- . acter such as would justify them in taking away his license. Betting men could be as honest as anybody else if they choose to be. He asked the Bench to he very careful before depriving Mr. Bullock of his house and living. Mr. Segar, speaking for Mr. Bolton, the owner (4 the Royal Exchange, said it would be a very great lossto his client if the license were refused. Mr. Bolton had paid £950 for the house and license, and only became pos- sessed of the house after the nth September, and there- fore he could not be guilty in the least degree of the al- leged offence. Mr. Segarthen referred to the long period during which the Royal Exchange had been a licensed house, and to the fact that Mr. Bolton had such a good character as to the conduct of his other houses.
Mr. Browne said Mr. Bolton was not a licensed victual- ler, and owned only one licensed house besides the Royal Exchange.
TIM MLOISTIZATHS CONSULT.

The magistrates then retired, and after consulting for some time again took their seats on the bench. The Mayor said they had decided not to renew the license to Edward Bullock; but that the question of the license to the house would be adjourned for further consideration. —Mr. Browne said that he should take that as a refusal of the license.—The Mayor (after consulting with the clerk) said that he was advised that there could be no further adjournment.—Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, who is secretary to the Licensed Victuallers' Association, urged , that the justices were legally entitled to appoint an ad- journed meeting any time before the end of September. —Mr. M'Keand: If you will give me an adjourn- , ment for four days, that will answer the purpose. 1 —Mr. Browne: What for 2—Mr. M'Keand: For Mr. Bolton to get a new tenant and apply for a , license.—Mr. Browne: You would have to give 14 days'l notice.—Mr. M'Keand: I do not think it necessary to I give any notice, and I should apply in the ordinary way for the transfer to a new tenant.—Mr. Jenkins: You can apply for a temporary authority to sell.—Mr. M'Keand : I think it would only be right and fair, for Mr. Bolton (the owner) is blameless in the matter.—The Mayor : We have not the slightest wish to jeopardise Mr. Bolton's property at all, but I am advised that, as far as this court is concerned, we can do 'lathing further than tell you to apply next year for a license.—Alderman Harri- son said that the magistrates never intended that the property of the owner should be affected.—Mr. M'Keand suggested that the bench should grant Mr. Bolton a tem- porary permit to sell.—The Mayor: I think the feeling is very unanimous that if we could protect Mr. Bolton we should only be too pleased to do so; but the feeling is equally unanimous that we could not grant a license to Edward Bullock. If our law-clerk could show us any means of supplying the license to Mr. Bolton it would be saved.—Councillor Voisey : Will Mr. Bullock say that he is ready to resign 2.-Mr. M'Keand: lie will.-Mr. Browne: It is an unfortunate :position for Mr. Bolton, but your worships are perfectly powerless.—Mr. M'Keand sug- gested that the license might be renewed to Mr. Bolton, and not to Mr. Bullock. It was not granting a new license, but was a renewal.—Mr. Swift said that a case went to the Queen's Bench division, and thence to the Supreme Court of Appeal, under circumstances which showed that the Bench had full powerto grant a renewal

.... in the name of any person that they pleased to accept. I It was entirely in the discretion of the magistrates. If I they thought the present occupier was not a suitable per- 1 son, they could put the license irs the name of the owner, I or any other person, without any delay or any difficulty. He had known it done over and over again, and the case of the Queen y. Lawrence, from Liverpool, showed that what had been the piactice was actually the law. (Ap- plause, which was at once suppressed.)—Mr. M'Keand put it forward as a further suggestion that the Bench might grant a license to the present tenant, with an un- dertaking from him that he would execute a transfer to some other person within area sonable time.—Mr. Browne: I, of course, object to that,but at the same time he should undertake that no actions for libel be taken. They have been threatened.—Mr. M'Keand said that his was a sug- gestion in the interests of the owner.—The Mayor: I am still advised by the Clerk that we can do nothing fur- ther in this case at the present time, and we must go on with the next business.—The license is, therefore, refused.
TRH MAN INN.

The license of the Swan Inn was next taken into con- sideration.—Mr. Browne called Inspector Spinks, who stated that the Swan Inn was situate up an entry off Bridge-st. There were three entrances to it. There were gates to all of the entrances. There were two urinals opposite the entrance to Mr. Dobson's workroom. The Swan Inn was not situate in as public a place as the

div.head: .IXA'MINIIt, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27:1890.
div.p: THE .IXA'MINIIt, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27:1890.

other public-houses were. There was good accommo- dation in the house. In answer to Mr. Mullholland, who appeared for Mr. Dobson, the owner of the house, wit- ness stated that he did not know the license had been in existence over 100 years.—lnspector Cox said that if the entry doors were left open the house was under sufficient control. The door leading up the entry by Mr. Roberts' shop was always shut at night.—Mr. Browne asked the Chief Constable if a Sub-Committee representing the magistrates had visited the various public-houses in the town, and the Chief Constable replied in the affirmative.—Mr. Browne : Is one of the houses the magistrates objected to the Swan Inn ? The Chief Constable: I do not know that they objected to it. It was adjourned for consideration.—Mr. Browne: ' Was not one of the grounds that it was out of the juris- dictionof the police ?—The Chief Constable: I km not ' aware of it.—Mr. Jenkins asked if t was just to allow the private opinions of the Sub-Committee of the Bench to be , brought in evidence either against a tenant or an owner of a house? The report of 'the Sub-Committee was a communication which should be held as sacred and as privileged.—Mr. Browne: Is the house properly placed for the supervision of the police ?—The Chief Constable: I cannot say but what it is 'under the proper supervision , of the police. It is certainly up an entry.—ln reply to Mr. Mulholland, the Chief Constable said the police had plenty of access to the house.—Mr. Mulholland contended that there was no evidence to prove that the premises were used for betting purposes, and the Chief Constable kad admitted that there wasplenty of arrass to the house.— The magistrates then retired from court, and on their re- trun, the Mayor said: I have to announce that the magis- trates have decided torenew the license of Henry Gittens. —At this point Mr. Robert Davies appealed to Mr. Browne whether it was worth while to go on with the other cases. The magistrates were perfectly well aware that every effort had been made by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. to disperse the cluster of houses to which reference had been made, but they had done so in vain. —Mr. Browne said he could not consent to stop the cases. He had witnesses present who were most anxious about them.—Mr. Jenkins said that the tenant of the Swan had instructed him to apply for costs, as he had been put to considerable expense in meeting the objection which had been raised—objections which had not sprung from the Bench sr the ,police. He considered it would only be fair to great him his oosts.—The Mayor said the Bench had not power te grant costs. At this stage tke Court ifdjourned for an hour. ITHEt SHAKESPEARE INIT.

The license of the Shakespeare Inn next came on for consideration.—lnspector Spinks said there was nothing to prevent certain tenants getting beer over a wall at the back of the house, without the police being•able to see them. The house was fairly clean. He could not say whether the house was required. It was frequented by persons of low -character.—ln answer to Mr. Swift, he said he had never made any report objecting to the renewal of the .license, nor any report tending in that direction. That was not a police objection at all. The landlady did aIL she could to keep the house respectable. —Mr. Swift contended that he had no case to answer. The officer hafisaid the house was frequented by persons of low character, but it must be remembered that it was situated in a low neighbourhood, and be supposed birds of a feather would to some extent flock together. People of low character were not deprived by English law from getting reasonable refreshruents. The landlady did all she could to conduct the house in a respectable manner. Mr. William Owen, architect, could prove that it was a good roomy house and fairly clean.
•TH.II KISUTTI3PatARXIti,ffrIIEET HOtTSIIR.

Inspector Spinks gave evidence in respect to the Fox, Corners' Arms, and the Pelioan.—Mr. Browne: In your opinion, is it necessary ta have three public-houses situ- ated one after another ?—Mr. Swift said the witnesses had all properly declined to give an opinionon that point, and he contenTded that that was not a fair question.— Mr. Browne: 'Then it comes to this, that you cannot get any person in the world to say there is any necessity for these houses- But that is an argument which speaks for itself.—The Chief Constable was then examined, and was asked by Mr. Browne if there was any necessity for three public-houses one after another in Buttermarket- st., or for eight public-houses and one beer+house in one street within a distance of 100 yards ?—The Chief Con- stable: As faras I am concerned I don't see any necess- ity, but the houses are as they were .when I came to Warrington 27 years ago.—Mr. Browne: Have you received complaints from the inhabitants of Buttermarket-street, with reference to the number of public-houses affecting their trade ? Mr. Swift: Icbject to the question, because if people have any complaint to make let them come here and give evidence on oath before the magistrates.—Mr. Swift (to the Chief Constable) : I believe you don't ohject to the renewal of the \ licenses in any of the five cases ?—The Chief Constable: I don't see howl can.—Mr. William Gleave was then sworn, and said he was a baker carrying on business is Buttermarket-st. He had been in business for over 22 years, and he should say there was no neces- sity for so many public-houses in that street. It very considerably affected his trade, owing to the characters who assembled in the street. Witness was then,examined with reference to •Mr. Brandreth's shop, and hendmitted that the want of a tenant was owing to the owner re- quiring too mucherent. Mr. Gleave added that what he objected to was the bad characters who associated in the streets, and the bad language they made use of. The sights they witnessed day after day interfered very considembiy %with the business of the shop-keepers. —Mr. Swift contended that he had no case to answer. The objections had,heen presented to the court in the most slipshod, bald, and meagre fashion. He wished it to be understood that no objection had been raised by the magistrates or by the police. He admitted that in some parts of the town a litttle congestion took place,

but that might be remedied; indeed, Messrs: Greenall and Whitley had for the last 15 or 16 years. with a view to relieve that. congestion, offered to remove certain licenses to the outskirts of the town. Their proposals, however, had not been accepted. There were only seven boroughs in the two counties which had a less number of public-houses to the thousand than Warring- ton had. Warrington had 3.2 to the 1,000, taking the Public-houses as they stood now and the population of 41 thousand odd, on the last census. Since that time, how ever, the population had very much increased, but there were only seven boroughs which had less public-houses, whilst there were more than twice seven pos sessing more public-houses. Clitheroe had more, Bury, Bolton, Lancaster, Crewe, Oldham, Wigan!, Chorley, St. Helens, Preston, Blackburn, Staly- bridge., Ashton - under - Lyrae, Macclesfield, Chester, Manchester Blackpool, also had more. Warrington seemed to I:eve an abnormally large number of grocerst licenses, and there lay the evil, as men who were com- petent to judge said that the existence of those licenses was to a great extent the cause of the drunkenness. Warrington had 87 fully licensed houses and 48 beer. houses under close supervision; but there were 70 grocer's shops which were not supposed to requite watching, and therefore a great deal of surreptitious work went on. People went in apparently for groceries, but no one knew what they brought out. He called Mr. John Allen, of the Pelican, who said he had been tenant of the house for 15 years. Messrs. Greenall and Company did not have managers. When be went into the house he paid about £5O for fixtures, and had spent something annually on the premises ever 'since. The Pelican was the headquarters of several friendly societies—the Ironfounders' Society of England ,and Wales, the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, the 'Stonemasons' Society, and the Shepherds' Society. He was treasurer of three of the societies. He found accommodation for members of that society. Cavalry were occasionally accommodated in the house; he had had as many as 14 staying in the house the same night. He had accommodated from 30 to 40 persons a week in the house. They had stopped in the house all night.—ln answer to Mr. Browne, witness admitted that he had been party to an application for the removal of the • license to another part of the town. The Bench, after considering their decision in private, decided to renew the whole of the licensee. NEW COURTS REQUIRED.

Mr. Browne t While we are congregated here, may I call attention te the condition of this court. It has been said on many occasions that the condition of the court ought to be improved. Seeing the manner in which it has been crowded on this and other occasions, some im- provement ought to be made for the benefit of the health of all who attend here. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause).—Mr. Swift: If my friend Mr. Browne had not named the matter, I had intended to ask permission to say a word or two about it. One cannot sit here several hours without feeling that the room is small, incon- venient, and ill-ventilated. I am sure it is not worthy of the Bench, or of the important business which has to be transacted here. It is not worthy of such a populous and important town as Warrington.—Mr. Hobert Davies: Will you allow me to add a word as the senior practicing solicitor In Warrington? I well recollect during the vacation, on my return from Rugby school in 1842, ask- ing my father to bring me to the :Police Court at War- rington. Mr. Nicholson was clerk to the magistrates, and he kindly found a seat for me. I remained to see what was going on. When the population of the town was 18,000 this room was just as large as it is aow, and it was in the same condition except that there were no ventilators. Then I had the honour to hold the office of clerk to the magistrates for eight years, and I know the Inconvenience which the public sustained was nothing compared to the inconvenience which the magistrates sustained c If more than three or four magistrates attend, there is nothing but a little closet—for it is nothing more than a closet—for them to sit in to see anyone ; and I think that now the popula- tion has increased from 18,000 to upwards of 50,000, a better police court ought to be provided. The town is rapidly increasing, and there is every prospect of a stili greater increase. I hope some of the members of the Bench will use their influence to get something done before long. It is not only of this court we have to complain; but of a most inconvenient, draughty, and misplaced County Court.—The Mayor: I am very much obliged to , you, gentlemen, for bringing the matter forward. It is very inconvenient for the magistrates to sit here, but it must be much worse for the public to be crowded together at the back of the court as they have been to-day. I shall certainly bring the matter before those ',rho will be able to guideme. I trust we shall have better premises be- fore long.—Alderman Harrison: If Mr. Davies had 'not alluded to the condition of the County Court, I should have said that there were two courts situated in Warrington which want improving off the face of the earth—(hear, hear, and laughter)—the Borough Court and the County Court. They are a disgrace to the town and a source of discomfort to all who makeuse of them.—Mr. Browne: One building belongs to the town and the other to the Treasury.

div.head: BENWELL MURDER IN AMERICA.
div.p: THE BENWELL MURDER IN AMERICA.

' The public interest in the trial of Birchen grows from day today. Woodstock is crowded with people from all parts of the Dominion, who have come to try and catch a glimpse of the prisoner and hear what they can at the trial. Mrs. Birchalt was not present in the morning. Wednesday's proceedings commenced with the hearing of the evidence of Dr. Wilford, who made a post-mortem examination of Benwell's body. Giving evidence as to the cause of death, witness stated that he found two bul- lets in the deceased's brain.

div.head: THREE LICENSES ABOLISHED AT LEEDS.
div.p: THREE LICENSES ABOLISHED AT LEEDS.

The licensing justices of Leeds, on Thursday, re- fused to renew three licenses which had been in existence for many years. In one case the objector was connected with a local temperance society, and in the others the Chief Constable lodged objections. The grounds submitted against the renewal ef the licenses were generally that the houses were un- necessary, and that two of them had not been pro- perly conducted. In respect to the house against which no complaint was made, it was statea that five years ago the tenant paid .£1,700—.£700 being for goodwill. The decisions of the justices greatly surprised the licensed victuallers.

div.head: STRIKE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE STRIKE AT ST. HELENS.
PEARS' SOAP has maintained its reputation as the best of all Toilet Soaps for more than One Hundred Years.
It represents a CENTURY'S EXPERIENCE of the most successful achievements in the Art and Craft of Fine Soap making.

An important meeting in connection with the strike at the Cowley Hill Plate-glass Works of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers was held at the Lamb Hotel, Coporation-st., on Tuesday. The casting-hall men have been out on strike for 14 weeks in consequence of the firm declining to grant an increase of wages, and their action necessitated the stoppage of the whole of the men employed in other departments of the works. On Tuesday afternoon the Arm conveyed intimations to a number of the "lock-outs" who were employed in the polishing or finishing departments thatthey could resume work on Wednesday. A meeting of strike hands and " lock-outs "was accordingly called for Tuesday night. Considering the extremely short notice, there was a very large attendance, and Mr. John Bradbury, president of the United Plate-glass Workers' Society presided. Re- porters were not admitted., but it was ascertained that a ;determination was unanimously expressed not to resume work unless the men's terms were conceded. It was ; understood that Messrs. Pilkington had in their works a ; large quantity of glass ready for polishing and finishing , and it was thought that if a gang of polishers could be ; induced to resume work the firm would be able to hold out against the demands of the men for a longer period than would otherwise be the case. The men were urged to remain firm and united, and not to accept work under , any considerations other than those for which the casting- hall men were out on strike. This opinion was generally entertained by the meeting. Another meeting of the strike-hands and lock-outs was held in the Public Ball, on Wednesday forenoon. There was a very large attendance. Reporters were again excluded, but they were afterwards informed that the proceedings had been of an enthusietic and unani- mous character. It was reported that on Tuesday . the firm sent messengers to eight of the lockouts intimating that they could resume work, but the men who had been asked to start attended the meeting and expressed their determination not to resume operations until the demands of the casting hall men had been conceded, and this announcement was received with loud cheers. Several speeches were made, and the following resolution was carried unanimously :—" That this meeting hereby agrees to stand firm ;until the employers give us what we ; are asking, and pledges itself to dean in its power to keep , the men from accepting work." On Thursday afternoon an open-air meeting of the strike-hands and lock-outs was held on a plot of land near the entrance to the Cowley Hill works. There was a very large attendance, and Mr. John Bradbury pre- sided. Addresses were given by Messrs. Bradbury, P. McKinley, T. Glover, R. Hunter, and P. J. King, and the men were -strongly urged to remain firm and not to resume work =till the demands of the casting hall men were conceded. No resolutions were submitted, but the proceedings were unanimous. Whilst the meeting was in progress, several men, who have been engaged doing odd jobs about the works, came out on their way home. They were hissed and hooted, but the disturbance was at once stopped by the gentlemen on the lurry, which was being utilised as a platform.

div.head: HALTON CASTLE HOTEL
div.p: HALTON CASTLE HOTEL

The adjourned Brewster Session for Runcorn district was held at the Police Court on Monday. The magistrates present were Messrs. Jas. Handley, G. L. Wigg and John Brundrit (who arrived late.) The only case for decision was the objection of the police to the renewal of the license to Thomas Idigginson Wolstencroft, tenant of the Halton Castle Hotel.—Mr. F. A. Lake appeared on behalf of Wolsten- croft, and of Mcssrs. Baker and Co., brewers, Langolleu, the holders of the lease.—lnspector Bowyer said the police objected to the renewal of the license on the ground that the applicant was not a fit and proper peison. He called P.C. Fryer, who proved that Wolsten- croft had been fined for being drunk on his licensed premises, and for keeping his house open during pro- hibited hours. The officer stated that he had visited the hotel on an average twice a week, and he had always found Welstencroft under the influence of drink. He had also frequently seen him driven home in cabs when he was drunk.—Mr. Lake oentended that the notice of objection had not been legally served, and said the officer was either exaggerating or had not done his duty in regard to Wolstencroft. Wolstencroft had been given notice to quit,and another tenant would be found by next Monday.—Mr. Baker said the firm had had a great deal of trouble with the present tenant, but they could only get him out on a convietion.—Wolstencroft : It was only about accounts and nothing else.—Mr. Baker: It was about the manner in which the house was conducted.— After a protracted deliberation, the Bench decided to renew the license on the understanding that a fresh tenant would be obtained.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Boardwas held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Alderman Harrison presided and there were also present Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Messrs. T. Jones, Davies, Aukland, Balharry, Smith, Hurar..lireys, Turton, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Mather, Eddowes, Gill, Kilshall, Clarke, Jolley, Dignum, Hood-Wright; J. C. Sutton, (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant-clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse master), H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padgate Schools). GIFTS. _ _
Gifts for inmates of magazines were acknowledged from Mr. Joseph Mercer and Mr. J. D. Buckton.
SCHOOL FEES.
The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 43 casrks 41 of which were old and two cases.
new
DEPOT!' MEDICAL OFFICER FOR NEWTON. Dr. Watkin wrote asking the Board to accept his son as deputy medical officer for the Newton district, and this was agreed to.
TIE LOCLL GOVERNMENT SWAM INTERPOSE.

The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board with regard to the proposal of the Guardians that a conveyanct should be hired to take the members of the School Committee from Warrington to Padgate Schools and back on the occasion of their meeting there. The Local Government Board wrote that they had always ' held that it was only in cases were members of Boards of Guardians were obliged to travel beyond the limits of of the Union that they were entitled to charge for travelling expenses. The Board therefore could not, consistently with this view, assent to the payment out of the rates of the expenses of the Padgate Schools Committee on visiting the schools which I were situated within the Union.—Mr. W. HotionyoN thought the Local Government Board had taken a very proper view of the matter.—The Criatinum said it ap- peared to him to be a very shabby and contemptible piece of business. Here were gentlemen who devoted their energies and time to discharge duties for which they got Ino monetary recognition whatever, yet when a neces- sary expense was to be incurred by reason of the dream- stance that the schools were at Padgate, they were prevented from providing a just and reasonable mode of conveyance to a place that was practically inaccessible by any other means. It was time centralisation was abolished and that they had Home Rule. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—Mr. W. HOUGHTON said that of all the Guardians the Warrington Guardians had the best facilities for getting to Padgate. A Id. railway fare took them there, while Guardians from other parts of the Union had to find their own means of getting there. —Mr. RATCLIFFE agreed with what the Chairman had I said, and he pointed out that the Guardians from Earles- , town and Newton, if they missed the 5.30 train at Padgate, did not get home until ten minutes past nine o'clock.—The CLERK suggested that the bill for the con- veyance as far as they had gone should be submitted to the auditor for him to pass or reject as he chose, but of course they could not continue the conveyance in the face of that letter.—Mr. AUKLAND thought it was a scandalous piece of business. It was not the railway fare they complained of, but the loss of time business men had to incur.—The CHAIRMAN : They would be in a difficulty if we refused to perform the duties.—The sub- ject then dropped.

div.head: I'HB ESTIMATES.
div.p: I'HB ESTIMATES.

In the course of a statement on the estimates, the CLIME said the estimates before them fixed the total contributions by parishes in the next half year at £6,981, following upon totals of £11,431, £9,101, £9,116, and £8,823. These substantial reductions had been effected by prudent appropriations of new common fund credits, by energetic and successful procedure in connection with the settlement of insane persons, by the diligence of their collectors, and, it might justly be also said, by a desire all round to adopt in that Union effective and economi- cal systems of Union administration.—lt was decided on the motion of Mr. NV. HomairroN, to print the statement of the Clerk, and circulate it amongst the Guardians.

div.head: TEE SUPPLY OP SOAP TO 1712 WORKHOUSE.
div.p: TEE SUPPLY OP SOAP TO 1712 WORKHOUSE.

On the question of tenders for the supply of provisions, &c., to the Workhouse coming up for consideration, Mr. IGILL said he had been told that some three or four tons of soap were used in the year at the Workhouse, but that the soap was bought out of town, although a large rate- payer in the town was a maker of soap. It seemed to be I rather unfair if the same quality could be got at the same price in Warrington.—The CHAIRMAN said that unless some good reason could be given for it, it seemed mon- strous.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said that the House Committee I had always taken the lowest tender. They got the soap through Mr. Owen. and they had nothing to do with Iwhere he got it from.—Mr. AIIKLAND thought the soap ought to be bought in town if it could be bought in a reasonable way .—Mr. RATCLIFFE pointed out that the Union consisted of other townships besides Warrington. —Mr. AITKLAND said his remarks applied to all who paid rates either in or out of town.—The CLERK said he be- lieved the soap came from Runcorn. It was their duty to issue an advertisement inviting anybody to send in tenders, and if a person living within the Union did not send in a tender it was his own fault. When a person's tender was accepted they could not say he should not go to Runcorn or anywhere else for his soap.—The CRAM- ?LAX : We might go to the manufacturer.—The CLERK: In that case it is for the manufacturer to tender if he cheoses.—Mr. GILL: Gould he tender for soap alone ? The Cuing said that he could. He added that the value of the soap used at the Workhouse in the year was about £los.—The Cusrnick.v remarked that the subject might be considered by the House Committee and the subject then dropped. PROPOSED NEW OFFICES.--A RETLECTION Ow THE PAIL AND TIDA VANS.

Mr. AIIKLAND gave notice that he would move at the next meeting that the Board erect new offices and Board room somewhere in the centre of the town.—The CLERK suggested that that subject might be left over till it was seen what further proposals the government intended to make with regard to alterations in local government.-- Mr. Auxuatia said they had about the worst approach in England to that workhouse. They had to pass about 28 or 30 closets and ashpits and as a rule there were a number of the pail and tub vans about.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said that the smell of those "jam carts" was certainly not pleasant.—The CHAIRMAN said that probably Alder. man Burgess would say the smell was rather pleasant than otherwise. (Laughter.)—Mr. AI:TALLER : I have my own opinion of what Alderman Burgess says; I don't think it is all gospel. He added that he should still bring forward his motion, as he thought, considering the rents the Board had to pay, that it would pay them to erect new offices.

Fifteen men were scalded on Wednesday, three of them severely, by a boiler explosion on board- the Australian warship Pandora, lying in the Tyne. Superintendent J. Grant, of the Hampshire Constabu- lary, was on Wednesday committed for trial by the Win- chester magistrates on a charge of forgery and misappro- priating moneys amounting to several hundreds of pounds. James Batchelor, described as a sackmender, was re- manded by the Clerkenwell Police Court magistrates, on Wednesday, on a charge of attempting to murder his wife by cutting her throat with a razor.

div.head: MAN OF THREE WIVES.
div.p: A MAN OF THREE WIVES.

John Clifford Arnold, of the Ferns, Edward-road, Bed— ford, was on Wednesday, committed for trial at the Central Criminal Court, on a charge of bigamy. The evidence disclosed an extraordinary state of affairs, being to the effect that prisoner had gone through the marriage ceremony with three women, all of whom are now alive.

div.head: MORE BOULANGIST DUELS.
div.p: MORE BOULANGIST DUELS.
A duel was fought on Sunday afternoon between M. Millevoye, the Boulangist deputy, and M. Canivet, the, director of the Pars. M. Millevoye was slightly wounded in the hand.
A duel was fought at Bordeaux on Sunday between M. Gounouilhou, an Opp )rtunist journalist, and M. Chiche, a Boalangist deputy. M. Chiche was slightly wounded.
It is stated that General Boulanger is preparing a reply to the story of Boulangism in the shape of a volume of: two hundred pages, to be pabli6hed in French and Eng-- lish in London.
THE BOLTON DROWNING I‘iYSTERE.

The adjourned coroner's inquiry into the mysterious, death of Thomas Mather, 27 years of age, labourer, of Warburton's-fold, Egerton, who was found drowned in a lodge at Dunscar, near Bolton, under circumstances which led to the suspicion that foul play had taken place, was held at the Globe Inn, Egerton, on Wednesday after- noon, when the man Thomas Macdonald, an ex-convict, who is in custody on the charge of being concerned in Mather's death, was present. It will be remembered that Mather and Macdonald were in each other's company, and that Macdonald on his own admission left Mather drunk besides a water lodge. Whatever truth there was in this, Mather's body was found in the lodge with cer- tain marks, assumed to have been caused by personal violence, OR it.—The jury after a long deliberation, re-- turned a verdict of found drowned.

div.head: WELSH BI7ILDLNG SOCIETY FRAUDS.
div.p: THE WELSH BI7ILDLNG SOCIETY FRAUDS.

Writing from Llanberis, on Wednesday, a correspon— dent states that Mr. Williams, chairman of the Carnar- Ivon County Council, who is one of the two gentlemen I acting as the Advisory Committee, has intimated that in his opinion, after careful examination of the rules, the mortgagors and also the holders of preference shares are safe. This places the responsibility for the deficit of £11,509 on the ordinary shareholders. It is also under- stood that very little will be recovered from the estate of the deceased secretary to make good this fearful loss,. and the ordinary shareholders will consequently have to bear the whole loss. The secretary was immensely popu- lar with the quarrymen. He was extremely liberal to religious and charitable objects. To one chapel he pre— sented a harmonium, and to another a set of Communion vessels, and judged even by the strict canons of Welsh religious thought, he led an actively pious and exem- plary life.

div.head: PROPOSED SHIP CANAL TO BIRMINGHAM.
div.p: THE PROPOSED SHIP CANAL TO BIRMINGHAM.

A special meeting of the Birmingham Chamber- of Commerce was held on Wednesday, for the pur- pose of hearing the statement of a deputation from the promoters of the Birmingham and Liverpool Ship Canal scheme, a proposal to construct a canal for boats of 400 tons between Birmingham and the Weaver Navigation at W insford. The promoters are engaged at present in soliciting subscriptions to a company the object of which is limited to the obtaining of an Act of Parliament authorising the construction of the canal by a larger company. It is proposed that on the Act of Parliament being obtained the shareholders in the preliminary copa- -1 pany shall be paid either in cash or in shares in the canal. The engineering features of the scheme were described by Mr. B. Shepherd, and its advantages I were pointed out by Mr. Alderman Johnson, Mr. J. Slater, and Mr. Samuel Lloyd. A resolution approv- ing of the project and commending it to public support was moved by the Chairman, Mr. J. W. Tonks, seconded by Mr. Wilson Lloyd, of Wednes- bury, and unanimously carried.

div.head: PREVENTING A GLOVE FIGHT.
div.p: PREVENTING A GLOVE FIGHT.
PUGILISTS IN COURT.

At Lambeth Police Court on Monday, before Mr. Partridge, Frank P. Slavin and Joseph P. M'Auliffe, pugi- lists, were charged under warrant taken out by Chief Inspector Chisholm, with having agreed to commit a breach of the peace by fighting a prize fight at Ormonde Club, Walworth-road, London. A large crowd of well dressed men assembled outside the court, but compara- tively few were admitted.—Lord Lonsdale occupied a seat on the bench.—When the evidence of Chief Inspec- tor Chisholm was read over, Mr. Purcell, for Slavin, cross examined him. He said he had received notice of the fight from a club proprietor.—Mr. Wiehtman Wood, for M'Auliffe, argued that if the defendants were guilty, gentlemen at Oxford and Cambridge who did the same thing were guilty.—The magistrate said he could not go so far as that.—Mr. Purcell urged that the fight was not a prize fight.—Mr. Crichton Temple, proprietor of the Ormonde Club, produced gloves, weighing four ounces each.—The magistrates asked witness if serious injury could be inflicted with them.—Witness could not say.— After further argument, the magistrates held that the proposed fight was illegal and a breach of the peace, and bound the defendants over in £l,OOO each, and one surety each of £l,OOO, to appear when called upon. If the defendants fought, the whole question could be decided by a judge. The promoters of the Slavin-M'Auliffe boxing match decided on Wednesday that tho contest should still take place, the number of rounds, however, to be reduced from thirty to fifteen.
THE CHEMICAL UNION.-EXTENSIVE

div.head: OPERATIONS.
div.p: OPERATIONS.

The "Chemical Trade Journal" of Saturday says— The meeting of the Alkali Trade, called at Liverpool at the instance of the promoters of the Chemical Union, turned out to be an unqualified success. In one finan- cial newspaper, " inspired " no doubt by the opponents to the Union, we were gravely told that only three mem- bers of the trade were present. This was totally false— nearly one hundred alkali makers were present, amongst whom were Mr. John Brock (who occupied the chair), Sir Charles Tennant, M.P., J. C. Stevenson, Esq.. M.P., Mr. James Tennant, Mr. GeergekPilkington, Mr. E. K. Muspratt, Mr. Huntley, Mr. J. E. Davidson (represent- ing the Newcastle Chemical Works Co.), Messrs. Hedley and Yryde (representing Messrs. Hutchinson's), Messrs. Barlow and Wylde (attending on behalf of the WidneS Alkali Co.), Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, senr., Mt. Eustace Carey, and Mr. Holbrook aaskell, jun. (representing the firm of Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.), Messrs. Davis, Clark- son, and Golding, of the firm of Golding Davis, and CO. ; Messrs. Robert Shaw, of the firm of Hall Bros. and Shaw; Mr. Thomas Matthieson, Mr. Thomas Snape, Mr. Mort, and Mr. Liddell, of Mort, Liddell, and Co.; Mr. Richmond, of the Liver Alkali Co. ; Mr. Cook, of the Atlas Chemical Co.; Mr. Charles Wigg, and Mr. G. Lloyd Wigg, of Wigg Bros. and Steel; Mr. Charles Hazlehurst, of Messrs. Haziehurst and Sons; Mr. J. H, Dennis, of the Globe Alkali Works; Mr. E. Baxter and Mr. W. Baxter; Mr. Raynor (representing Messrs. Kurtz), Mr. Thomas Walker; Mr. M•Bryde and Mr. Blinkhorn, of James M'Brydo and Co.; Mr. R. Rigg ; Mr. P. J. Worsley, of the Netham Chemical Co. • Mr. Richardson' of Newcastle; Mr. Cannington ; Mr. E. Bramwell ; Mr. Mawdsley ; and Mr. Chadwick, who is. both paper maker and alkali manufacturer. Mr. C. Stead, accountant to the proposed Union, and Mr. Haw- kins, solicitor, Li ve rpool ,were also present amongst others. A proof prospectus was handed to each member of the- trade present, from which it was gathered that the capital lof the Union is to be eight and a half millions sterling, of which seven millions is set against works, plant, land and buildings, and one and a half millions for, stocks and working capital. The capital of the Union will be allotted as follows —Two-and-a-half millions in 5 per cent. deben- tures. Three millions in 7 per cent. preference shares. Three millions in ordinary shares. It is understood that the vendors have agreed to take 70 per cent, of the pur- chase money in shares, so that it is quite possible that the public may experience a difficulty in obtaining the allotment of any ordinary shares.—The Chairman stated that the Committee had come to.the.C.Onelusion to' issue the prospectus themselves without the assistance of any financial intermediary. They were confident of suc- cess, and he mentioned that five firms, representing one- and-a-half millions of capital, have stated their intention of taking the whole of the purchase money in shares, and it is understood to be the intention of one firm to apply. for £lOO,OOO more shares than the amount of their par.. chase money. All the alkali works in Widnes, without exeeption, will fall into the Union. All in St. Helens will join, with one exception. All in Runcorn will go into the Union without exception. On the Tyne all will be Union. Works, without exception. and the same in Scotland and Ireland. All the country works of any importance, save one, will join the Union, and that one would probably join if the proprietors' own valuation werelecepted, but as moderation basso far been exercised by the-Committee- in their valuations, they do not see their way to exorbi- tant values for patents, the future value of which is only' problematical.

SCA.MTED work may be the work of Scam Ping Work, a scamp; but it is not necessarily so. It means work which is done

with bad material, or work so hurriedly or care- lessly executed as to be bad in character. Mr. " GLADSTONE, speaking at Saltney, the other day, put In a plea for all work being well done, and inciden- tally referred to the scamping which was known to take place. He was careful to guard himself against the supposition that he intended to con- demn any particular class ; but his language seems to have been misunderstood. Mr. W. J. DAVIS,

the General Secretary of the National Brass- Workers' Society, has elicited a communication freen the ex-PREMIER which places the matter I'eYend the possibility of misapprehension. Mr. GLADSTONE says :

I don't believe I used any expression which im- Plied that the scamping of work was characteristic ?f workmen more than any other class. It is icnown, I fear, to all classes. I see it in my own class—that of politicians, and I daresay I have been guilty of it myself. The root of it lies deep in !Inman nature, and it is the vice of all production. suppo-e that working below the proper standard is the vice especially of wholesale production, and here will, no doubt, come in the employer, if he has not a proper sense of his duty, which is also his Interest. But I made no reference to wholesale Production, and had it not in my mind. I was thinking exclusively of such manual work as is scuted in detail, and to a considerable extent tinder the control of the workman himself. Politicians are certainly, as this chief of politi- clans admits, guilty of scamping. There is too ranch business done after our legislators have dined not wisely but too well—not to say any- thing of slip-shod clauses which are framed in the aaaall hours of the morning. The result is Acts of l'arliarnent which are pitfalls to the public and 'Windfalls to lawyers. Scamping is :indeed " the vice of all production," and the consequences are Bnteetimes serious. Scaffolding,for instance, badly

erected frequently results in accident and some-- times loss of life. The life of the Prince Imperial of Prance was sacrificed in South Africa through failure to mount his horse and get away from the Zulus, and he failed to mount his horse through the breaking of a saddle girth. There had been a Piece of scamped work, and the Prince was its vie- But it is the jerry-builder who is the scamp scampers ; and we are sure we are within the Ilia& in saying that hundreds of people perish "ery year through pipes being so badly laid, and drains so badly made, that sewer gas is brought into houses by the very means which have, osten- 81blY, been devised for keeping it out. The jerry- builder might and ought to be taken red-handed, Promptly despatched, and buried without hope of resurrection in one of his ill-constructed drains. Wliat a contrast are the rickety structures of to-day to the buildings of our forefathers—going back a dozen or Sven twenty generations ! See the ruins of ancient mansions,castles, and churches --how the stones are bound together by good raortar and good workmanship, as though they meant to defy time and weather until the crack of I°ola. Of a truth, it may be said of those work- , ruen of old that "They builded better than they knew." It is contract work, we fear, which leads to a mat deal of scamping. Excessive and un- qualified competition results in low prices, and low Prices result in a low class of work. It is thus
_ that 80 many things come to be made like the

celebrated razors—not for use, but for sale. What we all, as a rule, want is, as Mr. GLADSTONE haB it, "to be continually braced up to a high standard in our work." Employers can do much towards mending matters—more, we are inclined to think, than workmen, for if a high standard is i'laisted upon by the employer, the workmen must Imost of necessity follow suit. Still, it is not to be denied that the labourer has an opportunity of Showing himself worthy of his hire, and, if he will c'ver have this in mind, there will certainly be less acamping.

„_ The school teachers of Warrington seem to have had a pleasant time of it, at Mr. Long's residence, at Windermere on Saturday. It is a sort of per- formance which they would doubtless like to 'll.core. ” Laking "is pleasant to teachers &swell as kholars.

"Sweet are the uses of adversity." The death (If the Workmen's Club in Warrington will result 111 the birth of •a gymnasium and reading-room, r the mind as well as the body is to be provided for. The Committee are working hard to obtain further funds, so that they may feel justified in commencing to build. More power to their elbow. The Emperor of Germany is here, there, and everywhere. He courts Courts as ardently as a .outhful lover. It is all very well for him to whom kingship is as a new toy, but visit upon visit Must be trying to the old stagers. It is costly, too, tthe people visited; but that doesn't count with mperors, and as to the people—why, they can gruMble and pay as usual. From later news received as to the foundering !3f the Turkish man-of-war off the coast of Japan, It seems that the total loss of life was no less than 87. It is a terrible disaster, and a great loss to ie Turkisk navy. It has transpired that the °sman Pasha who perished with the rest was a ice-Admiral in the navy, and not the Osman l'asha known to fame as the heroic and skilful 'le:fender of Plevna. A. Buttermarket-street tradesmen has been com- Paaining in strong terms to the Chief Constable of arrington of an over supply of what he called the finished article." Asked to explain, he said 'what he meant by the phrase "finished article" Ivas "Drunk and disorderly women." How sug- gestive ! Wonder if the manufacturers are proud Of" the finished article," and if their travellers Tlete according to sample. Leeds macistrates have followed the example et them in some other towns, for on Thursday they extinguished three licenses. Itis evident, that PUblic opinion is influencing the irre3ponsibles of the Ranch; and it is not unlikely that as many • 'iceases will be extinguished this year without corn- A•lnsation as would have been abolished with com- Pensation, if the Government proposals had been adopted. And this is only a beginning.

There was a collision between 'buses, and an in- , trloek-ing of wheels, at Warrington Bridge, on aturday night. It is not.so much a wonder ' that collision occurred as that accidents do not nftener happen at the bridge or in Bridge-st. It Is: clue to the drivers to say that they know the l'sks they run, and, as a rule exercise great care. 01 the good time coming, rule, will be a wider °l.idge and a wider street.

'Busmen and tramway men are moved by the a Pirit of the times, and are seeking a reduction in their hours of labour. There is no denying that I . tli present an exceedingly strong case, working ...' Illany of them do from fourteen to sixteen hours

div.p: a day, and a half day, in some cases, on Sunday. In the smaller towns, there are, comparatively speaking, so few men employed that they are naturally timid about organising. It is to be hoped employers will meet them in their wishes without waiting for threats of a strike.

The General Purposes Committee of the War- rington Corporation have settled upon the names of the nine new wards, which are to be as follows: —No. 1. Town Hall Ward. No. 2. Whitecross Ward. No. 3. Bewsey Ward. No. 4. Orford Ward. No. 5. St. John's Ward. No. 6. Fairfield Ward. No. 7. Howley Ward, No. 8. St. Austin's Ward. No. 9. Latchford Ward. This indication of tho locality by means of the name is in accor- dance with the suggestion we made last week. It is much better than naming a ward after an indivi- dual—living or dead.

The conversion of a big brewery firm into a Limited Liability Company has its disadvantages as well as its advantages. At the Runcorn Revi- sion Court, on Wednesday, the name of Sir A. B. Walker was struck off the owners' list for Runcorn North, his title to appear on the roll as an owner having vanished when his brewing firm was con- verted into a Limited Liability Company. Sir Andrew will doubtless still have a number of votes —far too many—as a property owner in various counties. When are we going to adopt the prin- ciple of one man one vote?

Strange and sometimes scandalous things do take place in Revision Courts. A scandalous thing happened at Battersea on Wednesday, when thirty working-class tenants were disfranchised because , their landlord—a Mr. Ryan—had failed to pay the rates. There could scarcely be a more glaring instance of the need of reform in the registration law. The landlord, it will be said, deserves punish- ing for his neglienco ; but why, in any case, should the tenants suffer for his sins? Rating and voting ought to have no relation to each other. We want full representation of men—not of rate-books.

The McKinley Tariff Bill of the United States is proving disastrous to a certain portion of the iron trade of this part of Lancashire. Its evil effects are being felt in Canada, too ; so much so that a section of the Canadians are preaching an- nexation to the United States. This is cowardly. It is not the part of brave or patriotic men to rush into the arms of those who are inflicting an injury. Let the Canadians exercise patience; they will find that the people of the United States will get tired of paying more for everything in order to please the tariff-mongers.

Mr. D. Crilley, M.P., has been rendering good service to the Liberal cause by giving addresses at Earlestown and at Ashton-in-Makerfield. The rank and file in the Newton Division are in good heart, and if their leaders can find a good candi- date for them, they will work with an ardour which will in all probability pave the way to victory. Mr. Balfour is on the other side, but he, too, is helping to ensure the success of the Liberal cause. He has only to proceed with the arrest and imprisonment of such men as John Dillon and William O'Brien to crown the triumph of the Home Rule party at the General Election.

It is like the Duke of Argyll to back up the Irish Secretary in ordering the arrest of Irish members. He argues :with a correspondent in his peculiar style. He says :—" If it is conceivable that Lord Hartington would be guilty in England of the violent and immoral acts and language which are now the subject of prosecution in Ireland, I pre- sume you would not hold that his high position should shield him from the law, and this view of the case reacts upon the 'mere question of expedi- ency." Bye-the-bye, as bearing on his argument, will the Duke explain why the Irish judge who suggested lynching was not "run in" by Mr. Bal- four F Was it because he was not a Home Ruler F

Mr. John Morley has been an unexpected wit- ness of the way in which the Irish police bully and baton the people. The "Daily News" des- cribing the same at Tipperary on Thursday says At this point Mr. John Morley arrived, but was apparently unknown to Colonel Caddell or his police. Mr. O'Connor called for a cheer for Mr. Morley, and the baton men, not realising that they had a distinguished ex-Chief Secretary in their midst, kept pushing the people off the path into the centre of the street. One man had raised his hand to strike Mr. Morley, but the mention of his name by Mr. O'Connor, who had seized his arm, made the constable's arm almost drop lifeless by his side. At length it dawned on Colonel Caddell that Mr. Morley was present, for he was heard shouting "'Sall these men back. Stop them," but they were almost beyond control, and at all events did not desist until they had given the right hon. gentleman a slight experience of present police methods in Ireland. Colonel Caddell grew quite livid, and stood irresolute as Mr. John O'Connor shouted close beside him, "A cheer for John Morley," which was given with a will. The hon. member then said, " Why don't you charge now, Colonel Caddell, as ' you would if Mr. Morley were not here. You are a coward, and I tell you so to your face." . . . . Later on without the slightest provocation, the people were batoned to the ground, amongst the number being the intrepid young member for Mid- Tipperary. Mr. Henry Harrison, who, while saving the people from the police savagery, was struck from behind with a baton which knocked him down.

div.p: ' .RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY._
The members of this Society are notified that the rehearsals will commence on Tuesday next in Bethesda schoolroom. There are vacancies for all voices.
POSTAL FACILITIES AT _WIDNES.

Mr. J. Payne, the postmaster at Widnes, has succeeded in obtaining sanction from the authorities, to establish a sub-post office at the Ball of Ditton, and of a town receiv- ing office at Halton View. Both these offices will be a great convenience to the public, and Mr. Payne deserves their hearty thanks. • MAIL CARTS for children.—Garland, Ironmonger, Warring- ton and Earlestown.—Advt.

HALTON PARISH CHURCH. A service of thanksgiving for the harvest was held at Halton Parish Church on Thursday evening. The sacred edifice was beautifully decorated, and at the request of Sir Richard Brookes, the gardener of the Priory had adorned the chancel with flowers and fruits. There was a large congregation, and an eloquent sermon was preached by the Rev. Canon Hamilton, vicar of Dove- ridge, Derbyshire.

UNTVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN. From an advertisement in another column, it will be seen that arrangements have been made for a course of lectures under the Oxford University Extension Scheme, onthe subject of "Wealth and Wages." The lecturer will be Mr. 11. Llewellyn Smith B.A. B.Sc. The first lecture will be delivered on Thursday October 9th (and not on the 2nd as stated on the tickets), and possesses the attractive title of • The making of wealth." UMBRELLA 9 RE-COVERF.D at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. _ .

9 meeting of this Committee was held on Wednesday. When on the motion of Mr. Simpson seconded by Mr. Grice the Rev. Canon Wood was re-elected chairman. On the motion of Mr.fGrice seconded by Mr. Hankinson, Mr. T. Riley was re-elected vice-chairman. The Rev. H. Burson was elacted to the vacancy on the Committee. It was resolved to purchase 75 volumes many of which deal with the subject of the University Extension Lectures. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest" notice.—J. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.
