div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBFR 27, 1R90:
CHRIST CHURCH, WESTON POINT.

The annual harvest thanksgiving service was held on Friday evening last . week, when the sacred edifice was beautifully and appropriately decorated for the occasion. Special music was sung, and the Rev. I). Wray, vicar of Halton, preached a sermon to a good congregation. The services were continued on Sunday, when the Rev. T. H. Wilcockson, the incumbent, occupied the pulpit. Collections were taken in aid of church expenses. ELEcrno PLATED Goons.—Garland's oldest established Ironmonger, Warrington.—Advt. AMBULANCES FOR WIDNES. - .

The WidneS-i;Oli'C-C. have this week received the two hand ambulances purchased out of the surplus fund,after providing for a horse ambulance which is in course of construction at Liverpool. The hand ambulances are constructed according to the patent of Mr. Tozer, super- intendent of the Birmingham Fire Brigade, and have cost £ll Sc. each. The beds of the ambulances are of spring wire, detachable, and at the head of each is a drawer for splints and bandages. - -

SIMMS CROSS PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES. Services of thanksgiving for the ing.athering of the ; harvest were held in this place of worship on Sunday, and there were good congregations. Mr. Berry, of Man- chester, preached morning and evening, and in the after- noon the Rev. G. S. Meek, Wesleyan minister, delivered a sermon. On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held, and was well attended. Addresses were given by several members of the congregation, and a musical pro- gramme was gone through by the Welsh quartet.
- - UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED a the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-et., Warrhigton.—Art. WESTON POINT WESLEYAN CIIAPEL. •

_ The annual harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday last when Mr. Robert Norman of Runcorn preached two forcible sermons to large congregations. On Monday night a further service was held and a nu- merous audience listened to an eloquent sermon by the Rev. John Simpson of Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Runcorn. The sacred edifice was most charmingly de- corated with the fruits or the season. Collections were made in aid of the fund for renovating the chapel. WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.

At the usual weekly meeting on Sunday afternoon, Mr. J. llowlin, in the chair, the following resolution was passed unanimously :—" That we fail to find words to express our feeling of condemnation of Mr. Balfour's latest attempt to imprison the political leaders of the Irish people, and we are confident that this outrageous policy on the part of the present Government will fail, as previous attempts have failed, to crush the aspiration of the Irish people." The resolution was moved by Mr. Delaney and seconded by Dr. O'Keeffe.

ST. EDWARD'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, RUNCORN. In connection with this place of worship, the annual charity sermons were preached on Sunday, by the Very Rev. Canon Clegg. There was a crowded congregation , present at both the morning and evening service, and , they had the pleasure of listening to two powerful and eloquent sermons. The choir rendered several pieces of music in an admirable manner, Miss Comerford presid- ing at the organ. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, the local pas- , tor, took part in both services. The collections, which will be devoted to the the school fund, were highly satisfactory. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, RUNCORN. The annual harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday, when the Rev. R. Davenport preached morning and evening to large congregations. In the afternoon the Rev. J. Martin, of Ellesmere-et. Chapel, occupied the pulpit. Specially selected music was ren- dered at each service. The chapel was suitably deco- rated with flowers, fruit, tkc., and the collections will be devoted to a fund for beautifying the sacred edifice. On Monday evening a number of the members of the chapel bad a coffee supper," and the fruit and vegetables were disposed of. BATHS, all kinds.—J. S. Garlands, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge Street, Warrington. Braneli—Earlestown.—Advt. ALBERT-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES. . . . .

_ For some time this chapel has been' considered too small for the wants of the neighbourhood in which it is placed, and the trustees have now purchased an iron structure, formerly used as a church at Stanley, Liver- pool. It will accommodate about 450 people, twice as many as the present chapel. In the interior it is lined with pitch pine, has a neat oak pulpit, well provided with cushions and hassocks, and will be a well lighted, and comfortable place of worship. It is intended to erect the building on the land adjoining the present chapel, and the Rev. Charles Garrett will conduct the opening services.

- - PROPERTY SALE AT RUNCORN. Mr. Luke Holmes, auctioneer, of Runcorn, submitted two lots of property for Sale at Wilson's Hotel, on Tues- day: The first lot consisted of six leasehold dwelling- houses, situated in Shaw-st., in the occupation of Mrs. Haddock and others. The property is held on lease for the residue of a term of 999 years, commencing Ist of June, 1861, and is subject to an apportioned yearly ground rent of £7 10s. 4d. This lot was knocked down to Mr. John Owen for £615. Lot two and six shares in the United Cheshire and Lancashire Permanent Benefit Building Society and Savings Fund. Mr. Samuel Walton was the purchaser, the price being £B6 12s. Messrs. Linaker and Linaker were the vendors' solicitors.

ASSAULT ON INSPECTOR BOWYER, RUNCORN. A navvy named John Cappell, a native of London, was brought before Dr. Steele and Mr. Cr; L. Davies, at Run- corn Police Court, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly and assaulting Inspector Bowyer. Late on the previous night the prisoner was drunk in Lowland's-road, and creating a disturbance. The Inspector requested him to go home quietly, where- upon the man struck him on the side of the head with his fist. As he attempted further violence the Inspector dosed with him, and with the assistance of P.C. Wood- row secured him and brought him to the Police Station. For being drunk the prisoner was find ss. and costs and for the assault 10s. and costs; total £1 7s. 4d, or 21 days' in default. The money was paid.

ANOTHER POLISH AFFRAY. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Joseph Gasbrousky 13, Water-St., and Martha Remarkis, 15, Water-st., were charged with assaulting John Dabrabousky on the 11th Inst. The complainant went to the house of the female defendant, and after having a drink of beer, it was alleged that he was assaulted by the defendants, who violently kicked and struck him. He had not since been able to work in consequence of his injuries. He had been a witness against the woman's husband.—Mr. Rideal for the defence, said the complainant behaved in an indecent manner to some women who were in the house, and he was ejected by the female defendant-- After hearing a number of witnesses, the magistrates discharged the male defendant, and bound the woman over to keep the peace for four months, herself in £lO and one surety of £5.

WIDNES GYMNASIUM. The annual meeting of members was held in the officers' room, at the Drill Hall, on Wednesday evening, 1 and there was a good attendance. Mr. T. J. Peters, who 1 presided, said he was glad the society showed some signs of vitality. The prospects of the coming season were bright, Mr. Alexander had promised to obtain an instructor for them, and Mr. Edwards Moss, M.P., was interesting himself greatly in their behalf. The society was only in debt on apparatus account, and they hoped to clear that off by an assault at arms.—Mr. D. J. Brookes presented a financial statement; which showed a balance in hand of is. 2d. on last years' working.—Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss, M.P., was re-elected president, treasurer, Mr. D. J. Brooks, secretary, W. Duggan, committee, Messrs. R. Evans, E. Welling, T. Jones, T. J. Peters, T. Atherton, jun. ,J. Treacy, G. Evans, R. Evans, jun., W. Pedder, J. Midwood, and J. Taylor. A discus- sion took place as to the wisdom of increasing the sub- scription to 55., but it was eventually decided to make the usual charge of 3s. 6d. THE VISIT OF THE CHANNEL FLEET. - •

The fleet will anchor in the river opposite the Liverpool Landing-stage at half-past nine on Satur- day morning. A complete programme of proceed- ings, entertainments, &c., with an illustrated des- cription of the various warships, has been issued. The work, which has been compiled by Mr. W. A. Brignal, contains much valuable and interesting information. FINEST KIEL BUTTER, one shilling per pound.—lmperial Tea Co.—Advt. _ _

- DEATH OF A CHF:MI.IE COUNTY MAGISTRATE. The death is anno mc-,1 of Mr. John 0. Kay, J.P., of Winsford-lodge, Cheshire, late member of the firm of Messrs. John Kay and Sons, salt manufac- turers, Winsford. The deceased gentleman was a Lancashire man, born in Manchester, and at Wins- ford he was extremely popular as a magistrate for the division, and as a liberal benefactor to all local charities. He was a Conservative in politics. • SEE OCR ALMANACK, entitled "Heavenly Light."— Imperial Tea Co.—Advt. LLANDUDNO AND NORTH WALES.

This resort has, we understand, had an unprece- dented season for visitors, and this in spite of the un- favourable weather which prevailed during many of the midsummer weeks. On all sides credit is given to the introduction of the sailing of the New North Wales Steamship Company's St. Tudno for bringing about this improvement. The company is now issu- ing tickets at 10s. 6d., available for all trips up to the 30th inst., which date ends the season, but early next year the St. Tudno will again commence her sailings on this station. LTINIIISELLAS RE-CON-ERE') at the shortest notice.-1. d; DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrinc,rton.—Adrt. EXTENSION OF WIGAN INFIRMARY.

On Wednesday afternoon a new wing, which has been added to the Wigan Infirmary by Mr. James Henry Johnson, of the Abram Colleries' at a cost of £2,500, was formally opened by Mr. Alderman Smith mayor of Wigan. Afterwards an address of thanks was presented to Mr. Johnson for his gift, the Rector, Colanel Blundell, M.P., Mr. Tomlinson, M.P., and other gentlemen taking part in the proceedings. A garden party was held in the grounds by the Mayor and Mayoress, and was attended by a large number of residents. UNIBRFLLAS 11E-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adrt,
FARM STEAD FIRE AT CIIERDLEY.

On Monday afternoon, about one o'clock, J. Thompsini," a' t:latelayer en the London and North. Western.Rsilway, observed that-a-large haystack on the Marsh End Farm, occupied by Mrs. Crosby, was on fire. An alarm was raised; and the news sent to the Warrington Fire Brigade. The brigade, under the direction of Superintendent Turner, immedi- ately turned out, and soon arrived on the scene. The wind had caused the flames to ignite a stack of oats close by, but as there was a good supply of water two hose pipes were in a short time got to play on the fire, and kept it confined to these two stacks. Great anxiety was felt for three other stacks which were in close proximity to the fire, but owing to the strenuous exertions of the firemen, the flames were confined to the two already alight. The damage is estimated at about X 2,00. but is covered by insurance with the General Fire and Life Insurance Company. Immediately the news was known in Penketh, a number of men from the Penketh Tannery went to the scene of the tire to render assistance. As they arrived part of one of the 'burning stacks fell upon one of the other stacks which the fire had not caught, and it was only by the assistance they gave that it was saved from destruction. The origin of the fire is unknown. _ _ . .

FORMATION OF A RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB. For some time past an agitation has been afloat in Earlestown, Newton, and the Vulcan, for the in- stitution of a football club, to play under the Rugby Union rules. The matter was brought to a crisis on Saturday night, when a large number of young men met in the district infant .school, in order to formu- late some scheme, by which such a club could be inaugurated. Mr. Samuel Williams, a well-known Rugby football player, and one of those who made the Australian tour, was voted to the chair. Some discussion took place,and ultinaately it was decided to form a club, to be called "The Earlestown Rugby Football Club." The following were then chosen as a committee to represent the three places named above-s Messrs. G. Edwards, R. Wright, R. Thorne (for Earlestown), J. Nicole, J. Williams, A. Williams (for Vulcan), T. Egan, G. Lane, and W. Rose (for Newton). Mr. C. H. Lea was appointed secretary, Mr. G. Slinn assistant secretary, and Mr. J. Bolton, treasurer. It was else decided that the club colours should be "navy blue, with red sash." Already about 60 members have been enrolled, and the club has a promising future. The committee are in ne- gotiation with Mr. T. Sanderson for a field, situate behind the Wesleyan Chapel, and it is expected that an opening game will be played on Saturday, the 4th October. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-1. dc W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. THli) MUNICIPAL CANDIDATES AT ST. RELENS.

The selection of two labour candidates for the ensuing municipal elections by the members of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, has occasioned a fluttpr of excitement in the political circles of the town. It is stated that Mr. G. Webster will oppose the return of Mr. J. B. Leach for Central Ward, and the Chemical and Copper Worker' Union candidates will be brought forward in . op- position to Messrs. Brown (Parr Ward) and Foote (North Windle). Mr. Robert Bunter, the secretary of the Lancashire Glass-bottle Makers' Society, has been asked to stand for North Bccleston Ward, the retiring councillor being Lieu- tenant-Colonel W. W. Pilkington. ;Among other names mentioned as likely claimants for some of the seats have been those of Mr. 13: M'Binley, who was last year beaten in Parr Ward by Dr. Gaskell, and Mr. Thomas Glover, miners' agent. !There will prob- ably be a contest in every one of the nine wards. At a private meeting of Conservatives held at the Conservative Club on Tuesday night it was decided to bring forward a candidate in each ward. No definite arrangements have yet been completed, but it is considered likely that there will be an equal number of Liberals in the field. In addition to the recognised candidates of the two great political parties, it. it expected that there will be at least three independent labour candidates brought for- ward. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Guion, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, " Examiner ' Office, Pewsev-at., Warrington.—Advt.

Carter, of Northwich, delivered a most eloquent and impressive charge to the pastor. The service was brought to a conclusion by Mr. Simpson pronouncing the benediction. • The choir; which was augmented for the occisioh, 'rendered the anthems "-Flow-Lovely •-are the Messengers" (the solos being sung by Miss Nellie Handley and Mr. Gowanlotk) and "Judge me, 0 God." Miss Handley. also sang the solo ." 0, Rest %the Lord," with admirable expression and taste. Mr. H. W. Handley was the organist.

EDDISBURY DIVISION. Mr. Burke Wood, revising barrister, on Thursday commenced the revision of the voters' lists in ,the Eddisbury Division, at Dunham-o'thcHill. Mr. W. Handley represented the Liberals, and Mr. R. N. Owen the Conservatives. nu:moans or OVERSEERS. The Barrister found that the overseer's lists for Haps- ford were undated ,and the clerk of the peace had not been • supplied ; and instead of pu‘3lishing the list of parliamen- tary voters he had simply published a piece of a County Council Register that is in force this year. The Barrister said it was a question whether any list had been pub- lished at all, but he ultimately decided to alter the form so that it would be taken to mean one for this year. The Barrister appeared to be highly amused by the blunders of this assistant overseer, and said in the country they were mostly farmers, who were not used 0 this kind of work, and he supposed they must take them as they found them. They ought not to do it, he added, but human nature is a bit weak. When the township of Ince came under review there was no evidence that the assistant overseer had published the lists, and the repre- sentative'of the clerk of the peace said he had received no list of electors. He had received allist purporting to be a list of claims. It transpired that a number of claims had been sent in by the occupants of the Ship Canal huts on Ince Marsh, and the assistant overseer said he had published the list on the Bth July, which was not the legal day of publication. He produced some pieces of rough paper, which appeared to have been dipped in water to make them appear weatherbeaten, and *aid this was the identical list he had published, but he could not accoant for the fact that he had not sent one to the clerk of the peace.—The Barrister found that the claims had been sent in on the 18th August, and were actually on the list the assistant overseer stated he had published on the Bth July. The Barrister said althought it was grossly irregular, he would take the lists and do the best he could. The claims were made out for division two instead of one, but the Barrister allowed them to stand for division one. In another township the overseer had omitted to publish a claim sent in by the Conserva- tives, but the Barrister having ascertained from the farmers present that the man was entitled, added the claim to the list of voters. TEE MOST PROPER PARTY After leaving Dunham, Mr. Burke Wood travelled to Frddsham, where he held a court at the Bear's raw Hotel for the revision of the voters' list for that district. —William Davies, Main-street. Frodsham, claimed a lodger's vote. He said he paid 10s. 6d. per week for rooms and attendance. The house was assessed at £25. —Mr. Handley said the local agent had witnessed this claim.—Mr. Owen: A most proper party, is it not ? Mr. Handley: The most proper party is the person who receives the rent—the landlord.—Mr. Owen: You don't mean to cast a reflection upon the agent P—Mr. Hand- ley : I don't mean to do that. There is no objection to the vote.—The vote was allowed.

HIGH RENTS AT FRODSHAM. Harold William Abernethy, engineer on the Ship Canal, claimed a lodger's vote. He lived at Holly Bank, and paid £55 a year for three rooms and attendance.—Mr. Handley: 225. per week! Rents are higher in Prod- sham than any other part of England. As there Was no objection to the claim, it was allowed.

SORRY FOR HIM. The Liberals objected to George Foster, farmer, who claimed as joint occupier of house and land. The appli- cant said he lived with his mother, who was rated for the property, but he was a partner in the farm and shared half the profits and half the losses. He received nowages. —Mr. Handley contended that Mr. Foster was neither occupier nor owner. The simple matter was he was go- ing to succeed his mother wheti she died.—The Barrister: Have you amy money of your own in the concern ? Applicant : Yes.—Mr. Handley : He is neither owner nor tenant.—The Barrister said he could not get behind that fact, and the applicant was not entitled. He must set himself right to be entitled. He ought to be on, but he could not put him on. He was sorry for him. • ---

BAD LODGER CLAW. Eight lodger claims had been made in the township of Helsby. Mr. Handley said the claimants worked at the telegraph works, and three lodgers were claiming for one house, which was only a small cottage.—The Barrister said none of the claimants appeared.—Mr. Handley said the claims were one and alt bad. It was better for them not to appear and, risk a• prosecution.—Mr. Owen: Discretion is the better part of valour.—The Barrister struck off all the claims.

RUNCORN RURA.L SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was htld at the Work- house, on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present—Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, P. Hall, Weir, Smith, J. Whitlow, Knowles, G. Priest- ner, J. Stokes, Lewis, Hewitt,Rate, Bretherton, H. Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker fdeputy clerk), and Dr. Adams (medical officer).
• THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR. 1 The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the reappointment of Mr. Farrington, as inspector of nui- sances, at a salary, of £l4O per annum.
- THE POLLUTION OF KECKWIC BROOK., . K. _

The Clerk said notices had been posted in the district, stating that Colonel Walker Mardon Ducat, RE., an in- spector of the Local Government Board, would hold an inquiry as to the alleged pollution of Keckwick Brook, at the Red Lion Hotel, Preston Brook, on Thursday, the 2nd October, at twelve o'clock noon. The Inspector would be prepared to receive the evidence of any persons inte- rested in the matter of the inquiry. CHARGE AGAINST OFFICIALS VISITING FEVER PATIENT'S. The deputy clerk mad a letter from Dr. MacLennan, of Runcorn, who complained of the conduct of two of the officials of the Authority with regard to a patient of his 17 years of age, daughter of Mr. Lightfoot, of Weston, who was suffering from typhoid fever. On the Bth Sep- tember a man describing himself as an inspector of nuisances called at the cottage and asked to see the patient. Mrs. Lightfoot told him the doctor had given orders that her daughter should be kept exceedingly quiet. He re- plied that he must see her, and thinking he had a right to do so, Mrs. Lightfoot permitted him to go upstairs. He sat by the bedside for a time and having made some remark about the position of the pillows went dossmstairs. The patient several times afterwards alluded to the visit of the Inspector by saying " he had hurt her head " or "made her head worse" and implored her mother not to allow him to sea her again. On the following Thursday this official called in company with a gentleman whom Mrs. Lightfoot was informed was a doctor, and who wanted to go upstairs. Mrs. Lightfoot objected, and be explained that it was his place to see the patient and he must do so. She told him that Dr. McLennan had strictly ordered that no one must be allowed to see the patient and that no official of any sort could against her will enter the sick room of her daughter unless he was provided with a writ for the pur- pose. After telling him this, and contrary to the mother's wish, he went upstairs to the patient's bedside, felt her pulse, asked to see the fever spots on her body and in short examined her. On the occasions when these officials visited the patient she was in a most critical condition. Her life was wavering in the balance and any undue excitement would be exceedingly dangerous to her. On each of the days following the visits, he found his patient distinctly worse and though for a short time she rallied the fever terminated fatally on Satur- day, 13th September. It was quite possible that her death might have been accelerated or hastened to some extent by any undue excitement arising in con- sequence of the visits. He (Dr. MacLennan) knew of no law .giving, the officials power to enter a sick room against the wishes of the tenants and contrary to the wishes of the medical man in attendatibe. —Dr. Adams said he had only just come home from his holidays and he opened a letter from Mr. MacLennan on Sunday. To this letter he had replied explaining exactly how the whole thing had arisen. 'The contention of Dr. MacLennan was absolutely correct. Neither the Medical Officer of Health nor any sanitary official had any right to enter the private apartment of any patient; but there was not a medical man within the Union with whom he had not a tacit understanding that he might exercise his discretion with regard to examining patients suffer- ing from infectious disease. He had explained this to Dr. MacLennan and he did not dream any further action would be taken in the matter. He had explained that his locum tenens (Dr. Melville) had visited the patient and had suggested an examination of the patient; which was demurred to on the part of the mother and that then he was rather surprised to hear, the Inspector suggested to Dr. Melville that it was really his duty to see the patient and under those circumstances a visit to the patient was made. He had explained to Dr. MacLennan that this was entirely improper and outside the powers conferred upon them by the Sanitary 'Act. He apologised to him , for the breach and requested Ihim to apologise to Mr. I Lightfoot. As to the insinuation contained in his letter —he did not suppose he meant it as an insinuation—he should be sorry to think that any medical man would use an insinuation of that kind. There would be no more detrimental effect upon the patient than there would every time Dr. MacLennan visited the house and exam- ined the patient. It was unworthy of a professional colleague to makean insinuation of that kind, and if Dr. MacLennan meant that insinuation it reflected upon him for all they did would be precisely what he would be compelled to do on his daily visit.—The Clerk: Then it was not yourself.—Dr. Adams :No, it was not me.—The Inspector admitted that he had examined the patient and contended that they had full power to do so in order to see whether it was typhoid fever or not.—Dr. Adams: That is quite a mistake. The Act only gives power to visit the spot.—Mr. Aaron: What has the Inspector to do? The Chairman: To visit the houseand see if it is in a sanitary condition.—Mr. Aaron: How can you 'tell when the , bedrooms are wrong.—Dr. Adams t It is for the Medical Officer. I may examine the bedroom but I cannot examine the'patient,

—ln answer to questions, Dr. Adams said the Inspector would only visit the place at the request of the medical officer. There was no doubt this was oneof those unfor- tunate cases of over zeal, and there was nothing to be said for it. There was scarcely a sanitary authority in the county, with any zeal about them, where something of this kind did not occur. He had been the medical officer for seven years and this was th,:: first time any- thing of this description had happened, and this had occurred through his locum tenens doing what he thought I to be his duty =instruction derived from the Inspector. —Mr. Mclntyre: Mr. Farrington did that which he had no right to do.—The Clerk: There is no doubt about that. —Mr. Aaron said there were some hovels in Weston that needed ransacking both upstairs and downstairs, and something should be done or there would be more fevers than there were.—The Chairman: He ha 8 power to inspect houses but not patients.—On the proposition of Mr. Brandreth, secoxded by Mr. Aaron, it was resolved that the Clerk reply to Dr. McLennan explaining the mat:..
FEVER OIITBREAYE,
The Medical Officer reported outbreaks of typhoid fever at Weston, Woods Row, Halton, and also scarlet fever at Weston. .
NEW HOUSES.
Certificates of occupation were granted with respect to number of new houses at Preston Brook. THE WATER SIMPLY OF RITDWORTH.

The Inspector presented a report with regard to the water supply of Great Budworth Village, which he said contained 60 houses four of which were farms, with a population of about 280 which included 179 adults and 101 children under 12 years of age. The present and only water supply for domestic purposes for the whole of the village is from a iunning pipe which is situate at the bottom of a very steep hill, and is known as "The Deane" and is 130 yards distant from the nearest house, and about 520 yards from the furthest house. The pre- sent yield of the pipe is 2,180 gallons in 24 hours, which ;3 a little 'over seven and a half gallons per head of the population. There was not the slightest doubt as to the quantity Or quality of the water, but it 'cannot by any means be considered to be within reasonable distance and an improved and more convenient supply is greatly needed, as it was a hardship and an expense to many of the inhabitants to have to procure their water from the present source.

div.head: ORDINATION OF REV. JOHN SIMPSON, OF RUNCORN. – –
div.p: ORDINATION OF REV. JOHN SIMPSON, OF RUNCORN. - -

An event of much interest to the members of the Congregational body of Runcorn and neighbour- hood took place at Bethesda Congregational Chapel, on Thursday evening, when the Rev. John Simpson, of Glasgow University, who has been the pastor of the church for several months past, was ordained according to the principles of the Congregational faith. The proceedings coinmenced with a tea party in the schoolroom, where a goodly company sat down to the excellent repast provided. Subsequently an adjournment was made to the sacred edifice adjoining and the assemblage was of ample proportions, the body of the chapel being well filled. After singing a hymn, prayer was offered by the Rev. Thomas Cole, of Garston, and the first and second lessons which followed were read by the;Rev. R. G. Hughes (Widnes), and the Rev. Dyer ;Bray (Frodsham), respectively. The Rev. H. Barnes, M.A., (Stockport), who conducted the proceed- ings at this point offered a few remarks, and introduced the Rev. S. B. Handley, of Stafford, to give an exposition' of church principles. In a powerful and eloquent address Mr. Handley expounded the principles and tenets of the Congregational denomination, and described their model of church government. The customary questions addressed to the church were then put by the Rev. F. Barnes, 8.A., of Chester, and Mr. W. Heatherinton, the secretary, explained what led Bethesda Church and con- gregation to invite Mr. Shnson to become their pastor. I Since Mr. Simpson commenced his pastorate, he said the congregations at St. Luke's Chapel had been much , larger, the mcnetary offerings had increased, the atten- dance at the monthly observance of the Lord's Supper had been larger, the week night meetings had been better attended, the church had added to the roll of member- ' ship, especially from the younger members of the con- gregation, and there were hopeful and earnest assurances of great activity of all the various forms of Christian work in Which the church and congregation were engaged. The Chairman then put the questions to the pastor. The first was: Favour us with some account of your rellei- ous life, especially of your conversion to Christ.-111.r. Simpson, in the course of his reply, said looking back at his past life he could not distinctly point to any day on which he was converted. Brought up under religious influences, he was early taught to love the Lord. Amongst the first things he could remember was that of his mother teaching him to read the Bible. Through the sacred in- fluences of his home, guided by the tender love of a devoted mother, he was early taught to love Christ and pray to him. That love,planted by her, had grown with his growth, strengthened with his strength, until it had, now become master of his heart. In answer to the second question" What led you to chcose the Christian ministry as the vocation of your life," Mr. Simpson said the desire to become a Christian minister had always been most powerful in him. It seemed to have been wrapped in his very being and grown with him until it was to-day the all absorbing passion of his souLto which all other desires were subordinate. He felt that he had been called by God to this work. To the next question " Why have You decided to exercise your ministry amongst the Congregationalists," Mr. Simpson replied that he was not a bigot and he desired not to be thought such. There was something to admire in every religious body if they only looked for it. In his youth he was surrounded by other than Congregational principles and influences. The great influence of Presbyterianism, the religion of his fathers, was brought to bear upon him, but the principles of Congregationalism seemed to him nmre in accordance with the nature of man himself and ,the will of God. He adhered to the congregational church because it was democratic in Government, and spiritual in nature ; because in it man was respected as a man—as an individual ; and because the opinion of the poorest man in the church was as much respected and listened to as that of the elder or priest. There were in their Church no little popes whose word was to be taken as infallible. Christ was their only head—the supreme head whom they acknowledged. Perhape the ,greatest reason of all was because in their church the christian man is free to follow the dictates of his own conscience and had more liberty to preach the truth as he found it. The Congregational church was a spiritual democracy under the direCtion of Christ and His Word, and for that reason he decided to select the ministry of the Congrega- tional church. In conclnsiOn,Mr. Simpson was asked what faith beheld and meant to make the basis of his preach- ing, and said his creed was a very simple one. It was, God is love, God is our Father, and thouah there were many mysteries in this life,many things which made the heart sore and tears spring to the eyes, yet God was making all things work together, not perhaps for our happiness, but most certainly for our good. God was in Christ Jesus reconciling the world to Him. Christ was his Saviour and the Saviour of mankind; sin was his enemy; Christ came to save him from it; and round the Cross of Self-sacrifice he threw his arms and there he took his stand. The ordination prayer was now offered by the Rev. R, J. Ward, of St. Helens, and the Rev. Fred

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS,
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse. Colonel Ashton presided and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Mclntyre, Brandreth. Aaron, Lewis, Hewitt, Stokes, Bate, Bretherton, Weir, Knowles, W. Fisher, J. Whitlow, Priestner, H. Linaker (clerk), and H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk).—The Clerk reported that the balance in the Treasurer's hands was £1,984 17s. 9d. All the calls had been paid. The following contracts were accepted for the ensuing half year :—Groceries, Kyckl, Frodsham ; carting, William Grounds, Aston; clothing, Unsworth Bros., Runcorn; drapery, Thomas Wright, Halton; boots and shocw, Shar- rocks, Runcorn ; coffins, Lightfoot; butcher's meat, Gill, Warrington ; wines and spirits, Jones.

div.head: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CLASSES.
div.p: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CLASSES.

- - - _ The ninth session of these classes was inaugur- ated on Tuesday evening, when a public meeting was held in Ellesmere-street schoolroom.. There was a good attendance. Mr. J. J. nowitt presided and in opening the proceedings proclaimed himself an old sol-fnist, and described the system as the English grammar of music. A great many people advo- cated the old Notation in preference to tonic sol-fa, but it must be remembered that these people had been educated in that system, and had they gone through a I series of lessons in the sol-fa method, and acquired the system thoroughly the transitions to the old notation would have been few and far between. Since the commencement of these classes, Mr. Holford had taught 510 persons a knowledge of music, and 166 had taken certificates. The annual average was 63 students and 21 certificates obtained. This state of affairs was highly creditable to the teacher and to tl-e students, but he did not think they were satisfied In Mineorn they had a population of about 20,000:and there ought to be about 5,000 people taking lessons in tonic sol-fa music. (Applause.) He strongly advised elderly people, middle-aged people, and young people, to acquire a knowledge of tonic sol-fa music as an indoor recreation, so that they might take their proper part in the sacred music at the churches and chapels. There was nothing so excrusciating to a musician as to hear a tolerably coarse voice taking the soprano part in the church. (Laughter.) If anything should be well done, it should be praise to the great "I am," and after a course of tonic sol-fa people would be able to take a more intelligent and graceful part in praise to the maker of us all. (Applause.) In conclusion Mr. Hewitt commented upon the simplicity of the system, and the ease with which It could be acquired, and strongly urged all present to join the classes.— Mr. R. Griffiths, G. and L.T.S.C., secretary of the Tonic Sol-fa College, Landon, delivered a speech on the advantages of the tonic sol-fa method, illustrating his points in a very apposite manner, and instituted a criti- cal comparison between the old notation with consider- able point and humour. Speeches were also delivered by Mr. E. Mason, F T.S.C., and A. Mos. T.C.L., director,of music to Ilurslem School Board, and Mr, Skaife, of St. Helens. During the evening a well-trained choir ren- dered several glees and part songs in capital style, and also sang, at first sight, a piece of music, written for the occasion by Mr. Mason, a performance which evoked loud applause. Mr. J. Holford, the teacher of the classes, who is also the musical instructor to Widnes School Board, was the conductor, and at the conclusion of the meeting that gestleman and the choir were cordially thanked for their services.

div.head: RUNCORN REVISION COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN REVISION COURT.

On Wednesday Mr. Clement Elphinstone Lloyd, revising barrister, held a court at Runcorn for the purpose of revising the voters lists for the Runcorn, Halton and Aston polling districts. Mr. W. Hand- ley represented the Liberals, and Mr. G. J. Hughes assisted by Mr. A. Lightburn apppeared for the Conservatives.
8111 L. B. \TALKER.

The name ol Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, brewer, appeared on the owners lists for Runcorn North, Mr. Handley objected on the ground that the firm was now converted into a limited liability company.—The name was struck out.

_ MLINCOUN 130TTLING COMPANY. Mr. Alfred Lightburn, of Greenway-road, claimed for a vote as tenant of premises in Brindley-st., used as a bottling stores.—Mr. Handley objected, because the premises were not rated of sufficient value to give a qualification to more than one person and being the Runcorn Bottling Company there must be more than one in it.—Mr. Hughes : Who is rated.—Mr. Sutton : Mr. A. Lightburn.—Mr. Hughes: Mr. Lightburn is the ten- ant of this place, he pays the rent, and he is rated • and he trades under the name of the Runcorn Bottling born- pany.—The Barrister : Is it not Wregistered company under the Companies Act.—Mr. Hughes: No sir. Mr. Lightburn simply trades under the name and he holds the license in his own name.—The Barrister: What does he want a license for P—Mr. Hughes : Bottling and sell- ing—Mr. Handley. The license must be put in some persons name, I take it:—Mr. Hughes: But still it is ' additional proof that Mr. Lightburn is tenant and that there is no company.—Mr. Handley: On the signboard Mr. Lightburn is stated simply secretary.—The Barris- ter : Mr. Lightburn says he is the Company and he is the person who knows most about it.—Mr. Handley : There ' was no evidence before that it was not a Company.— The Barrister: It is a very reasonable objection.—The vote was allowed. THE SPIRIT OF THE ACT.

Superintendent Large claimed to be placed on the list of Parliamentary voters, in respect'of his occupation of a house at the police station.—Mr. Handley did not wish to object to the name, but drew attention to the fact that the premises were not entered on the rate book.— Mr. Sutton said it was struck out of the book by the Assessment Committee on appeal by the county authorities. There were police stations about to be erected in various parts of the county and it would be well to know the law on the subject,in order that they might know how to act.—The Barrister having looked up the law upon the subject, said he was in considerable doubt as to whether there was any proper ground of exemption from local rates of a house attached to a police station, as it was not crown propPrty.—After some discussion the Barrister decided that he would act in the spirit Of the act and allow the vote.

AN ABSENT OVERSEER. When the list for Aston should have been revised it transpired that Mr. Robinson, the assistant overseer was not present.—Mr. Handley said as there was no conten- tious matter, Mr. Robinson thought the lists could be revised in his absence.—The Barrister said Mr. Robinson was a schoolmaster and ought to know the law. He must attend. Mr. Robinson was accordingly telegraphed for and at a later stage appeared.

FIGURES. From a table compiled by Mr. W. Sutton, the assistant overseer for Runcorn, it appeared that in Runcorn North there. were 220 owners, last year 221 ; 2,351 Parliamen- tary and County Council voters, last year 2,194 ; 22 Parliamentary voters only, last year 20 ; 241 County Council voters only, last year 237 ; 44 lodgers, last year 76. The total number of voters In 1890 was 2,878, last year 2,527; increase 351. In Runcorn South there were 99 owners, last year 86 ; 725 Parliamentary and County Council voters, last year 613 ; one voter, Parliamentary only, last year 4; 83 voters, County Council only, last year 77 • 23 lodgers, last year 23. Th 3 totals were, this year 931',last year 805 ; increase 126. The total electorate of the town was 3,809, being an increase of 477 over the previous year. CONGRATULATORY AND APPRECIATIVE. At the close of the Revision, Mr. Hughes, on behalf of the party he represented, expressed his thanks to the Revising Barrister for the very impartial manner in which he had conducted the Revision, and for the cour- tesy he had extended to both himself and Mr. Handley, and he trusted that he would for many years preside over that Court.—Mr. Handley expressed his thanks on behalf a the party he represented, and said he felt sure

that if every Court was presided over with the same ability as the Northwich Court was there would be far more satisfaction expressed at the decisions of the barris- ter than was often the case as they saw from the public papers, and he trusted Mr. Lloyd would preside over the Court for many years.iz-The Barrister, in-acknowledging- - the kind expressions, ..did he always tried toxic) his duty in the spirit of the Acts for lie thought ev4yone who could be said to be entitled to vote should ceitainly have 1 a vote. He had been very greatly assisted in his work 1 by the manner in which the respective agents had pre- , sented the cases ;and in fact, were it not for that assist- ance, it would be almost impossible to get on with the work as it was got on with in the Northwich Division. He should like to bear testimony to the efficiency with which the overseers throughout the division prepared • the lists ' • in no division of the county were they better prepared. He hoped if he were appointed another year he would meet the same agents and that they would have as pleasant and genial a revision as they had had since he had presided over the Court. The Court sat from 10.15 a.m. to 3.0 p.m., with an interval for dinner, and in that time the lists for the Runcorn, Halton, and Aston polling districts, which con- tain one-third of the whole of the voters of the division, were revised.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held on Thursday afternoon, at the Work- house, Whiston. There were present—Mr. W. Tyrer art the chair), the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. E. Syder, J. Whalley, C. B. Johnson, G. Davies, J. Peover, J. Marsh, R. A. Graves, J. Mercer, W. Middlehurst, J. Ran- son, P. Longton, W. Borrows, J. Burchall, Mr. F. Stapleton-Bretberton, J.P. (es-officio), and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk). WORKHOUSE INMATES.—Mr. Hale, master of the Work- house, reported that there were 484 inmates in the nork- housethis week, 487 last week, against 486 in the corresponding week last year. There had been 68 vagrauts relieved during the week, against 54 in the corresponding week last year. THE CHAIRMAN.—Mr. Davies stated that the chairman of the board (Major Wareing), was sorry he could not possibly be present at the meeting that afternoon, in consequence of an important business engagement. RE-APPOINTKENTS.—The Local Government Board wrote consenting to the employment of Mr. William Cooper as medical officer of the lower Widnes district until the 29th September, 1891, at a salary of £7O. The Board also saw no objection to the re-appointment of Mr. Robert George Waterman as assistant relieving officer, at a salary of £l5 per annum. THE NEW OFFICES AT Sr HELENS.—The Clerk said that some time ago the St. Helens Guardians were ordered to get in tenders for alterations at the relief offices at St. Helens. That was done, and Mr. Middlehurst found the tender of Messrs. Crake and Marsh was the lowest, and instructions were given by Mr. Middlehurst to that firm to go on with the work.—Mr. Middlehurst said that be- fore he gave the order he submitted the tender to the rest of the committee, and they were unanimous. He moved that the seal of the board be attached to the contract of Messrs. Crake and Marsh.—The motion was adopted. COUNTY MAGISTRATES WANTED.—MY. Middlehurst stated that Mr. Barton, relieving officer, had considerable I difficulty at times to obtain the removal of a lunatic to the asylum, in consequence of not being able to get at a county magistrate. He repeatedly had to go down to the works of Messrs. Pilkington, but of course at times he could not find them, and he had on some occasions to drive beyond Prescot to Mr. Pilkington's. He would advise that they should try and get Alderman McKechnie, of St. Helens, created a county magistrate. He could readily be got at his new residence, The Grange, Eccleston. If he was appointed a county justice it would be a great saving of time and expense.—The Chairman did not think it was for a Board of Guardians to advise the ap- pointment of justices.—The subject then dropped. A NEW INSPECTOR.—The Clerk said that the assistant wasasic oLnocathle Govpret snenze nh to tB oo an rl unless ei inspector, Aiairn.s Mreoqourisreemd to, him any questions he did not desire to be present at the meeting.—None of the Guardians expressed a desire to ask any questions. This was the only business. .

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BT AN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BT AN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

That the Chemical Union is practically an accom- plished fact, and while it may be a very good thing from a manufacturers' point of view, the workmen, and the subordinates generally, do not favour the project. That the Union will have a bearing upon the in- corporation of Widnes, which will now not meet with opposition from any quarter, and can be quickly carried through. That Dr. O'Keeffe, who has been the pioneer on this important local question, will rejoice when he can speak of the borough of Widnes. ' That, of course, he will be one of those placed on the elevation of the Aldermanic Bench, not only for his advocacy of the measure, but for his long and valuable services to the ratepayers on the Local. Board. That on the ninth of the next month the first of a series of University extension lectures on " Wealth and Industry," will be given by the talented lecturer, Mr. H. L. Smith, BA., B.Sc. That the subject is of the utmost importance to working-men, and, as the price charged by the committee is the lowest possible and well within the means of all, it is to be hoped that large audi- ences will assemble. That pupil teachers and monitors are admitted at a reduced rate, and that customary arrangements will be made for an examination of students. That after this week the familiar form of Captain Clark will be missed from Weston Point Pier. He has been the manager and harbour master for the Weaver Trustees at that port for very many years, and he will carry away to his new house in Devon- shire the good wish of numerous friends and acquaintances That the revision of the lists of voters for the Northwich division is at an end, and when the results are cast up,there will be shown a considerable gain for the Liberal party.

div.head: L Y 3131.
div.p: "HIGHLY COMMENDED."—Mr. Joseph Stott, of Lymm, at the sixth annual exhibition of foals sired by Lord Egerton's horses, held at Tattoo Park on Saturday, was highly commended for a nice chestnut roan filly. AnnvErissaY SERVICES. —At the Congregational Church, on Sunday, the anniversary sermons were preached, morning and evening, by the Rev. T. W. Rinn, M.A., of Stockport. The congregation was large at each service. In the afternoon a cantata, entitled "Daniel," was given by the choir and friends, Mr. A. Leather pre- siding at the organ. The collections, which were taken on behalf of the Sunday school funds, realized £l9. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL. —The ha.rve4t thanks- giving services were held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, on Sunday, when sermons were preached, after- noon and evening by Mr. J. Manley, of Manchester. The little chapel had been tastefully decorated for the occa- sion with a profusion of choice fruits, flowers, and plants, and grain. The congregations were very good,the chapel in the evening being filled. Special hymns were sung at each service, the choir being led by Mr. Edward Mairs. Miss Florrie Shore officiated at the organ. The decorators were—Miss Katie Guest, Statham; Messrs. E. Mairs, G. L. Welferd, Astbury, T. Mairs; the Rev. W. Evans, and others. On Monday evenine,in the same place of worship, a service of song, entitled "Two Autumn Evenings" was rendered by the choir. There was a large congregation, and the piece was creditably performed. Duets were rendered by Mrs. Pearson and Mr. T. Appleton and Miss Littler and Mr. T. Appleton, whilst Mr. E. Mairs contri- buted a solo. The choir was under the conductorship of Mr. J. Appleton, Miss F. Shore presiding at the organ. The connective readings were given by Mr. G. L. Welford. The collection, which was in aid of the new chapel build- ing fund, together with the amount realized at the Sunday services, amounted to £B.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

DRINK AND VIOLTEXCH. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Patrick Fallon was charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly in Rose-yard, on Saturday night, and with hav- ing assaulted his wife, son, and daughter. Ile was fined 10s. and costs. It was his 37th appearance. W. White and John Newen were each fined 10s. and costs for drunkenness and assaults on police officers. When ar- rested White struck Constable Wood in the mouth, and Nevrens assaulted Constable Griffiths._
ONI WAY OF GETTIWG A DIZINS.

-- On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, a man named Thomas Noon, described as • " professional singer," was charged with stealing beer by means of a trick. He and two other men went into a public-house in Buttermarket-St., and prisoner called for three half- pints of beer. He afterwards tried to leave the house, but the landlord intercepted him and demanded pay- ment for the beer. This was refused, and prisoner became violent. The magistrates sent him to prison for 2.1 days.

FATHER AND SON IN THS Dom. On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, Peter Baguley, and his son Thomas, who live In Rose-yard. were together brought up in custody on a charge of drunkenness. Evidence was given by the police to the effect that the two were fighting together in Rose-yard, and created a great disturbance. The elder prisoner said that his son came home drunk, and began to beat his mother. He (the father) then proceeded to put him out of the house. On the other hand, tha son blamed his father for what had occurred. Peter Baguley, who made his 88th appearance, was fined ss. and costs, and Thomas Baguley was sent to prison for a month. A "Tnicxv " THEFT IN • PAWNBIZOKSR'S SHOP. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, a married woman named Mary Alice Healy, living in Playdoek-st., was charged with stealing by means of a trick from the shop of Elizabeth Tunstall, pawnbroker, Winwick-st., a bundle containing a shawl and a dress, value 55., the property of Ann Taylor. Prisoner went tothe pawnshop to pledge some boots. Taylor was there at the same I time, having come to redeem a shawl and a dress. The bundle containing those articles was brought forward by an assistant and claimed by the prisoner, who went straight across the road and pledged the shawl at another pawnbroker's. She was afterwards apprehended by P.S. Bowen, and in reply to the charge, said "I had sonic drink. I don't know where the frock is. I mast have lost it when I went to pawn the shawl." A fine of 40s. and costs was inflicted, the default being one month with hard labour. JOHN 'WARRINGTON IN TROUBLE AGAIN. Among the prisoners brought before the Warrington! Bench on Thursday was the foundling John Warrington, who was charged under the Vagrancy Act with sleeping out. Ile was discovered at an early hour in the morning lying on an ashtub on School-brow. The attention of a police officer was called to the lad, who, the constable was informed, had been sleeping in ashpits for the last three weeks. He had had a pistol in his possession, but that had been taken from him by the Pa.dg,ate police. The Chief Constable explained that it was a toy pistol. Warringtm said he had given 4d. for it. The Chief Con- stable also mentioned that the lad had many times run away from Padgate lndustral School, and on one occa- sion he rode from Warrington to Liverpool on the buffer of an engine. The Bench decided to remand the lad, in order that the parochial authorities might be communicated with. He was again brought up yesterday morning, when Mr. Harbourne, relieving officer, said that he had been discharged from the Clio, and had been sent to Denbigh lunatic asylum. He was afterwards in the Workhouse, but took his discharge. The Chief Constable thought prisoner was not responsible for his actions, but Mr. Harbourne said that the doctors did not think he was a fit person to be in the asylum. The Chief Constable: He used to have a pipe and a dog. Constable Chantler He's a very heavy smoker. (Laugh- ter.) The magistrates ultimately sent Warrington to prison for a month. SERIOUS CHARGE OF Taarr. Yesterday, at the Warrington Police Court, a man named Joseph Birchall, alias Smithson, alias Williams, was brought up on remand on a charge of stealing from the officers' quarters at Orford Barracks, between 9 p.m. on April 18th and 10 a.m. on April 19th, an overcoat, value £3, belonging to Captain Stapleton Cotton ; also withstealing from a bedroom at the Patten Arms Hotel, between 3 p.m. on July 29th, and 1 a.m. on July 30th, a brown leather portmanteau, containing four shirts, 15 collars, a gold scarf ring, a pair of patent leather boots, brown coat, pair of trousers, gold and silver sleeve links, gold pm, and other articles, together value £B, the pro- perty of Mr. F. C. Morley, a commercial traveller.—John Dickenson, tailor, Cartwright-st., was charged with re- ceiving the portmanteau, knowing it to have been stolen. —Mr. Arthur Browne appeared to prosecute, and Mr. P. Davies was for Dickenson.—From a statement made by the Chief Constable when the case was first before the Court on Monday, it appeared that on the night of the 18th April the prisoner drove a fare to the Barracks. The next morning, an overcoat, belonging to Captain Cotton, was missed. A few days later it was pledged by the prisoner at a Salford pawnshop. On Saturday last the prisoner went to the shop to redeem the coat, and was then given into custody. Whilst at the Bridewell he made certain admissions, which caused Inspector Spinks and P.C. Monaghan to go to his home, where they found part of the proceeds of the Patten Arms robbery. At the residence of the prisoner's father-in-law, Dickenson more of the stolen property was discovered. Yesterday the -case was remanded, Dickenson being admitted to bail.

div.head: MINOR. CASES.
div.p: MINOR. CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), Alderman Davies, and Alderman Holmes. _ . _

DRUNILENNESS.—The following persons were dean with for this offence :—Sarah Wilkinson, Market-place, Satur- day afternoon, fined ss. including costs ,• Martin Kelly, Buttermarket-st., Saturday night, fined ss. including costs; William Bailey, Scotland-road, Sunday night, fined ss. and costs; Richard Bailey, Scotland-road, Sun- day night, fined ss. and costs; and John Smith, Wilders- pool-causeway, Saturday night, fined ss. including costs. _

PITCH AND Toss.—Peter Hanlon, a lad was charged 1 with playing pitch and toss in Crown-st. on Sunday morning.—The Bench ordered the prisoner to be detained in custody until six p.m. SLEEPING OllT.—George Cotton, who had been found asleep in an outbuilding in Church-st., was discharged.— William Yates pleaded guilty to sleeping in the Market abed. He was sent to prison for 14 days without hard labour.—Thomas Kearns was committed to prison for seven days for sleeping in a shed at Arpley. ALLEGED NIIISANCE.—David Walsh was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to abate a nuisance which was alleged to exist at 116, 118, 120, and 122, Winwick-road.—lnspector Norman said that the yards and outhouses were in a foul and defective condition. Defendant was served with a notice to abate. He had the outhouses attended to, but not the yards. He had seen green water standir g in holes in the yard.—Mr. Arthur Browne, for the defendant, called the tenants of the houses, who denied that any nuisance existed, and explained that the water spoken of was blue water. In- spector Norman paid his visit on washing day.—The case was dismissed. A DEFECTIVE CANAL BOAT.—PObert Dough was sum- moned for keeping a canal boat in a defective condition. William Cooper was summoned as owner for allowing the boat to be so kept.—They were ordered to pay a fine of Is. and ss. costs each. MAINTENANCE Cssfs.—William Dennett, dascribed as a fle cutter, was summoned in respect of a sum of £2, arrears due from him with respect to the maintenance of his son on the training ship Clio.—The defendant : It is a great shame to send my boy away when he ought to be working for me. He was only sent away for neglecting to go to school. I consider iE a great hardship; there will always be boys who will not go to schools. I think the law is extremely hard.—The Mayor: You should get into the House of Commons, then, and endeavour to alter the law.—Defendant: The Secretary of State the other day sent a letter to the newspapers condemning severity in carrying out the education laws.—The Chief Constable: The lad is one of Mr. Riley's incorrigibles.—Defendant : Not half as incorrigible as he (Mr. Riley) is. (Laughter.) —The Chief Constable said he had been asked to press the case at the request of the Government Inspector in London.—Defendant : Do you want to starve me and the family to death 7—The Chief Constable replied that he tad no such intention, but the law must be obeyed.—De-

fendant : The lad ought to be bringing me in 10s. or 'As. a week. Instead of that I have to pay to his mainter .anot. —Defendant was ordered to pay 2s. 6d. a week, or . go to prison for 14 days.—Henry Thompson was oThdered to pay 2s. a week towards the maintenance of his who is detained on board the ship Clio, and Michael Feeny, whose son is an inmate of St. A-sme,s Industrial School, Liverpool, was ordered to pay a .similar amount. MISCELLANEOUS .—Patrick Gillick, " tor allowing a cart to remain in Market-st. longer tha in ry for loading or unloading, was fined Bs. 6d. • , Charles Thornley. Thos. Dakin, John Holden, and M; . duel Mitchell, for throwing stones in the streets to the . 1, danger of passengers, were heed 38. dd. efhik„,,i; M" ',sad Kelly, James Lawless, Henry and Patrick McDonough, playing 'rat igpgiitchns,anJadmcoss..oi_ •4 ~ii .tied' .3s. 6d. each, and James Kenny, charged with -.owing his house chimney to be on fire on the 14th Septe ,„. r. ,mise ordered to pay a shilling including costs.—Jarr,e3 Hayes was summoned for allowing his son, who is or3m six years of age, to sell newspapers in the streets_ y --John Ward was summoned for a similar offence. Tnhe, case against Hayes was dismissed; Ward was fined 44. 68.
TUFSDAY.—Befare Aldermen Davies, and Harrison, - - -
Ebnd Mr. Garnett.

FELONY.—Andrew Wood, charged with having stolen a coat and vest from the lodging house of Mary Clarke, on Town Hill, on the 21st inst., was fined 20s. and costs. DRUNKENNESS—For this °fence James Taylor was fined ss. andcosts.—Thomas Burke, who also assaulted two constables, was sent to prison for a month, and Mar- garet Dooney was sent to prison for a fortnight.—John Mullholland and Ellen Rabbit were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Sohn Fairclough, Alderman Holmes, and Alderman Chandley. REFUSING TO Qum—Michael Melia was charged with having been drunk on tha previous day, and with hay- ing refused to quit the Rope and Anchor Inn when requested. He was fined 103. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. A DESEATER.—Frank Mackley, who admitted being a deserter from the 2nd East Kent Regiment, stationed at Aldershot, was remanded to await escort. &soot. ArratinANca.—Several persons were summoned for neglecting to send their children regularly to school, and the usual fines were imposed. Mr. George Riley prosecuted on behalf of the School Attendance Com- mittee. THURSDAY .—Before Alderman Sutton.

SLEEPING Our.—John Williams and Mary Unsworth, were summoned for sleeping in Arpley-fields on the night before. The former was sent to prison for seven days, and the latter for fourteen days. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gornall. SLEEPING CWT.—Gilbert and John Warburton, youths, were charged with sleeping in a shed at Arpley, on Wednesday night. Gilbert Warburton,who was described as incorrigible, was sent to prison for a month, and John Warburton was allowed to go on promising to obtain work. THEFT BY A Bor.—Joseph Frangleton (11), pleaded guilty to having stolen a florin from the shop till of Robt. Kennedy, Crossley-st., on the previcus morning. He was ordered to be detained in custody until the following evening, and to have six strokes with the birch rod. DRIINHENNESS.—For this offence Elizabeth Smith was sent to prison for a month, with hard labour. MAINTENANCE CASE.—Thomas Bailey was ordered to pay is. per week towards the maintenance of his 9011 on the ship Clio. CHARGES or ASSAULT.—James Gleeson was summoned for having assaulted Rosannah Finn, on the 20th inst. Rosannah Finn and her daughter were also summoned for assaulting Mrs. Gleeson. The cases were dismissed, each party having to pay 4s. costs.—William Hunt and Charles Darbyshire were summoned for assaulting each other on the 21st inst. The cases were adjourned. THREATS.—Catherine Gerrard was summoned for hav- ing used threats towards Mary Smith, on the 22nd inst. She was ordered to be bound over.
WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before Alderman Crosfield.

MrscErAmeous.—Two lads named Laurence Dunn (16) and Walter Parr (14) were charged with stealing two silk pocket handerchiefs, value 7s. the property ot Messrs. Rylands and Co., of Go'borne, on the 19th inst. The evidence was to the effect that a traveller for the firm engaged the lads on Saturday to wheel his handcart, and he subsequently missed the pocket handkerchiefs. He charged the lads with having stolen them, and they admitted the offence. The prisoners were remanded to the Newton Petty Sessions, bail being granted. At the same court, on Saturday, before Mr. James Tinsley, Benjamin Smith, for being drunk and disorderly at Golborne, was fined ss. and costs,
FRIDAY. —Before Mr. E. Greenall.

VAGRANcy.—Mary France and Henry Wilson were brought up charged with vagrancy at Poulton, and with having done damage to a haystack. Both prisoners, who have been convicted over twenty times for various offences, were fined 10s, and costsm regard to each case, or 28 days' imprisonment.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. F.-131—Goasa-- ge-andlifr. H. Craskotl. jun. Danwir.—Elizabeth Glasheen, Caroline-st., and Bernard Cruse, St. Helens were each tined ss. and costs for being drunk.
SLEEPING Ouv.—Michael Mannion, a tramp, was charged with sleeping in the Widnes Alkali Works, and he was discharged on promising to leave the town.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. James Handley and G. L. Wigg. DRUMS AND DISORDBRLY.—Jane Butterworth and Bridget Rawlinson were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs for this offence, and Thomas Sutton was fined 10s. and costs. FIRING FIREWORKS.—Joseph Woodfine, Martin Gilligan, Levi Bothwell, and William Hartley young boys, were summoned for firing fireworks on the Belvedere on the 13th inst.—On promising not to offend again, the defendants were discharged. FooTes.ru Onsranornm—John ,Christie a young man was fined 6d. and costs for obstructing the 'footpath in Bridge-st., by loitering thereon. SCISOOL BOARD Cases.—Several persons were sum- moned for not sending their children regularly to school and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case.

A VIOLENT PAllPHR.—Richard Bilton, a deaf mute,was brought up on remand charged with having absconded from the workhouse with clothes belonging to the Union. Mr. A. Linaker who prosecuted, said it was impossible to make the prisoner understand the charge, or he would have been accused of assaulting the Master, Mr. Cunnah. —The prisoner was discharged and taken to the work- house. PROPOSED TO ASSAITLT.—George Gilbert, formerly employed on the Ship Canal, pleaded guilty to assaulting a woman named Ann Scott. It was alleged that he had ' struck the woman on the face blackening one of her eyes.—The prisoner, who said he received great provoca- tion, was fined 20s. including costs or in default a fort- night's hard labour. THEFT OF A COA7.—John Burns, a labourer, was charged with having stolen a coat from the shop of Arnold Unsvrorth, of High-st., on Saturday night. It was proved that the prisoner had given the coat to a girl named Mary Stanton, of Granville-st., to pledge. The prisoner was remanded in order that his antecedents might be ascertained.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. H. Wade Deacon, and Lieut.
Col. Gasket'.
DRUNKENNESS.-Dwi:r-idi&,M;-, of Violet-street, was fined ss. and costs and James Longshaw, of Warrington 10s. and costs, for this offence. _ _

FIREWORKS IN THE STnewr.:-Andrew M'Cann, a boy of Sankey-street, was summoned for discharging fire- works in Waterloo-road. On promising not to offend again he was dismissed. FOOTPATH Oesmucriox.—Richard Tebbutt, draper, Waterloo-road, pleaded guilty to obstructing the foot- path by placing a quantity of oilcloth there. He was fined ss. and costs.

BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—JuIia Quinn, WalMSley-St., and Mary Mularkey, Chapel Entry, were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, for creat- ing a breach of the peace. ASSAULT AT DrrroN.—Anastasia Stafford, charged Mary Ann Rimmer, of Ditton, with assaulting her on the 20th inst. by striking her on the face. The defendant was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. BREACH OF THE HIGHWAY ACTS.—James Murphy, Wid- nes-road, was fined 10s. and costs for leaving his horse and cart an unreasonable time in front of the C.istle 1 Hotel.

RESISTING A Cosisrarax.—Margaret Healey, Charlotte- st., and Mary Ann Murph7, Sutton's-lane, were charged with resisting and assaulting P.C. Moore. On Saturday evening Moore arrested a man for fighting, and while he was struggling with his prisoner, the defendants seized him and resisted him to that extent the man escaped from custody.—Each defendant was fined 2s. 6d. and costS.

IN A TRUANT Scnooz.—William Melton, 37, Elizabeth- St., plumber, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the support of his son who is an inmate of the Highway Truant School.—The defendant refused to pay because the child was taken without his knowledge and against his will.—Tke Bench made an order for 2s. a week.

- UNJUST Scm.Es.—John Barton, Peel-st., was summoned for having in his possession a potato scale which was un- just. -Mr. Johnstone,inspector of weights and measures, said the scales were 5 drachms against the purchaser.— Mr. A. Browne, who defended, said the case was a very trivial one, and the Bench being of the same opinion dis- missed it.

ASSAIILTS.—Kate Bailey a girl, of 42, Milton-st., was summoned for assaulting a married woman named Jane Ingram. There was a cross summons. The parties are neighbours, and had had a general ,quarrel. The Bench dismissed the girl and fined the woman ss. and costs.

WARRINGTON v. Sr. HELENS.—The return fixture be- tween these clubs was played at Warrington on Saturday. Neither side was fully represented. The home team in- flicted a severe defeat. Winning the toss, Crosfield and Lawton faced Joseph Simm and J. Marsh. At 13 Lawton was bowled. Smith scored four out of 23 put on during his stay. Crosfield was next out for a well-played 29. Jolley should have caught a short leg off on first ball, after which he scored 11. Clarke by vigorous hitting scored 26—four 4's. Jefferson, like Jolley, gave a very easy chance first ball, and then settled down to pretty ' cricket, scoring 16 before he was beaten by A. Simm, who had gone on in place of his brother at 82. The in- flings closed for 105. St. Helens, with an hour and a half to bat, never had a chance of saving the match, as ' Jolley was simply unplayable, and the greatest caution had to be exercised with Lawton's deliveries'. Only Marsh reached double figures (14). his defence was very good. Two of the St. Helens men fell to splendid catchee in,the slips. Both were taken by Jolley with his left hand. Score :

Wantintozox Siscown v. Nnvrros.—Played at Newton on Saturday. Newton won the toss and Hindley and Longton opened, the latter being quickly caught in the long field, and Hindley bowled by a beauty from Bell, the batsman doubting whether the wind had not blown the bail off. Heaton played a steady game but found no one to stand with him against the fast bowler, nine wickets being down for 51 runs. Owing to an easy chance being missed (which nearly cost the visitors the match), the last wicket put on 20 runs. Bell's analysis reads 18 overs, 5 maidens' 23 runs, for live wickets. On the visitors going in to bat Adamson was splendidly caught in the slips, and Unsworth bowled by one which came in a lot from the off (three wickets for 23). The fourth wicket added 15 when Jolley was bowled by a big break back. Brown was hitting away merrily all the time he was in, but no one stayed long with him, and eight wickets were down for 60, and things did not look so rosy for the visitors. But on Parry joining Brown both batsmen hit out at everything, and, with a large slice of luck, soon put the issue beyond doubt, Warrington win- ning by six runs. The visitors were without a wicket keeper. After the match the players sat down to the cop- ital knife and fork tea at the Pied Bull, to which ample justice was done, especially by the Warringtonians, who were justly elated on bringing the present season to such a successful close.
