div.p: FOOTBALL.

.„* Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

Iturstootur Honaers v. Dirrox 'Nos.—Played on Satur- day at Runcorn. Score :—Hornets: one goal, three tries, two minors; Ditton : one try, two minors. WATERLOO WHITE SPAR. (Runcorn) 17. SIMI/EY-ST. Raxosas.—This match was played on the ground of the former, and resulted in a win for the Stars by 1 goal snd 1 try to 1 try. A. Dyer scored a try, which was con- verted into a goal by P. Green. Green scored another, which he failed to convert. Gough scored the try for the Rangers. WIDNES "A" TRAM v. BOOPLII WASPS. The Bootle Wasps opened their seAson on Saturday, at the Bootle North Park, against the" A" team of the Widnes Football ; Club. Just on half time, Tonkins crossed over, and ; Foster kicked a grand goal from the place. The interval r arrived with the score—Widnes one goal, two tries, and five minors to Bootle nil. Final score: Widnes " A," one goal, two tries, and five minors; Bootle Wasps, one try, and one minor.

WARRINGTON " A" v. SWINTON" A."—The above match was played on the ground of the latter en Saturday in sultry weather, before a moderate assemblage of on- lookers. Warrington started with the sun in their faces, and they at once rushed into their opponents' territory. For some time the game partook of a loose scambling nature, Lawless and Mather by some smart play getting the ball to the home line. Ultimately the Swinton for- wards succeeded in getting the oval well out of danger, but after Sampson had cleverly returned, a kick by the same player was allowed to roll dead. Following the drop out the home forwards, amongst whom Hotchkiss and Bradburn were prominent, gained a considerable advantage, the leather being taken rapidly to the oppo- site end, where Sampson saved. Although some capital play by Lawless and Webster relieved, Hotchkiss, by a strong burst, was looking extremely dangerous until Webster by an effective tackled stopped his progress. Bdge lost ground by trying to round his opponents, and then Lawless threw to Daniels, whose strong kick went dead. The drop out was of little advantage to the home side, Davies, Byres, Thornley and Holmes by a rush carrying play to their antagonists' quarters. A free kick to Swinton was a welcome relief, and caused the leather to be taken to neutral territory. Shaweross im- proved matters for his side by a good dribble, but his efforts received no support from his colleagues, for some capital transfers between Mather, Heesom and Daniels completely nullified any advantage gained. Some lively play ensued, and then Mather gained possession and racing round threw wide to Webster, and the latter, after a capital run in, had the mortification to be pushed into touch in goal. Still the home team had to defend, which they did in sterling fashion, but another minor was given, the outcome of some passing between Mather, Lawless, and Daniels. Succeeding this a couple of capital runs by Webster and Pegg livened matters up a little and when the home man looked dangerous, the Warringtonians, amongst whom Barnes, Isherwood, Nield and Beard were very prominent, cleared the danger, and took the .scene of hostilities to midfield This was further enhanced by a good run by Davies along touch, and Eyres, Holmes, and Isherwood dribbled over, forcing Greenall to kick dead. On Swinton dropping out Thorniley, made a run and pass, which was not taken and a good chance lost, and half time was called with Warrrington, five minors to nil. Immediately on re-starting Webster by a grand pick up and run caused play to be waged in the home stronghold, and the same player improved the position by a strong rush. From a line out, Holmes passed the ball well out, but it was mulled under the posts, and a beautiful chance lost.

Through some unac.countable mulling of the ball, some splendid chances were lost by the visitors, and Swinton were at last enabled to relieve a strong pressure through a miskick. Nield, Davies, Eyres, and Barnes soon retrieved the lost ground, but a bad mistake by the visitors' full back almost enabled the home team to score under the posts. This proved their last chance and Lawless by a severe tackle relieved,and being supple- mented with a run by Eyres and pass to Ileesom, the , Swinton quarters were again the scene of operations. Some in and out play fpllowed, but Mather intercepting a had pass raced down midfield, and when pressed threw wide out to Daniels on the left, who romped over the line behind the posts, and succeeded in obtaining a grand try, which Heesom failed to convert. The drop out was mulled, but Heesom saved splendidly,and then Thornley, Beard, and Davies got away with a rattling rush to their opponents' quarters. Some effective play by Sampson followed, and Greenall was floored on the line. Heesom again saved from a bad pass, and then Daniels by a beautiful piece of play got right up to the line before being stopped. A piece of tricky play by Mather from a line out ensued, and getting clean away he threw right across to Heescarl, who ran over the line, but losing possession Lawless completed the try, which was not converted, leaving Warrington winners by 0-2-5 to nil. The following were the teams :—Warrington : Sampson, back; Webster, Deesom, and Daniels, three- quarters ; Mather and Lawless,half backs; Beard,Jones, Nield, Holmes, Barnes, Isherwood, Davies (captain), Thornley, and Eyres, forwards. Swinton: Greenall, back; Pegg, Edge and Wood, three-quarters; Edge and Sbawcross, half backs; Allen, Buxton, Holker, Howard,

div.head: Bradburn, Parkinson, Hulme, Hutchkiss, and Williams, forwards.
div.p: Bradburn, Parkinson, Hulme, Hutchkiss, and Williams, forwards.
RUNCORN v. BRADFORD.

The second fixture for the present season on the Run- corn card was played off at Bradford on Saturday. The ' Bradford club is one of the most prominent the Run- cornians have to meet, and speculation was rife as to the result. The Runcornians went by an early train on Saturday morning accompanied by a number of their admiring friends. At 3.30 there was quite 10,000 spec- tators lining the enclosure, and the game was witnessed with much interest. Runcorn was represented by B. Houghton (back), Davies, Crompton, and Wainwright, (three-quarter backs), Hughes and Evans (half backs), Broady, Hughes, Faulkner, Dolan, Rigby, Hancock, Hampson, Gayter, Davies, (forwards.) Bradford's team was Doyle (back), Moulson, Bairstow, and Jenkinson (three-quarter backs), Bonsor and Smith (half backs), Richards, Fieldhouse, Toothill, Fisher, White, Noble, Dewhurst, Gill, and Wilkinson (forwards.) It will thus be seen that both were representative teams. The ball was put into motion by Toothill, two thirty-fives being agreed upon. Play for a short time was confined to the Runcorn half; but Wainwright relieved the pressure, and kicked the ball back into touch. Some exception- ally fine as well as fast play then ensued, the forwards on both sides exerting themselves most energetically to gain a point. Davies showed good form and kicked well, but Doyle put in a saving clause, and punted to touch. Bonsor, who received after the throw out, passed to Richards, who mulled the ball. The restart was made by Faulkner, and owing to the deter- mined pressure brought to bear by Crompton and Wain- wright, Bradford were forced to give way. White came to the rescue, and rushed the ball on to the left wing. Houghton, however, was on the alert, and brought White down by a fine piece of tackling. A free kick conceded to Runcorn was met by Jenkinson, who spurted in capital style, and made an attack on the Runcorn quarters. Here a stern struggle took place, but Cromp- ton obtained possession, and passed to Wainwright, whose career was checked by Doyle. Scrimmages en- sued, and Bairstow, by dribbles, took the sphere to the Runcorn line. A disappointment, however, was in store for the Bradfordians, Houghton and Wainwright coming quickly on the scene, end checking further danger. Davies gave the home team an example of his dodgy runs, and at this point the greatest excitement prevailed. Bairstow, who secured, passed to Jenkinson, who made a capital run, and gained a try. The place at goal, however, failed, and at half-time the register was—Brad- ford. 1 try; Runcorn, nil. After the usual interval W. Hughes started the ball. The play was not of so com- bined a character as in the first half: but the forwards proved very strong. Bradford got near the Runcorn goal posts, and dribbled over the line. After the drop out Wilkinson broke through the visitors' line, but again the home team failed at goal, the kick being essayed by Doyle. A little later on Bradford, being encouraKed by its success up to this point, entered most spiritedly into the game, and Noble scored another try, the needful being done by Doyle. Jenkinson then dropped a goal. Had not Houghton tackled well, the home team would have added snore to their score. The game resulted s Bradford, 3 goals, 2 tries; Runcorn, nil. WIDNES V. HULL.

The first 15 of the Widnes feotball club played their second fixture on the grounds at Lowerhouse-lane, on Saturday, against Hull, before about 3,000 spectators. The weather was favourable, but a strong wind blew across the field, and interfered to some extent with the game. Smith started the ball with the wind in his favour. Howard got possession In the visitors' quarter, ' but was brought down just in time, while Clarke com- ing to his assistance, further advanced the position of the home team. The pressure was continued for a few minutes, when Hull were compelled to concede a minor. On restarting, a temporary visit was made to the home quarter, where Brennan, owing to the strong wind, failed to take a pass, but subsequently got possession and saved further disaster. Farmer, Johnson, Peters, and Howard here defended grandly, and a long punt by the latter repulsed the visitors to their own line, where the pressure being continued, a second minor was placed to the credit of Widnes. Smith was next conspicuous , with some good play, and evith the assistance of Gordon, carried the ball to the Hull line again. Mansell returned to the centre, where Brennan got possession, but being challenged he passed to Peters, but the ball was not taken, and Brennan, getting the ball again from a flying kick, made his mark close to the centre line. Plumpton took the place kick, which fell short, and the Widnes forwards following up, Hull were again compelled to touch down. Brennan subsequently again carried the ball to the visitors line, where it was again kicked dead. Three other minors followed in quick succession to Wid- nes, and from a free kick which fell to Widnes, Plump- ton would certainly have obtained a goal if the ball had not been turned aside by one of the visitors' hand. Some _ _ . . . .

further ineffectual play followed, in which Widnes had the best of game, and the scores at half-time stood as follows :—Widnes seven minors, Hull nil. On changing ends Widnes immediately invaded the visitors' quarters, but though no advantage was gained, the play on both sides was excellent. Hull now having rthe benefit of the wind seemed to take heart, Only on one occasion were Widnes compelled to concede a minor when their goal seemed in danger. Play for some ' time continued in the centre and home quarters, when Drennan failed to get through. At this point Brennan was put full back, and his place was taken by Plumpton. ' The game now became very exciting. Hartles, Howard, Peters, Farmer, and Whelan were conspicuous, and a series of passes started by Johnson, between Farmer, Whelan, and Stubbs, resulted in Gordon getting over the line, but the ball was called back, and a minor allowed. Gordon again got possession, and got over, but the ball was again called back, and a scrimmage followed in the visitors' Quarter. A few minutes later the ball was carried over the line, and was immediately pounced upon by Stubbs and Farmer, a try resulting. Plumpton made a good attempt at goal. but failed. Hull then invaded the home quarter, when Plumpton allowed the ball to pass him over the line, and a try for the visitors seemed inevitable, until Howard coming up just in the nick of time kicked the ball dead. The game ended in a win for Widnes by one try and eight minors to Hull one minor. The following were the teams :—Widnes : Plumpton, back H. Peters, D. Brennan and J. Clarke three-quarter backs • G. Howard and J. Hartles, half-backs; G. Hewitt, J. H. Smith (captain), Gordon, Farmer, Whelan, Johnson, Carroll, Pearson, and Stubbs, forwards. Umpire, Mr. Chadwick. Hull: W. Mansell, back; Ireson, Hill, and Shillit, three-quarter backs ; McLachlin and J. Mansell, half-backs; McWatt, Galbrath, Chaffer, Calvert, Allan, Wright, Harrison, Pinder, and Mennell, forwards. Um- pire, Mr. Brewer, and referee, Mr. Seddon, Broughton Rangers.

div.head: WARRINGTON T. STOCKPORT.
div.p: WARRINGTON T. STOCKPORT.

After their victory over Swinton, the Warringtonians encountered Stockport at Cale Green. on Monday even- ing, a game of an hour's duration ending in an unex- pected victory for the homesters by one goal (dropped), wne try, and two minors, to one try and three minors. The Warrington team differed slightly from that which did duty on Saturday, Eyres, Davies, and Thorniley re- placing Turner, Donohue, and Dillon. Before a large at- tendance Potts kicked off at 5.10, and after the opening exchanges, some faulty passing by the Warrington backs gave Stockport a footing in the visiting quarters. A mark to Boscow was followed by a fine kick by Barnes, who caused the Cheshire men to defend. A fine run by Ashton from a line out was spoiled by holding the oval too long, and Ogden intercepting some passing of the Warrington men, neutral ground was the scene of opera- tions. A spell of monotonous give-and-take play was witnessed, until Bate, with an effective run' took the oval in the mouth of the Stockport goal. The home forwards, however, were playing a determined game, and, although they relieved slightly, a brilliant run by Barnes took the game again on the home line. A dribble by Dain was met by Lawless, who compelled a hasty re- treat, Bandies meanwhile failing to put the finishing touoh en an excellent dribble, Stockport 25 was the scene of operations. The homesters forced the game, and a useful kick by Legge changed the venue, and a combined rush by the Stockport forwards sent the oval dead. The drop out was but feebly responded to by Legge, and then a characteristic run by Evans found Stockport once more on the defensive. Ashton and Jol- ley showed up well, and from a pack on the line a spell of passing between Bate, Antrobus, and Barnes, resulted in the latter running in a fine fry, his kick at goal striking the post. Following this success, a change same over the scene, for after Bandies, Berry, and Eyres had displayed rare form, the homesters swept down in a body on the Warrington goal, and from some scrambling play which ensued, Pain scored near the corner flag. A poor attempt was made at the place, but fortune was with the Stockport men directly after, Ogden dropping a fine goal, this latter point bringing half-time, with the score as Stockport 14-1; Warrington 0-1-0. On resuming, the Stockport men again presented a bold front, their forwards playing well to a man. Despite good runs by Lawless and Evans, the homesters held the upper hand, and dribbling with accuracy, the Warrington defence was sorely tested. Boscow put in some clever kicks which gained consider- ablelground, and a shot at goal by Evans went a little wide. Warrington now seemed to realize the situation, for on the drop out the Cheshire men were called upon to defend, and although Antrohusand Lawless successively put In brilliant runs luck was not with them, and their efforts had a futile result. Ogden cleared his lines in smart style, but Boscow was equally safe. Although Warrington pressed the major portion of this half, they lacked combination when a final effort was required. Repeatedly they were within an ace of scoring but some hasty pass, faulty picking up, or selfish act would spoil the otherwise brilliant effort. During the last few minutes, Barnes had a drop. Murray again being com- pelled to save, Evans finally forcing a third minor. Time was eventually called with the score as stated above, Stockport team :—Murray, back; Dr. Blades, Ogden, and Legge, three-quarters; Parrott and Naylor, half-backs; Potts, Bailey, Dain Duckers, McLure, Dr. Smith, Ankers, Abbey, and Kitchen, forwards. Referee, Mr. McLean, Manchester.

WARRINGTON V. SWINTON. That football has now "caught on "in the Warring- ton district was plainly proved on Saturday, when fully 6,000 spectators lined the enclosure at Wilderspool to witness the first engagement this season with the famous Swinton team. The match in question had been the

theme of conversation for the past few weeks, and the fine form displayed by the Swintonians in their recent engagements with Oldham and Mossley, rendered the match on Saturday, in the eyes of many, as a foregone conclusion,. However, there was not wanting a few who pinned their faith to the Warringtonians, believing that they would improve on their form against Lancaster, and rise to the occasion. The Swinton men mustered their strongest possible, whilst Warrington were still without Massey. Nevins also being too indisposed to take part in so important an engagement. Warrington won the choice of ends, and Valentine kicked off towards the pavilion goal. The preliminary movements found the play at neutral ground, where from the first pack fermed, Bumby effected a pass to Marsh, but Barnes and Bate, ' ever on the alert, intercepted, and Swinton defended. The stay here was only temporary, for the homesters, who did not seem to thoroughly get into their stride, were overpowered, and a rush by the burly Swinton for- wards caused play to ho located near the pavilion goal. Boscow was frequently called upon to save his charge, and admirably did he accomplish his task. Passing by Valentine, Marsh, Buxton, and Winterbottom, raised the hopes of the visitors, but as eagerly as did Swinton attack so cleverly did Warrington defend. Valentine made several efforts to get in, but either Evans or Barnes awaited his coming with remarkable accuracy, manag- ing to pull hhin up before he travelled far. Boscow made his mark when pressed, but a moment of anxiety was experienced when Lawless had his kick charged close to i the line. Luckily he saved, and again the Warrington forwards cleared, Turner, Ashton, and Berry being especially prominent. Marsh put in a neat dodgy run, but a combined dribble by Povey, Dillon, and Jolley negatived the effort. The relief was only momentary, for Buxton passing wide to Valent ne, the game was again on the Warrington line. Walker and Hallum almost notched a try from a clever dribble, and with less experienced hands than the Warrington backs, suapess would surely have attended the Swintonian's effort. Barnes got in a good kick to the half way flag, but Murray saved from a rush, and though Warrington were afforded a free kick it availed them little, for after a spell of passing by Winterbottom, Bumby, and Marsh, the last-named, effected a grand run and pass to Valentine; who ran over amidst loud cheering, the same player failing. This success did not deter the Warringtonians from playing up, for on the restart we found them exhibiting rare ; dash. Antrobus, Jolley, and Ashton were in turn ap- plauded far their efforts, and although Turner put in a ' tremendous kick, which gave Warrington a footing in the Swinton twenty-five, no addition was made to the score, and half-time was called with the score as Swin- ton one try; Warrington nil. On change of ends, play was confined for a considerable time at neutral ground. Boscow respouded brilliantly to a kick by Marsh, but the visitors by combined play forced the game to the War- rington end. Lacks by Ashton and Littlewood caused Swinton some anxiety, but their backs getting the oval travelling, it was quickly back at the railway goal. Warrington's defence was admirable, and Boscow saved at a critical moment. From a free kick by Lawless, Murray put in a good run along touch, Evans ultim- ately pulling him up. The Warringtonians now rallied and after Littlewood, Bandies, and Jolley had put in a useful dribble, Valentine punted well to Lawless, who responded with a long kick, and the movement being taken up by the home forwards, Turner being prominent and Murray being at fault, the ball was rushed down the field, and Berry ultimately made the game equal. Loud , cheers greeted this effort, but the enthusiasm broke all bounds when Fair Turner landed a magnificent , goal. 'On the restart Swinton rushed the game near the, Warrington posts. Valentine almost got in after a pretty display between Bumby and Buxton, but Evans, Bate, and Antrobus repeatedly saved. A drop at goal by Val- entine was short of its mark, and from a pass by Bate, Evans punted down the field, changing the venue to the Swinton quarter flag. The excitement during the last few minutes of the game was intense,every movement be- watched with the keenest interest, and when Valentine in the last second of the match dropped at goal and grazed the post on the outside, and the whistle sounded "no side," the spectators cheered to the echo at the suc- cess of Warrington the final score being—Warrington, 1-0-0; Swinton, 0-1-1. Teams :—Warrington Boscow, back; Evans, Barnes, and Lawless, threequarters ; Bate, and Antrobus, half-backs; Turner, Ashton Bandies, Povey, Littlewood, Donohue, E. Dillon, *Tolley, and Berry. Swinton: Murray, back; Valentine, Marsh, and Winterbottom, threequarters ; Buxton and Bumby, half- backs; Hall, Lomax, Walker, Astall, Hotchkiss, Sharpies, IRothwell, and Evans. WEST LANCASHIRE LEAGUE.

_ WTDNE.S ST. MART'S V. LITHERLAND.—WidtIeS St. Mary's who last season won the West Lancashire Junior Cup, met Litherland at Litherland, on Saturday, and fortunately the weather was more propitious than could have been hoped for. Litherland started the ball against a powerful wind, and could therefore make no headway. At length from a penalty kick, Harding made a fruitless shot at goal, but from a scrimmage Cosgrove scored without improvement. After some scrambling play Litherland got beyond the half-way line, but the posi- tion was not tobe held, and they were compelled to retreat. Not discouraged, however, play again settled In the centre, when Clay made a brilliant run on the left, and passed all but the full back. Now for the first time Litherland pressed, and had hard lines in not scor- ing. The score at half time was—Widnes St. Mary's, one try and one minor; Litherland, nil. On changing ends, McCafferty, taking advantage of the mull by one of the home three-quarters, ran in and Hardman kicked a neat goal. St. Mary's continued to have the best of the game, and Litherland rarely got beyond the dividing line. A second goal having been got by the Saints, the game ended as follows :—Widnes St. Mary's, 2, goals, 1 try, and 2 minors, to Litherland nil.

div.head: FLOODS ON THE CONTINENT.
div.p: FLOODS ON THE CONTINENT.
200 PERSONS DROWNED.

A despatch from Mustapha Pasha-, --er town on the Turco-Bulgarian frontier, reports that 200 persons, 100 of whom were Tutkish soldiers and the remainder in- habitants of Mustapha Pasha, were drowned in the recent great floods caused by the overflowof the Maritza. Railway communication with Constantinople has been re-established, and the trains are now running as usual. A violent tempest broke over Marseilles and its vicinity on Sunday Morning. The streets were flooded, and the waters invaded the shops and the cellars of the houses, while in many places the paving of the promenades was to up. The country districts round also suffered severely from the effects cf the storm, great damage being done to property of all kinds. In one place a wall fell in, killing a woman and two children and injuring three men. Storms are also reported from Nimes, Alais, and Bessexas, while heavy rains are prevalent through- out the department of Gard, where the rivers are inun- dating the low-lying lands.

div.head: MURDER OF A POLICE SERGEANT.
div.p: MURDER OF A POLICE SERGEANT.

Mr. and Mrs. Kettlewerl, fruit and vegetable vendors, were driving to Rickmond (Yorkshire) market, early on Saturday morning, when they found a sergeant of police, named Weedy, lying on the road opposite the garden gate of a married man named Kitching, a gardener. In- formation of the discovery was conveyed to Constable Nixon, of Catterick, who followed the gardener Kitching, and arrested him at Richmond market, on suspicion of having murdered Weedy. He was locked up at the Police Station. An inquest was held on Saturday night on the body of the deceased man. Reporters were not admitted, but it transpired that Kitching, who is in cus- tody, had been drinking at a public-house, and at closing time on Friday, when requested by deceased to go home, threatened that he would shoot him. Weedy appears to have followed accused to his house at Leeming, and while he was in a paddock in which Kitching's house stands, the latter is alleged to have shot him with a gun in the left side of the neck, breaking the spine, and causing instantaneous death. The jury returned a ver- dict that death was caused by a gun shot wound in- flicted by Robert Kitching, whom they found guilty of wilful murder.
THE CONFESSION OF MURDER CHESHIRE.

Mr. 11. Churton, coroner for Cheshire, on Sunday morning received the following letter from the Rev. H. 11. Waters, of St. Paul's New Orleans, re- specting the confession made by a man in New Or- leans of having, about 30 years ago, murdered a gamekeeper at Tarporley, Cheshire. for which crime a man named Blagg was executed : "Windsor, Ontario, Canada, September 10, 1. . "My dear sir,—Your letter of August 20th to Mr. James Sowers has been forwarded to me here. I have written to the man in New Orleans urging him very strongly to put himself in the hands of the British Consul at New Orleans, or to go and see Mr. Sowers. My intention in making the inquiries in the first place was with this view, assuming that the representations made to me were correct. Ile wrote out a statement of several pages, giving all the minute details of the case, and when I return I will try and procure this statement. I shall return to New Orleans probably about the first week in October, and then may be able to write you more fully.—Believe me, yours sincerely. "I-I. 11. WATERS. "Henry Churton, Esq."

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

It would seem that there is to be a kind of crusade against veiled" professionalism "amongstcertain Rugby clubs in Lancashire. If professionalism is to be kept out of the Rugby game, it is certainly time some notice was taken of tha manner in which certain clubs get their crack players. One cf the first to have to undergo the ordeal is • Buff " Berry the famous Tyldesley half-back, who has been called upon by the Lancashire Referees' Unionto explain why he has transferred his services from the Kendal Hornets to Tyldesley. The Referees Union is certainly late enoughin taking action in this case, but still it will be interesting to know how Berry comes out of the affair. The case of W. Ashworth, of Werneth, too, is being examined into, so that it would appear that players are no longer to chop and change about without a valid reason.

Several matters of interest will occupy the attention of the Rugby Football Union at their annual meeting next week. Not the least of these will be the attempt to decide the question of county championship on a new basis, which it is proposed should be done by a series of competitions. The present method of selection by the Rugby Union Committee has not given satisfaction. If carried, however, the proposal is hardly likely to take effect this season.

Mr. S. IL Payne failed to obtain the consent of the Lancashire County Football Union the other evening to his suggested curtailment of the playing season, which in the opinion of the majority of the members is already short enough.

Runcorn team travelled far on Saturday, big with hopes of victory, and they entered the arena confident of upholding the reputation built up by the successes of the past six years. But fate was against the champions of Cheshire. From first to last the Yorkshire forwards held the upper hand, and the speedy and tricky backs of the Cheshire team had no proper opportunities to die- play their skill to advantage although despite their ad- 'verse circumstances, they became dangerous on several occasions. Crompton, Davies, and Wainwright put in good work and the former player might have crossed the rubicon once, had he not unselfishly passed to Wain- wright, whon he thought had a better opening, but the speedy sprinter mulled the ball ift his eagerness, and the Bradford citadel was safe. In the first half the balance of points was not great but in the second half, the home team piled on the agony and ran out winners by a score that has not been made against Runcorn for many years past. Had it not been for the magnificent tackling of Houghton, a still more woeful tale might have had to be told.

On Saturday Widnes received a visit from the Hull team who are invincible at home, but they had to lower their colours before the players of the Chemical Metro- polis. The game was of a very exciting nature, but the strong wind that prevailed, rendered long kicking almost impossible and accurate passing extremely difficult. In the first half the home team held the upper hand, but they could score no tangible point minors being the order of the day. In the second half when labouring under greater disadvantages Widnes added a. try, and on handsomely. It is to be hoped this Is only the pre, cursor pf further suceesses.:

Attack and defence in football was to be seen in a high degree on Saturday in the match Warrington and Swinton. The Swinton play was strong dashing and ageressive, while the wirepullers' defence was of the toughest and most unflagging description. The specta- tors who saw the fine combination and the splendid passing of the Swintonians, quite acknowledged that this team still knows how to uphold the high fame it has won 1 in past years, and in fact it was probably never stronger than it is at the present time. When a well-known team ' is down for a visit disappointment is often caused by the absence ef one or more of the crack players, but on this occasion the visitors put their " very hest " in the field, and a formidable lot they looked as they defiled from the pavilion, led by the famous" Val."

It was perhaps rather hard lines that after doing the majority of the pressing, the Swintonians should come off second best in the scoring, but after all the strength of a chain is according to its weakest link, and the Swinton chain had a weak link on this occasion in the full back. Murray certainly did not play up to his repu- tation en this occasion, and it was through his bungling that Warrington scored the decisive point. On the other hand Warrington would have been a long way behind if they had not kept up their defence in a way that few clubs could emulate. Their tackling throughout was splendid and try as the visitors would, with their big forwards and combined passing, they scarcely ever found lan opening.

One thing seems pretty certain,and that Is that a Rugby club which wishes to keep in the front rank must have some strong heavy forwards. The Yorkshire clubs owe a lot of their success to this class of player, and the Swin- t.onians follow suit. As a result they generally had the best of the scrimmages, and this gave their half-backs and three-quarters a great advantage which they made the best use of.

div.head: CYOLING.
div.p: CYOLING.

A very strong wind assisted the competitors for the first half of the 100 miles North Road Cycling Club road race on Saturday, but its effects were severely felt dur- ing the return half. Dangerfield rode very strongly , throughout, and won in 6hrs. 10min., Ilsley and Bates being his two' nearest opponents. Bidlake was first Iman in on a" three-wheeler," and Ward was second. Wilson created a record in the first fifty miles by riding the distance in 2hrs. 32min., but it must be remembered that he was assisted by a very high wind.

div.head: CRICIEST.
div.p: CRICIEST.

The el-lard averages for first-class English matches fairly well follow the results of the Australian tour. The bowling shows better than the batting. No English batsman reaches last year's total of 2,00 q runs, and Chinn heads the aggregate with the grand total of 1,621, Shrewsbury coming next with 1,568, and the " Doctor " being a good third with 1,476. Nominally Mr. Hewett is at the head of the batting averages, his figures being 43 to Shrewsbury's 41.10, but as he has only played eight innings he can hardly be said to be in the running, the real head of the batsmen being Shrewsbury, Gunn, and Abel amongst the professionals, and Cranston. Webbe, and Grace among the amatetirs. Grace has played a larger number of innings than any other player, amateur or professional, his total being 55 against Gunn's 53. Among the bowlers Briggs just takes the honours from Attewell, Sharpe and Lohinann, and behind these per- formers come Woof, Peel, Martin, and Lohmann. Briggs' average is 12.54 per wicket, and probably he has never bowled in " snakier " form during the whole of his career.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The Salford Harriers' contingent a champions, Messrs. Parry, Morton, Morris, Nicholas, and Morgan, who sailed last week for New York, intended taking part in the Canadian championships to-day (Saturday) at Montreal, an early getting into harness which it is to be feared will not prove successful unless the passage is a particularly good one. The climate of the Dnited States has proved a great trouble to most English athletes who have pre- viously essayed the task of meeting the flower of the American athletic world on their own shores, and not a few of them have thus fallen far short of their true form when at home, notably Conneff and Thomas. C. G. Wood's lack of success was more owing to an unfortunate sprain than climatic influences. It is to be hoped, how- ever, that this team will be more fortunate, and that they will return with their laurels in no wise tarnished. Morgan is almost certain to run up to his best form, as for many years he "lived the life of a sailor," and he used often to be seen emerging from the dressing-rooms at local athletic meetings resplendent in a mercantile midshipman's costume.

div.head: CARDINAL NEWMAN'S SUCCESSOR.
div.p: CARDINAL NEWMAN'S SUCCESSOR.

A Rome telegram says the report that the Archbishop of Dublin is to be made a cardinal is premature. The Pope has been too much annoyed lately at the almost defiant manner of the Irish bishops towards his autho- rity even to think of creating a new Irish cardinal.

div.head: CONFESSION OF MURDER.
div.p: A CONFESSION OF MURDER.

A man giving the name of William Turner. of Hatton, Essex, was charged before the local magistrate, at Pick- ering, Yorkshire, on Monday, on his own confession of having murdered Amelia Jeffs at West Ham, last year. The prisoner, who is a short, dark man, stated that his father resided at 7, Morris-place, Brentwood, and while the confession was being read he trembled violently. Dr. Thornton Combea said the prisoner was suffering from delirium tremens and hallucinations. Asked If he had ' anything to say, he said" I don't know." He was re- manded.

div.head: SHOCKING WELSH TRAGEDY.
div.p: SHOCKING WELSH TRAGEDY.

Mrs. Evans, wife of a wheelwright at Neath, ran from the house on Monday wounded and bleeding. The neighbours went in, but were driven back by Evans, who flourished a knife. Re-entering, they found him dead in the kitchen with his throat cut. Mrs. Evans, who is in a very precarious state, says her husband first unsuccess- fully attacked her with a hatchet, then struck her head with a hammer, and afterwards cut her neck. Deceased had been greatly straitened in circumstances owing to four months' illness from rheumatic fever, and lately there had been a marked depression of spirits. There is a family of four children.

TOWN, MR. D. CRILLY, M.P., AND THE GOVERNMENT. ....An enthusiastic meeting was held in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom,' Earlestown, on Saturday 'evening, under the auspices of the local branch of -The Irish National League of Great Britain, to pro- titit against the arrest of Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien. _Pere was a very large attendance. Mr. F. A. R. Veild,of Bold, presided, and lie was accompanied on the platform by Messrs. D. Crillv, M.P. for North ~.eYo, G. W. Rawlins, of Rainhill, P. M. Campbell, •7, Prescott, Thomas Flood, D. Boyle, C. Downes, T. ‘Talligan, L. Murphy, D. Caffrey, and J. Rodger*. The Chairman said he was very pleased to see s good , atidience, considering tUat, the meeting was partly in . SUPport of criminals. He was told by a friend the other 1:44'14W that there were some Irish members of Parlia- !lent imprisoned. He wanted to know what the cause Za4 ; whether they had been picking pockets, or what L'e.Y had been doing. His friend said he did not know, tit it was under Mr. Balfour's Government,and that was ,s_elleugh to show that they required some sort of sym- "4l9. There were supposed criminals in Ireland, who Were not called criminals. It was for a Government Sitting in London to pass resolutions in London,incrimin- atlag Iple living in a country they knew nothing at all at when the people of that country met criminals ilway station, and drove them in the Lord :arriage to the police court, where they had to resident magistrate, it showed there was not ninality about them. (Applause.) In Ireland vay to make themselves criminal, was to make popular representatives of the people. (Hear,

W. Rawlins said it afforded him very great M be there that night, and in company with Ir. Balfour's criminals. He was sorry to say tad not had much experience of meetings of the rue. He knew that they had been doing a iunt of good In furtherance of the Home Rule it he was surprised to see the orderly aspect of ;ing. He had expected to see a good many $ flying about. (Laughter.) He had been told had no love of law and order, and that they dened criminals, and very oven when he had itionalist leaguemeeting it reminded him of that Razors flying inthe air," but he did not see any ing about that night. (Laughter.) He then the following resolution "That this meeting ;, in the most emphatic manner, the latest . Mr. Balfour's policy in Ireland in arresting the leaders of the Irish people, John Dillon and IWllliarn O'Brien, and begs to 'assure them that at the arst opportunity, we shall leave no effort untried to tßh 13ecure the overthrow of the present coercionist Govern- 'lnent and to sent into power a Government pledged to Rive Home Rule to Ireland, and to legislate in the inter- tit of the masses iri Great Britain." (Applause.) They liad got to the time when the fight began again. It was Iheetings of that description which would decide the ,Aght of the Newton division, so far as they were per- olially concerned. (A voice: " Mr.:Rawlins.") No ...ere would be one forthcoming, but it . would la; t "nether man. They were asked to condemn the latest i Phase of Mr. Balfour's'policy in Ireland, and he thought tilliat expression was a very good one, Mr.' Balfour ad had a good many phases- in Ireland. It was ithia the knowledge of those present, that this '4,o°Bs outrage had been perpetrated upon the leaders the Irish people. He supposed the Government tq thought it necessary to restore their position, but mis-government seemed to have the faculty of ng the wrong thing at the wrong time; they did not to be able to grasp the position of affairs, to see Zbat the people wanted in this country, and they seemed ,{1) grasp at a policy which was the root of their own dis- Vernberment i . The potato crop n Ireland had been a vitter failure, and it was feared a famine might ensue, al_it how had Mr. Balfour answered this cry? By leaving `ue People of Ireland to do the best they could; by stop- tlie; the miserable warfare that was going on between dlord and tenant? No, nothing of that sort, but by t'resting the men who were going to America with the wievi of raising funds for the amelioration of the people Ireland. (Applause.) And if Mr. Balfour had done uais stroke of policy, with the deliberate idea of starving ine Irish people, he could not have done better from his point of view. A policy of that sort always failed, •d it would fil in this case. There was no doubt her A. raesty's Government had proved themselves utterly iajrapable of governing; all they wanted to do was to Old on as long as they could. If they should find, le Aur- r, ~, next session, a little turn of unexpected popularity, ▪ ea' would use that moment for an appeal to the coun- r ; otherwise they would hold onto the bitter end, and Zere was nothing for it but for himself and his hearers • Peg away at Home Rule, and to do their best to secure the Irish people the fulfilment of their just demands. (Bear, hear.) . . Mr. T. Flood, in seconding the resolution' said he had 480rne regret to be there to enter a protest against the foul blot that had been put upon Ireland by the present overnment. (Cheers.) The circumstance that occur- the other day might to many seem a trifling matter, i_ut constitutionally considered, was a violation of the iliberty of the subject, a violation of law and order. (Cheers.) It was only one of the many crimes the pre- -I),ent Government had committed whilst in office. The , ‘l, avernment had tampered with the faith of the people. arfear, hear). D. Crilly, M.P., who was received with loud and llnetiauous cheering, said he had a sad satisfaction in suPporting the resolution which had been proposed so iltkquently by Mr. Rawlins, and seconded by Mr. Flood. r..Flood,in the course of that speech to which they had all listened with pleasure, declared that the story of Ireland had been repeated so often, that speakers who rke on behalf of Ireland were tired of repeating it, and 7 who had heard it so fre.quently were so familiar .tli it that they also where tired of it. (Applause). 4 heY were called together that night to listen to the old Stories of Ireland, the old story of the persecution of her tople, the old story of the sorrows of their race. They d a resolution proposed similar in terms and in spirit, to. hundreds and thousands of resolutions that had , iren passed on English and Irish platforms ever since 'lreland lost her legislative independence. They were raet that night, not for the purpose of congratu- a_tling each oi her upon the fact that the old quarrel amtween the two countries had been settled satisfactorily, 0a to proclaim that the homes of Ireland were filled at 14 :Ist with comfort and prosperity ; not to declare that the , i„„wl quarrel was over, and that the English and Irish , were settled down to the discharge of their own traonal duties. They were met once more, as many of 1 A fli met in other towns of Lancashire before, to con- as the resolution condemns, in the most emphatic , ~,kanner, the outcome of the present and past '''''licY of governing Ireland, the arrest and im- ' Trisonment of the chosen leaders of the, Irish , Veople. (Cheers.) That night they had to I 4ee ognise th 3 fact that two leaders of the Irish people, I 1.1,1 the persons of Mr. William O'Brien and Mr. John I !anon had been arrested, because, like many other men ' 'oef ore them in the history of Ireland, they had been true to's the idea of legislative independence, and because they Zad done their best according to their lights, and accord- ;`,. ,; to the capacity which God had given them, to lift up ir people in the scale of nations, to lift them up in the , !t e•ale of prosperity, and not allow them to be for the ,ctiture, as they had been in the past, objects for the pity I.s.rid cbarity of the world. (Cheers.) For doing that Mr. llon and Mr. O'Brien had been arrested, and probably 4tter next Thursday, when the two Tipperary remov- •ables, and Mr. Balfcfur, had heard their case, they would t: it3e the inmates of a prison cell. (. Shame.") Mr. Bal- ,lar had wakened up, and he (Mr. Crilly) trusted that e result of his efforts would be to bring him as much aat tistaction and rest and enjoyment, as the holiday he had tTen enjoying since Parliament arose. Mr. "Balfour as "ief Secretary for Ireland had been enjoying himself in otland, and indulging in the game of golf, while the hrish people had been calling for bread to satisfy the rl,uger of themselves and their children.' He and his e1,12W Irishmen did not know much about the game of tc-ht, but they were pretty good wrestlers, and before they ad done with him, they would give Mr. Balfour and his t'o, ileagnes a heavy fall. (Laughter.) But although he he speaker) had never seen this interesting and aria- , cratic game of golf, he understood the main object of .: Was to put a little ball into a hole. Mr. Balfour had "Wakened up for a social game of golf to a political game _golf, whether he had potted his ball often enough to ' win the game, all he could say was that by his latest INv rtion in Ireland he was unquestionably playing well for success, because he had, as he has done ever ee he took office, put the Government in the same .11 le as he often put them in before. (Applause.) Za thought he was now by this new outbreak of a Trutal policy putting himself and the Government a hole, out of which he never would escape. What ~,ati he done? He had simply given another. ( s `II natr ati on of evil which attended the present system of tverning Ireland. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Balfour had al- . inflated between the bully and poltroon. Mr. Balfour 11.3e'a at times terrorised over the Irish people; cruelly ,anaten them, been responsible for imprisonment and ch„ttths,—at other times Mr. Balfour had run away from Irish people. ("Shame.") The people of Ireland ri4"ll,_ld not go to sleep until their movement had resulted phurinaina back to Ireland the splendid and glorious 6 e vilege of legislating for the Irish people upon Irish (Applause.) From that purpose they should not ~.b. diverted, either by Lord Salisbury or Mr.! Balfour. ~.n.!• Balfour, since he assumed office, had tried every ,1 'ae ' thod except one method, of governing the Irish )so 1 . Iv_ Pe. He and his associates had looked one in calm- fas and content, while thousands and thousands of the Rsh People were leaving the shores of their island home. , ,la had done all this, as well as for a longtime lying in Ireland. He had not for some months been ad- „ yirarasterin.g the Coercion Act in Ireland very' brutally. :te bad tried to convey the impression abroad that sOrcion had conquered. That policy had been, equal . th his former policies, a brutal and absolutii failure. -1,5 had been awakened by the taunts thrown in his teeth 1Y the Liberal party in England and the Irisht people in tie land, that his cowardice had failed to turn them from . 10°Ir.lie Rule. He wakened up now to convince, la. and Liberal Unionist supporters in England, that he, not afraid, that the Irish people had not conquered and beaten him inch by inch, and foot by foot, until '.. an ay he was a beaten despot. He comes te the frcnt " says "there is some, power and life left balme yet." t

However, they would knock the power out of his hands in a little time. (Hear, hear.) They were perfectly prepared to continue the fight in Ireland with patience, *ith even tempers, and with determination until the English people had an opportunity of declaring at the polls, whether this policy was to obtain for evermore. It was only one question now for England, whether in Ireland the awakened conscience, and the educated in- telligence of England, are to prevail for evermore, or whether the old brutal,prejudiced, ignorant, persecuting policy of Dublin Castle, directed by such men as Lord Salisbury and Mr. Balfour, is to continue until the day of judgment. (Hear, hear.) They had no feat for the result. They had a just cause, they had a brave and unbeaten people, and they knew that at the earliest Opportunity on which side the English people would decide. They knew that the enlightened conscience and educated intelligence of the English people would decide in favour of the policy represented by William Ewart Gladstone—(cheers)—and not the other policy, the bad evil policy of centuries as represented by Mr. Balfour. (Hooting.) They were willing at the earliest moment to see these two champions go into the arena, one repre- senting justice, right, and truth, the other representing cruel treatment and injustice, and they were not to be merely spectators in the fight, but actors in it, and they would say when they stood face to face on the day of election, "May God defend the right." (Applause.) He had no fear of the result, and he was quite sure from their presence that night, in such large and healthy num- bers, that they were determined to do their share, and put an cnd to this policy of Mr. Balfour's, that every man by his presence recorded the fact that in so far as his capacity and time would allow, he should contribute , something towards the return of a man for that division of Lancashire who would range himself, not on the side of Mr. Balfour, but on the siae of W. E. Gladstone. (Cheers) Could they say,as men of common sense, that the past policy of England in Ireland had been a success? (" No.") The Government had failed as statesmen all along the line, they had only been successful in one thing, and that was in perpetuating in Ireland the old state of things in which, the Irish people and their fathers before them, had made war unrelentingly. It was a usual thing for their opponents to say that the Irish leaders were liars and hypocrits, and that they were only making statements to deceive the English people. He could only say that men who made such statements were not worth arguing with. They came to the Eng- lish people and said—" We are willing to bury the hatchet; we only come to you to say that we desire to put in operation the ambition of Mr. Gladstone." Let , them at the general election carry London and Lance- shire, and they had not merely carried Home Rule for Ireland,but they had carried the main reforms that were I here in England. It was an old saying that what Lan- cashire thought to-day. England would think to-morrow. They wanted to help at the first opportunity in giving an expression of opinion on the part of Lancashire ; they had only a majority of about 800 to smash. The Irish leaders had smashed larger majorities than that, and he hoped they would respond to the call of Mr. Rawlins, in winning the Newton Division at the general election. (Hear, hear.) It was pnly the term of a madman to say that Home Rule meant separation. If they were fools, the Irish people, were not, and they were not going to jeopar- dise the prosPerity of their own country by cutting off every approach to the markets of England. It was not necessary for him to come there and say Home-Rule does not mean Rome Rule. Home Ride did not mean that the Catholics of Ireland would interfere with those who knelt at another shrine. They knew what it was to suffer for belonging to -a certain church, and they cer- tainly were not going to visit upon their own fellow- countrymen the sufferings the Catholics had undergone. (Hear, hear.) Be could say as an Irish Catholic, as an Ulster Catholic, that if he thought, for one instant, that the cession of Home Rule to Ireland meant that one single man in Ireland,that one of his own fellow-country- men, should be tortured for conscience sake, he should leave the Nationalist platform, and leave to other men the task of winning Home Rule for Ireland. (Applause.) It was because he had no belief in such a thing that he was there to advocate Home Rule, because it would bring liberty of conscience to Ireland, it would bring back to her those industries of which she had been robbed, those manufactures which had been killed in Ire- land, and would bring to her people prosperity. It would be no longer necessary for them to leave their shores to earn a week's wages on the shores of America or Australia; it was not merely that the cession of Home Rule would liberate Ireland, but it would liberate Eng- land as well, and would bring to the English people peace and content. (Cheers.) Mr. P. M. Campbell, in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Crilly, said it was rather difficult for him to follow after the very eloquent remarks which he had given upon the subject of Ireland, and mis-government of that country. Perhaps he should be well within his province and jurisdiction by confining himself to matters connec- ted with his own position in the Newton Division. They had just come through the revision, and no doubt they would be entertained with the figures showing the fabu- lous victories the other side had gained, but figures were not always facts. He looked upon Mr. Crilly's visit there as being a very opportune visit indeed, to awaken their conscience to the fact that there were enormities being committed in Ireland in their name. He claimed that they had a majority in that division if the people were fairly got at. Certainly they must adtnit from re- cent events that they had a political preponderance in that centre, and that centre was growing. The Irish element had a great power, and he hoped the result of that meeting would be that they would think over the Matter, and assert that power. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. Prescott seconded the resolution, and Mr. C. Downes, of Golborne, having spoken in support of it, it was put to the meeting and carried. After the usual vote of thanks to the Chairman, the meeting terminated.

HARVEST FESTIVAL SERVICES AT ST. JOHN'S CHURCH EARLESTOWN. Special services of thanksgiving for the ingather- ing of the harvest were held in St. John the Baptist Church on Sunday. The sacred building, which at ordinary times presents a bare appearance, was transformed into, literally speaking, a bower of roses, much time and labour having been spent in its accomplishment. Looking .from the main en- trance, the chancel was hidden by an open screen work, composed principally of cereals, embellished here and there with gay coloured flowers and plants. On the steps approaching, were a couple of miniature stacks of hay and corn, made and pre- sented by Mr. Berry, of Crow Lane, while surrounding them were vegetables of various kinds. The choir stalls also were prettily decorated with flowers and sheaves of wheat ; father on the steps along the Communion rail were loaded with vegetables and loaves of bread. The pulpit was prettily adorned with flowers and fruit en- closed in a fringe composed of cereals, the whole being relieved by a background of white, with floral ornamen- tations the work of Miss F. Matthews. From the lectern was suspended a huge bunch of grapes, the base being a perfect bevy of dahlias and other flowers. The pillars were also relieved by garlands of corn while the window recesses were filled with vegetables and fruit. The font was nicely decorated, and altogether the church pre- sented a very pleasing appearance. The work of decora- tion was carried out under the supervision of Miss M. Matthews, Miss F. Mathews, Mr. J. Matthews, Rev. E. W. W. Kay, assisted by the wardens, sidesmen, Sunday school teachers, choir and members of the congre- gation. At the morning service there was a large congregation, when hymns appropriate to the occasion were sung. The choir also sang in good style the anthem "Fear not, Oh land," the bass solo being nicely given by Mr. John Matthews, Miss Tripp under- taking the treble solo. In the quartette, which was tastefully rendered, Miss Tupps, Miss Mayhew, Mr. Inman, and Mr. Waddington took part. The Rev. W. J. Melville, M.A., rector of Ashton, was announced to preach, but owing to indisposition, his place was filled by the Vicar, the Rev. T. R. Matthews, who chose for his text Joel 2nd chap. 24 and 25 verses, from which he delivered an earnest exhortation. In the afternoon, a novel feature in the service of the church at.Earlestown was introduced, the Viaduct Institute Brass Band being present. The band turned out from their headquarters, and playeo on the way to the church a quickstep " Adeste Fideles." The church was crowded, and the band, which was under the conductorship of Mr. John Makin, of 'Platt Bridge, played "The lost chord" arranged by A. Owen. The piece was admirably executed, light and shade being carefully, adhered to. The cornet solo was taken bv Mr. J. Appleton, and soprano by Mr. J. Stevenson. 'They also played with spirit "The Hallelujah chorus." In addition to this they played the accompaniments to the variotis hymns sung during the short service which followed, the effect being of a most pleasing nature. The Vicar again occupied the pulpit, and delivered a *Mort discourse from Ecclesiastes Ist chap. 9 verse. "There is no new thing under the sun." His remarks were directed chiefly to the presence of the band in church that afternoon. He supposed some of them would say that this was a new thing. It might be new to Earlestown, but it certainly was not new to other places. 'He had heard that a lady in the neighbourhood had said that she was very much shocked at the innova- tion, and he quite sympathised with her, but it only wanted a little thought: He then proceeded to quote front the Old Testament to show that in those days instruments of various descriptions were used in the services, but he had not time to enumerate all the different kinds. They had the organ then but it was not in such perfection. People might say they had the organ now, why not use that. There was no reason why they should not have such splendid instruments, as they had had playing in the church that day, in the service of God, no matter whether they had been used for a wrong purpose before or not. If they put a little bit of thought in it, the text wag proper and right, because there was nothing new under the sun. At the evening service the church was again crowded, the choir singing in a capital style the anthem "The Earth' is the Cord's," Mr. J. Matthews again taking the solo, in which he acquitted himself with advantage.—Mr. Weeks presided at the organ during the day. In the evening the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, rector of Winwick, preached from Genises 8 chapter, 22nd verse. " While the earth remaineth, seed time and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall never cease." The collections during the day amounted to a little over £lB.

- _ Sir,—As a shareholder in the London & North-Western Railway Company, and, like Mr. Alderman Davies and others interested in minimising the bad influence of the -drink traffic, I was warned that, if I took any part in adjudication, steps would be taken to recover penal- ties, &c. (ssctosuus.) Dear Mr. liforris,—First let me say I do not yet know who it was that published the handbill you com- plain of. However, I adopt the course you say you would do under similar circumstances, and readily ex- press my disapproval of the paragraph you and your friends object to, and regret that anything issued in my interest should have given you pain, or affect the friend- ship between us. TIEOS. MORRIS.:
MUST RENT BE PAID FOR UNSANITARY HOUSES?"

Sir,—Can any of your readers inform me on the fol- lowing important points (1.) Has a tenant (lodger, household 3r, or shopkeeper) a legal right to refuse payment of rent in the case of the house which he occupies being in an unsanitory condition —his due notices to the landlord or agent concerning such unsanitary condition having been neglected or ignored? (2.) Considering that licenses are required for the sale of many necessaries of life—that chemists and doctors cannot practise their professions without proper certifi- cates—that shopkeepers dare not sell adulterated articles injurious to the health of their customers. Why should landlords enjoy the valuable privilege of supplying and making a profit out of the homes of the people without a proper certificate (renewable at definite periods) having been previously- obtained from the Sanitary Authorities of the District that their houses are thoroughly fit to live in? Foreign politics and party politics have their several claims upon the attention of the community, but I con- tend that far above either of these are the claims of domestic legislation, in which all classes and parties can unite, and upon which depend the health, stamina, and comfort of the crowded populations of our towns and cities. Let us spend twenty times the present amount upon the employment of sanitary officers, even if it be at the sacrifice of a. little military glory, or as a last resource even in the substitution of harmoniums for pianos in our elementary schools.—Yours, &c., JAMES HAYSMAN, President of the Working Men's Home Union. Finchley-road, London, N.W.
THE GRIFFIN LICENSE AT EARLESTOWN. "Fools are my theme, let Satire be my song." 9, • teeto-

- Sir,—A letter in your last issue, signed "J. H. Pro- fit," reminds me that one of the most practising tallers of his day was once askea : " Who he considered the most insufferable creature under the sun ?" His reply was characteristic, and ran thus: " Professing teetotallers, for they meddle and muddle all the days of their lives; and are utterly worthless from a commercial point of view, for you can't make a decent, nor even an honest " Profit " out of them!" It is not a little singu- lar that these rabid faddists are the first to bellow out " Do as you would be done by," and the last to act upon it. Your teetotal parson will preach by the hour that man is accountable to a Higher Power for his own actions and deeds; and the Sacred Book nowhere autho- rizes self-appointed meddlers to interfere, unless, indeed, the law of the land is being broken. I assume that this " J. H. Profit" is aware that a publican's business is per- fectly legal—yea, as legal and as equitable as the business he himself follows ; indeed, as legal and as honest even as that of a parson or scripture reader, and this being so, what earthly right has he to poke his nose into it? Tread on his toes in the same manner, or on the toes of others of his own meddling kidney, and you would hear a howl of rage, to which the yells of a pack ,of beagles couldn't for one moment be compared! I suppose, however, that this teetotal craze will go on in spite of all considerations to the contrary, and will, as of yore, make itself contemptible by its monstrous inter- ference with others' rights, in defiance too, of all the teachings of Holy Writ, and the country's laws. " We were gittin' on nicely up here to our village, With good old idees o' wut's right an' wut ain't" ; We kind o' thought Christ went agin war an' pillage. An' that" blue ribbons" worn% the best mark ot a Saint, But John P. • Profit,' says be, This 'fair' kind o' thing s an exploded idea I"
EaTlestown, 25th Sept., 1890.
YEASTING RUNCORN OFFICIALS.

- think the ratepayers of Runcorn ought to thank the gentleman who signs " Ratepayer " in the columns of your paper for his exposure of the hotel bill connected with the officials at the recent election. These men of such intellectual expansion must be some- thing in the -form of living wonders. Their salaries all range high, and besides their salary they receive an ad- ditional ifee of one guinea for their heavy duties of recording votes given to each ambitious creature. I believe a man ought to be amply paid for his services. But these men cannot be accustomed to having a sixteen shilling dinner. If not—why should they get such—at other people's expense? I am certain I would be able to provide my own meals out of the guinea—and would feel myself very much degraded if I stood like a pauper with hat in hand as stated. I feel confident if they had to pay the bill, they would exercise their intellectual region as acutely as they did the digestive region; and I further think they would hook upon their nasal organs their observing apparatuses to discover if a gross mis- take was not made. There cannot be any reasonable excuse for such extraordinary gluttony. I presume it is useless to speak on the subject as long as the ratepayers and their flattering and gulling work- ing-men's representatives are dumb. My idea is that we have every need of a Ratepayers' Association in Run- cont. lam thinking if I eat sixteen shillings worth at one meal I should require the aasistance of a Medico and ' his stomach pump, or a couple of stout men to wheel me home in the town ambulance cart. I admit that we have some cause for thankfulness. Though our town is not a borough, we possess a good " Corporation," I think. I will eonclude at !present. When I pass my next standard, I may send another ; perhaps the subject may be the emptying of ashnitN. &c., as scientifically done in Rune( na.--J am, most truly, ONE OF THE GULLED.

THE GOVERNMENT LICENSING PROPOSALS.' IMPORTANT LETTER FROM MR. RITCHIE. The following correspondence settles a disputed point as to the late licensing proposals ot the Government ; and will be the means of removing a singular misapprehension on the part of at least one Warrington magistrate. (LETTER TO Mn. R/TCHIE.) Warrington, Sept., 19th 1890. To the Right Hon. C. T. Ritchie, President of the Local Government Board, London, Sir,—ln conversation with a magistrate of War- rington. on Monday last, on the Licensing proposals of the Government's late Bill. 1 was told that there was a clause giving County Councils power to abol- ish a License, without compensation, in case they failed to come to terms with the holder of the license land other persons interested. My impression is that no such power was proposed to be given to the County Councils, it being under- stood that it was sufficient to leave the power to abolish a license, if need be, in the hands of the present Licensing Committees. Will you kindly set us right on the point? I am, Sir, your obedient Servant, JOHN W ALEER. (MR. RITCHIE'S REPLY.) Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W. 20th September, 1890. Dear Sir,—ln reply to your letter of yesterday, Mr. Ritchie desires me to say that your impression is quite correct. It was not proposed by the Local Taxation Bill to confer such power upon a County Council as would enable the Council to extinguish a license in a case in which no agreement with the licensee had been entered into.—You,rs faithfully, —T. H. CELIOTT. John Walker, Esq.

div.head: SLUM LIFE IN LIVERPOOL
div.p: SLUM LIFE IN LIVERPOOL

A terrible story of slum life in Liverpool has been dis- closed. A youth of seventeen, who had lived for three years with a girl now sixteen, died on Wednesday week, and the body lay for nine days unburied, repeated collec- tions made with the ostensible object of paying the funer- al expenses being expended in wild debauches.

div.head: SUPPOSED DEATH FROM EXPOSURE.
div.p: SUPPOSED DEATH FROM EXPOSURE.
BODY FOUND IN A DITCH.

At about nine o'clock yesterday morning, the body of an old man was found in a dry ditch near the Longford depBt, Winwick-road. The deceased was seen on the previous evening on the farm premises of Mr. Fisher—about 100 yards from the spot where the body was subsequently found—and was ordered to go away. He did so, and it was surmised that he lay down under a hedge, and while asleep fell into the ditch. The death is attributed to want and exposure. The deceased, who was about 70 years of age, is said to have told a police constable that he was "troubled with bronchitis." He had been several times during the past fortnight seen wandering about the district. There were no marks of violence on the body, which. was removed to the Horse and Jockey Inn to await identification and inquest.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW GYMNASIU3L
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW GYMNASIU3L

MORE MONEY WANTED. A general meeting of the subscribers to, and mem- bers of, the Warrington Gymnasium was held on Tuesday evening, at the Workmen's Club. Mr.Thos. Morris presided, and amongst those present were-- Alderman Sutton, Alderman Wright, Councillor Pierpoint, Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Mr. Snell (Ship Canal), Mr. James Critchley, Mr. H. 11. Evans (lion. sec.), Messrs. W. Iteid, H. Furguson, W. Gorse, and W. W. Dimmelow. - - _ .

The CRAInmAN reported the result of a Committee meeting held last week. At that meeting a letter was read from the Charity Commissioners, acceding to the request .of the Gymnasium Committee that the £650, proceeds from the sale of the Workmen's Club, should be handed over to them. With that sum, the total amount in hand at present was £l4OO. A further sum of £4OO was needed before the Committee would feel themselves justified in commencing building operations. The Com- mittee had recommended the following gentlemen for election as trustees :—Messrs. Thomas Morris, Joseph Harrison, T. H. Sutton, D. Jones, J. E. Wright, W. Pier- point, and John Evans. On the motion of Mr. CRITCHLEY, seconded by Mr. REID, the gentlemen named were elected as trustees of the building when it is erected. Alderman Wniour submitted plans of the proposed building, and mentioned that they had been approved by the Government architect and the Charity Commis- sioners. He explained that the intention of the Commit- tee WAS to erect a gymnasium having one large hall, 84ft. long by 42ft. 9in. broad. To comply with the trust of the Workmen's Club, they would provide a reading room 171 t. 6in. by 15ft. in front of the hall ; on the other side would be a dressing room 12ft. by 10ft. 6in , with lavatory and other necessary apartments. There would be a vestibule /ft. wide, an entrance to the main hall ; and, overlooking the hall, a gallery 9ft. wide. Commit- tee, dressing, and other rooms would also be pro- vided. The CHAIRMAN expressed the opinion that if the War- rington team had happened to win at Liverpool they would have had money showered upon them. If any gentleman had, before that competition, any idea of giving the gymnasium a £5 or a £5O note, he ought not to have drawn back because the team happened to lose. He(the Chairman) considered that although the Warrington men lost they really won a magnificent game. They wen in coming so near to a team representing a gymnasium which had been in existence 20 years, whereas the War- rington gymnasium had been started only two years. (Hear, hear.) In answer to a question, Mr. WHITTLE stated that the gymnasium and reading-room would remain for all time a public charity for Warrington. Mr. J. PonmonE moved the appointment of Messrs. , Thomas Morris, J. E. Wright, W. Pierpoint, John Evans, W. W. Dimmelow, J. Lyon Whittle, W. Tinsley, J. Pod; more, George Vernon, LI. Jones, IV. Gorse, H. Ferg,uson, J. liesketh, J. McGregor, E. Warren, and H. Evans, as the Committee of Mana,gement for the ensuirg year. Mr. PEMBERTON seconded the proposition, which was agreed to. A vote of thanks to the Chairman trougl.t the meeting to a close.
