div.head: TETE EXAVFN ER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27. 1890
div.p: TETE EXAVFN ER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 27. 1890

DEATH OF THE HON. A. J. F. EGERTON, M.P., News was received on Thursday at Worsley Old- hall of the death of the Hon. A. J. F. Egerton, mem- ber for the Eccles division of South-east Lancashire. He died on Thursday morning at Burwood, Chob- ham, Surrey, the residence of his .mother, and he had been ailing for two years. He was the son of the second Earl of Ellesmere, and was born in 1854. Ile was therefore at the time of his death 36 years of age. In 1881 he married Isabella Coresaide Gertrude, daughter of the late Mr. Hamil- ton Gorges, of Eilbrew, county Meath. He sat for the Eccles division since Nov.' 1885. He was elected in 1886 by a majority of .292 over his Gladstonian Liberal opponent, Mr. E. D. Gosling. Both parties in the division had been preparing for an early retirement of Mr. Egerton from parliament- ary life in consequence of his failing health, al- though his death was not expected. The Liberals in the constituency had invited Mr. H. J. Roby, a local manufacturer, to contest the division whenever a vacancy should occur, and he consented. The Con- servatives also made overtures recently to several gentlemen to contest the seat; including Sir W. T. Charley and Mr. Jno. 11. Gartside, a Manchester manufacturer, and ultimately decided to invite the latter to stand.

THE CONCLUSION. The whole of the lists for the Newton Division having been completed, Mr. Brook said he had very great pleasure in proposing a Vote of thanks to the revising barrister for the manner in which he had carried out the work, and for the courtesy, kindness, and assistance he I had extended towards himself and Mr. Catnpbell.—Mr. Campbell had equal pleasure in seconding the motion,and endorsing the observations of Mr. Brook. If it had not been for the uniform consideration that had been shpwn to him (Mr. Campbell) he did not know very well how he could have carried out the work, as he had done, on 1 behalf of the Liberal part.—The Revising Barrister briefly acknowledged the compliment. He reciprocatsd the sentiments which had been expressed, and said he had to thank them for the assistance they had given him.

div.head: IVESLE YAN QUARTERLY MEETING.
div.p: IVESLE YAN QUARTERLY MEETING.

The quarterly meeting of the Warrington 1 Wesleyan circuit was held in the large vestry of the Bold-st. chapel on Monday. The Rev. John Gunnell, superintendent of the circuit, presided, and he was supported by the Rev. A. Freeman, and the , Rev. T. S. Ross, the newly-appointed ministers, with a considerable number of officers, trustees, and stewards. The September meeting is usually alight oue, the business of the Methodist body being mostly transacted at the December and March meetings. Mr. Gunnell reported the additions to the member- ship to be satisfactory, and a considerable discussion took place upon the efforts to be made for further extensions through the coming winter. A warm welcome was given to the two new ministers, both of whom addressed the meeting and spoke hopefully , of the prospects of Methodism in Warrington and neighbourhood. A few 'remarks were made as to . the necessity for further work in the country , parishes,and particular mention was made of Apple- ton and Antrobus, at one of which it is expected i that an evangelist from Mr. Champness's home may . shortly be expected.

div.head: 2ND WARRINGTON STARR BOWKETT
div.p: 2ND WARRINGTON STARR BOWKETT
SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of the members of the second Warrington, 920th, Starr-Bowkett building society was held on Wednesday evening, in Legh-st. school- room. Mr. John Gandy presided, and there was a fair attendanca. In the course of a few opening remarks the Chairman referred to the favourable character of the report, and said that the business of the Society was going on in a very prosperous manner. He thought that they had every reason to look forward to increased success next year. The directors, he added, had been very careful about advancing money on property, taking every pre- caution to see that the property was worth it. —The second annual report, submitted by the Secretary, Hr. J. Titchett, read as follows: " The total income for the year ending July 28th, 1890, from all sources, amounts to .£1,766 Is. 91d., balance profits being £64 is. 90. During the year eight appropriations have been made, amounting to £1,900. The fifteenth appropriation will be made on the evening of the annual meeting, September 24th, 1890. While congratulating the members on the prosperous state of their finances, the directors wish to urge upon then the importance of paying their subscriptions regularly, and so make the appropriatirms more rapid. The following directors retire and, being eligible, offer themselves for re- election :—Messrs. Gandy, Auldand, Haynes, and Winstanley. The auditors, Messrs. Harrison and Reddish, also retire and are eligible for re-election." —The retiring directors and auditors were re- elected, and the fifteenth appropriation resulted in the drawing of number 209, entitling Sarah Birch, of Haydock-at., to an appropriation of £2OO. Messrs. Bennion and C. Sudlow were the scrutineer, and a boy, named James Barlow drew the balloting balls.
_ - NEWTON DIVISION REVISION COURT,

The revision of the lists of voters for the Newton division residing within the St. Helens polling district was resumed at St. Helens County Court, on Friday. before Mr. J. T. Foard, revising barrister. Mr. P. M. Campbell (registration agent) appeared for the Liberals, and the Conservatives were represented by Messrs. W. H. Brook (solicitor) W. Holbrook, and W. Lamb (registration agents.)

AN ARMY COLONEL AND HIS VOTE. Colonel Majendie, of Hill Cottage, Salcombe Regis, Sidmouth, claimed an ownership vote in regard to Chorley Farm, Eccleston, in the occupation of Mr. Molyneux. The case was mentioned on the previous Tuesday, when his Honour stated that he could not deal with it unless the deeds were produced. On Friday Mr. Brook said he had received the probate of the will of the late William Pemberton, under which the estate was left for life to his wife, who died many years ago, and subse- quently to his niece, the mother di the present claimant. The niece died in 1857, and he (Mr. Brook) produced the succession account showing the payment of succession duty by the claimant.—The Revising Barrister : He claims for the house and land? Mr. Brook : Yes ; but as a matter of fact he owns the whole estate. That is quite sufficient.—The Revising Barrister: He resides at Hill Cottage, Sidmouth ? Mr. Brooks: He is a colonel in the army, and moves about a great deal.—The vote was allowed.

div.head: TOWN COUNCILLOR IN THE BOX.
div.p: A TOWN COUNCILLOR IN THE BOX.

Ccuncillor J. P. Mearns, solicitor, appeared to support his claim in respect to his ownership of a freehold house in Park-lane, Eccleston. This case had been adjourned from the last sitting of the court for the attendance of Mr. Mearns. It appeared that the claimant purchased the equity of the property, upon which was a mortgage of £550. The rental was stated to be £3o.—The Revis- ing Barrister said it was a question as to the value.—Mr. Mearns said he would like to ask for the objector before his case was gone into.—Revising Barrister: I don't know about that now. I have allowed the claim sub- ject to the question of amount. You had a notice of objection? Mr. Mearns: Yes, but I got it late; it is out of date—the 21st August.—The Revising Barrister : That is too late.—Mr. Brook: It was posted on the 19th. Mr. Mearns: I made a note when I got it.—The Revis- ing BarriSter : If you should have got it in the ordinary course of post on the 20th it would be good enough.— Mr. Mearns said he was at home and did not receive it. —The Revising Barrister said if Mr. Mearns persisted in the point he should have to ascertain where it was posted, when it was posted, and when it was delivered. —Mr. Mearns: As I have been put to the trouble in be- ing brought here,! shall make a point of all I can.—The Revising Barrister examined the notice of objection and said it seemed to have been posted all right on the 19th, and if it was not delivered on the 20th it must have been delayed in passing through the post.—Mr Mearns said his honour would see the pencil note of the date when he received it.—The Revising Barrister: I don't dispute that. It may be either that the postman neg- lected to petit into the box, or something of that kind. —Mr. Mearns : Then I won't pursue the matter any fur- ther; but apart from that, I say that the qualification is over 40s. The Act does not say that it shall be 40s. clear.—The Revising Barrister : I think it does.— Mr._ Mearns said . the act__ provided that the

holder must be worth 40s. The- Revising Barrister : It must te clear. Mr. Mearns: It does not say clear.—The Revising Barrister : But if it says of the value of 405., it must be clear.—Mr. Mearns : But has your honour ruled that I can call for the objector before we go into this ?--The Revising Barrister : I think it is rather late. The objection was made and duly signed and received by you, and you are now here to answer.— Mr. Mearns : I appear to answer anything. Then I want to take another objection. There is no ground of 4 objection stated on the paper.—The Revising Barrister : It is a new claim. Asa point of fact, there was no dis- position to strike you off.—Mr. Mearns : I think I can satisfy your honour. Part of the mortgage has been paid off.—Mr. Brook : What is the amount now owing? Mr. Mearns : £soo.—The Revising Barrister : What is the rental P—Mr. Mearns : £3O. The real rent is £32, but I made an allowance.—Mr. Brook : The assistant overseer says it is £25 gross.—The Revising Barrister : We are not dealing with the assessment, This is an ow n•r- ship qualification.—Mr. Brook : But it is a guidance as i to the value.—The Revising Barrister said he thought t wasa very close thing, but he would allow the vote.— Mr. Mearns: I don't know whether I ought to ask for expenses.—The Revising Barrister : No.—Mr. Mearns: It is my second attendance.—The Revising Barrister : Yes, but it was to afford us information. SIR GILBERT GREENALL AND MS "OLD BARN." As the list of ownership claims for Windle was being gone through the Revising Barrister came across the name of Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., of Walton Hall? War- rington, who had a vote for houses and land described as "No. 1, Flardshaw-brow, and another." Tpe Revising Barrister said that "and another" was not very clear. Was it another tenant, another house, or what ?--Mr. Lamb :It is another house, your honour.—Mr. Twist (assi:tant overseer: They used to call them "Old Build- ings," Hardshaw-brow.-IMr. Lamb: There is a No. 1, but the other house is not numbered.—Mr. Twist : It is an old barn which has been made into two cottages. Old Buildings, Hardshaw-brow, would be the best descrip- tion.—tlis Honour amended the register accordingly.

THE LIBERAL AGENT AND HIS FRIEND. Some singular proceedings transpired in connection with the ownership claim of Joseph Whalley, Knowsley View, Denton's Green-lane, Windle. When the objection was called, Mr. Campbell stated that the objection had been withdrawn, and his Honour said the vote would be allowed.—Mr. Brook remarked that the objection had not been withdrawn.—The Revising Barrister : Mr. Campbell said so.—Mr. Campbell We objected to his but afterwards found he was one of..onrs, and we withdrew the objection. There has been another claim put in., and that has not been printed.—Mr. Brook : We have objected to the man and he does not appear. He must be struck off accordingly.—The Revising Barrister : Then what about the objection being with- drawn 7—Mr. Bro3lc : Mr. Campbell has withdrawn his notice of objection.—Mr. Twist : Only one claim and one objection have come to me.—The Bevising Barrister : Someone has objected, and he does not appear. He is struck off the register.—Mr. Campbell : But it is our claim and our objection, and we have withdrawn it.— Mr. Brook : But we objected, too, and we have not with- drawn ours.—Mr. Twist : There has no objection come to me except the one signed Richard Boardroan.—Mr. Brook: And that is ours.—Mr. Campbell remarked that it was rather hard the man should lose his vote because he had accepted the withdrawal notice sentto him.—The Revising Barrister : You must settle it with him. There is an objection on the other side, and unless you can induce them to withdraw it, I cannot allow the vote.— Mr. Campbell : It is a pity,

div.head: REGIMENTAL SPORTS AT WARRING TON.
div.p: REGIMENTAL SPORTS AT WARRING TON.

On Thursday, the annual sports in connection with the Bth and 40th regimental district were held at Orford Barracks, Warrington. WARRINGTON SCHOOL TEACHERS AT

div.head: WINDEItMERE.
div.p: WINDEItMERE.

On Saturday afternoon about 160 Warrington schoolmasters and mistresses and assistants enjoy- ed a trip to Belfield, Windermere, the lake country residence of Mr. W. Long, J.P., of Thelwall Heys. The party left Bank Quay station by the 7.10 a.m. train,ancl they reached Windermere about half-past ten. Conveyances were there in waiting to convey them to Mr. Long's residence which is beautifully situated overlooking the lake and commanding a charming view of the surrounding colantry. Lun- cheon was partaken of in a large marquee, and afterwards boating and other amusements were in- dulged in. Between four and five o'clock tea was served to the party at Beifield. At the conclusion of this, Mr. J. DEWHURST proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. , Mrs. ,and Miss Long, for their kindness.—Mr. D. W. FINNEY seconded the vote, and said Mr. and Mrs. Long had done the teachers a very great honour, and, in th,ing honour to the teachers, they had done honour to education. (Hear, hear). Education was taking a very great and important position in • the country, and Mr. Long recognised that fact. (Hear, hear.) He trusted that Mr. and Mrs. Long would live many years to en- joy what they so richly and well-deserved—the appreci- ation of their labours and kindness by their many friends in Warrington and Windermere. (Applause). Ho would ask his old friend, Mr. Brewtnall, who was a former schoolmaster, who took the lead in elementary education years ago, and who was very far before his time, to say a few words. (Applause.) —Mr. BREWTNALL said he felt in an exceptional sort of position. He was returning thanks on behalf of teachers, and he was nolonger a teacher, but he thought he was, perhaps, the professional progenitor of a good many teachers. (Laughter.) In a certain sense he was the father of the profession in Warrington—(applause)— in point of time, at any rate. It was 42 years since he came to Warrington as a schoolmaster. At that time there were only three public schoolmasters in the town. He understood that at the present time there were 160 teachers—heads and assistants, besides pupil teachers— practising in the schools of Warrington. That was a very important and salutary fact, of which, occupying the exceptional position he did, he was very proud in- deed. It had been a great pleasure to him to recall re- miniscences of those old times, and to associate again with the friends of education. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Finney had spoken very kindly of the sort of work he did. He must say that he was very much in earnest in that old work. He felt that it was a very important work, and he threw himself into it with all the vigour and earnest- ness he could ; and he was very glad to see one of the living results of his work there, in his friend Mr. Twiss, whom he had the pleasure of training, and who suc- ceeded him in his position, and who, he knew, was do- ing a very important educational work in Warrington; doing it, too, with very exceptional success. (Hear, hear.) He was very glad to sea that Le work of education was growing in importance and appreciation in the country. A very painted fact was adduced by Mr. Swire Smith when presenting the prizes at the Leeds School of Art last week. He was speaking id the competition between American and English manu- facturers, and he told how the Americans took the lead and obtained for a time almost the entire trade of our laTest towns through their protectionist proceedings. The people of Bradford, who had been hard hit by Ameri- can Protection, mettogether to consider what the exigen- cies of their position aemanded,ln order to recover their lost ground and they came to what might seem a very singular, but what proved to be a happy, conclusion. They determined at once to spend £40,000 in founding and equipping a technical school, the result being that in ten years the fruit of that school brought back all the prosnerity which had been previously lost. (Applause.) Bradford, after ten years of technical instruction, was able to send to America such beautiful fabrics, so ex- quisitely designed, so artistically ornamented, that the American ladies eagerly bought them in spite of the fifty per cent. duty they had to pay. That, he believed, was the direction in which education was now pro- ceeding. We were about to have throughout the country a,series of excellent technical schools, and he looked upon a higher sort of fruit of the work that elementary teachers had been laying the foundation for duringthe last 40 years. (Hear, hear.)--Mr. LONO, in acknowledging the vote, said he was very glad that they had taken his invitation in the, light of an honour to education, for it was meant as such. (Hear. hear.) It was intended also to be a personal compliment, because he felt that the work teachers were engaged upon was, taken in its right sense, a very solemn and responsible one. In 'their hands was the training of the young Eng- land of the coming,day, and that, he was sure, they all felt. (Hear, hear.) There had been in the past too much of the "cram" system, too much of anxiety to obtain results, and too little cultivation of the intelligence of the children. The Education Act of 1870 was a great stop forward, but they were hoping for greater things yet. The establishment of technical schools marked a great advance. The more we educated our children—he did not mean mere book learning, but the education of all the faeulties—the better England would stand in the future. (Hear, hear.)—Hearty cheers were then given in honour of Mr. and Mrs. Long and family, after which several of the company contributed sorws. At six o'clock the guests were driven back to the st'ation, and arrived home shortly after ten o'clock.

Mr. G. B. Samuelson has intimated to a meeting of his constituents in the Forest of Dean, that he is unable to. support any legislation in Parliament for limiting the hours of labour. He added that trades unions could effect the object, and if they failed then he would sup- port it. A number of men went on Tuesday into the hold of the steamer Harrogate, lying at Cardiff, and immediately afterwards it was found that they had been overcome by some noxious fumes. They were got out with all haste, tut one of the number, named Airs, succumbed.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
THE McBINLEY BILL.

BERLIN, FRI DAY.—ACCOrding to the Imperial Official Gazette, there is reason to believe that the American McKinley Tariff Bill will come into operation on the 10th or at the latest the 15th of October.
THE TIPPERARY TRIALS. THE PROCEEDINGS ADJOURNED.

The special correspondent of the Press Association, telegraphing on Friday morning, says things are much quieter at Tipperary to-day. The military and police still hold the street outside the Courthouse, and in the main thoroughfares of the town there are strolig patrols, but little is heard in the way of cheering or other demon- stration. At the sitting of the court, Mr. Ronan, Crown prosecutor, said a communication had been made by the County Court judge saying he would require the Court- house till two o'clock. Mr. Healy protested against the proceedings of the court being interrupted for the convenience of the county court judge. Defendants were being treated with every discourtesy. He urged the bench to sit on despite the county court judge, or at any rate to proceed with the business of the day in some other building, say the police barrack, or the Mart at New Tipperary. r Mr. Irwin said they had no option but to adjourn. I It is stated that Mr. P. O'Brien is indisposed. THE AMERICAN IRISFI LEAGUE AND THE TIPPERARY STRUGGLE. New Yorttc, FRIDAY.—Mr. Fitzgerald, president of the Irish National League of America, has sent the following telegram to Mr. Harrington, M.P. :—" The National Council now in session at Cincinnati has just read of the Tipperary atrocity. America abhors and resents the brutality there displayed. Tender our admiration to that honest Englishman, John Morley." Nnyv Yoax, FRIDAY.—At a mass meeting at Detroit resolutions were passed protesting against the arrest of Messrs. Dillon and William O'Brien, members of Parlia- ment. The speakers included Mr. Dickinson, ex-Post- master-General.

-- At a large meeting of employers engaged in the coal trade, held in London, on Wednesday, a resolution was carried binding those present to employ only unrestricted -labour. A Sydney telegram of Tuesday states that the asso- ciated steamship owners have concluded a three years' agreement with the marine engineers at increased rates of wages. At the annual conference in Edinburgh, on Wednes- day, of the Scottish Home Rule Association, Dr. Clarke, who presided, said the battle of Scotch Home Rule had been won and was now a plank in the Liberal pro- gramme.

At Woolwich, on Tuesday, Walter Jamea Lyons, aged twenty, was committed for trial for the wilful murder of Quartermaster-Sergeant Stewart, at Plumstead. A great miners' strike has ;wain occurred in the Moravian mining district, and such is the attitude of the men that troops are being despatched to the scene in special trains.

COUNTY OF CHESTBR. --- ' LOCOMOTIVES. --- NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the following BYE-LAW, made by the Cheshire County Council ma the 7th day of August, 1890, and ,ronfirraed by the Local Government Beard on the 18th day of September. 1890, regu- lating the hours during which Locomotives shall not pass along.any Highways in the County, is now in Operation, viz. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF' CHESTER will be holden at the COURT HOUSE., NETHER KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on Idomney,the 13th day of Oetoiser next,at Half-past Eleven 6:cloak in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, foaming the Knuts- ford Districts:and the trials of all prisoners committ,d from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY ALSO GIVEN% that at the time and place aforesaid, a proposal will be made to the Jus- tices then and there assembled to make a Provisional Order to dissolve the Ltteaway District for the Eastern Division of the Hundred of Braxton, ,n the said County, which sada Highway District consists of the Townships or L_Parishes fol- lowing, viz. : Agden Egerton Aldersey Farndon Aldford Grafton Barton Hampton Bickley Harthill Bradley Horton Broxton Handley Bickerton King's Marsh Bulk eley Larktort Burwardsley Ma-cfen Caldecott Haloes Carden Newton-by-Malpas Chidlow Oldcastle Cholmondeley Overton Chowley Shocklach Church Chorlton Shochlach Oviatt Churton-by-Aldford Stockton Churton-by-Farndon Stratton Coddington Threapwood (part in Ches- Clutton hire Crewe Tilston Cuddington Tushingham-eum- Duckington Grindley Edge Wichhough Edgerley Wigland and the said Court at the time and place aforesaid will also be moved to make a Provisional Order to dissolve such Highway District in accordance with such proposal. lighted state of the river side contributes to render this 1 road an attractive one for these nefarious people, coup- I led with the fact that the police seem to confine their attention to Bridge Foot. That such attention is wanted there I admit, for the scenes that are enacted in that locality, especially on Saturday evenings, are anything but edifying. But from Bridge Foot to the borough boundary, such is the evil state of the road that it is pos- itively risky for any respectable person to be out after nightfall. Drunken men reel about, uttering fearful lan- guage, and abandoned women have obtainedfull license. The other Saturday night, a sober man was resting on the " traveller's rest ' opposite the Foundry, when a lewd woman sat beside him without invitation and at- tempted to rob him. He complained to me of the attempt, this making the second such complaint I have heard in a short interval. Again, only last Monday evening. as I was returning to town about 7 o'clock, I passed a questionable character, and, directly I had done so, a respectable workingman complained that the brazen face had banged him against the stone fence by St. James's Church. Last week a re- lative of mine was walking slowly along the Causewav, when a man followed her;for a considerable distance, and at last accosted her. As to the sights across the river in Arpley Fields, they are of such a character as to put even the opponents of the borough extension to the blush. Scenes have recently been witnessed there in broad daylight that can only be hinted at in a newspaper. I trust, sir, I have written sufficient to show that some further oversight is required along this rapidly-develop- ing road to ensure passers by from the attacks of depraved humanity, and I further trust that the gravity of the subject will atone for the length of my letter.— Yours faithfully, A PEDESTRIAN. September 24th, 1890.

THE SHIP CANAL. ACCIDENTS AT RUNCORN. George Rowe, 14 years of age, the son of a ganger, was seriously injured at Runcorn, on Monday. The youth was employed at a travelling crane, and while he was underneath oiling, the machinery started, and he was terribly crushed about the loins. He was at once conveyed by special engine to the hospital at Latchford. Shortly afterwards another youth had his fingers crushed on the same works, and later, at the Big Field, two engines with wagons, came into collision, but no person was in- jured, and the damage done was very slight. £60,000 MORE CAPITAL TO BE RAISED. An extraordidary meeting of shareholders of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company was held yesterday at Manchester to authorise the borrowing of £60,000 for the construction of railway sheds, warehouses, and graving docks along the Canal. Resolutions were passed authorising the directors to borrow the money at interest not exceeding 4 per cent., such moneys to rank after the mortgages or debenture stock of the company, and bind- ing the directors to give to the holders of terminable mortgages the option of perpetual mortgage debentures.

SCALDED TO DEATH. A lad named Clements fell into a vat of boiling dye at the Harbertonford Woollen Manufactory, near Totnes, yesterday, and was scalded to death. A PAINT WAREHOUSE BURNT OUT. A large paint warehouse in Ramsgate took fire On Thursday night, and was burnt out. The place blazed like a furnace, threatening the adjoining property. No personal injury was sustaine4. STRIKE AT BARROW. Over one thousand miners employed by the Barrow Steel Company will strike work to-day (Saturday,) if theirdemand for sixpence per day increase in wages be not conceded to. The employers say they will not accede to men's demand. THE MURDER OF CAPT. BROWNE. A " Times " telegram from Calcutta gives particulars of Capt. 13rowne's death. He was proceeding to meet the Chief Commissioner, and while riding across a stream was shot from an ambush. Although seriously wounded, he made his way to Chang Sie, where he died from loss of blood. MR. GLADSTONE AT FIAW ARDEN. Mr. Gladstone, who is not due in Edinburgh for his Mid-Lothian engagements until the 20th of next month, is still removing books from Hawarden Castle to the newly-erected library near the church. Staying with Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone at the Castle are Mrs. Lyttelton and the Hen. A. Lyttelton, Lady Phillimore, and Mr. , and Mrs. Henry Neville Gladstone. TRAGIC SUICIDE OF A YOUNG LADY AT CREWE. I At cnd o'clock yesterday afternoon a young lady named Kate Latham,who had come to:Crewe to visit her brother, the manager of the Barrel Hotel, Nantwich-road. one of ,1 Messrs. Walker's houses, committed suicide in a fright, I ful manner. She possessed herself of a razor, and stand- ing before the mirror, almost severed her head from her body. She appeared in the best of health and spirits just previously. MORFA COLLIERY DISASTER. RECOVERY OF TWO MORE BODIES. On Thursday evening two bodies were recovered from the Cribbur vein of the ill-fated Mona Colliery, Port Tal- bot. The corpses are those of two brothers, viz., Evan Thomas and Thomas Thomas, both of whom lived at Tairbach, and left behind them widows and families. Six months have elapsed since the accident occurred. The bodies were in a wonderful state of preservation in consequence of the dryness of the place where they were found. TWO COLLIERS KILLED AND A WOMAN FALLS DEAD. During last night a shocking accident occurred at• Coopers' Bank Colliery, Sedgeley. Whilst two young men named Greenvray and Guest were loading coal in a gate road a heavy fall of coal occurred, burying both men. Upon the removal of the coal both were found, horribly mutilated. Greenway was dead and Guest died upon being removed home. A woman named Watton, upon hearing of the occurrence, fell down dead. Greenway had only recently been married. SMOCKING DISCOVERY AT BINGLEY. At the Bingley Police Court, Charles Dixon, over- looker, and Maria Dickenson, widow, weaver, were charged under the act with being in possession of a quantity of piece end in an unfinished state, supposed to have been, stolen from Messrs. Ackroyd's manufactory at Bingley. The prisoners were searched for the material, and it has transpired that the searchers came upon the dead body of a child in a pail, and secreted in the chimney of one of the bedrooms of the woman's house. She is known by the neighbours to have been enceinte, and about a fortnight ago she was absent from work a week, alleging that she was ill. An inquest will be held, and some sensational levelations are expected.
